items.question: A parcel rests, without moving, on a stationary conveyor belt that slopes upwards at an angle to the horizontal. Which of the following lists all the forces acting on the parcel? weight and normal contact force weight, normal contact force and friction acting down the slope weight, normal contact force and friction acting up the slope weight, normal contact force, friction acting up the slope and the component of weight down the slope
items.ms: Without friction the parcel would slide down, so friction acts up the slope; weight, normal contact force and this friction balance. A leaves out the friction needed for equilibrium on a slope. B has friction in the wrong direction: it opposes the tendency to slide down. D counts a component of the weight as an extra force; a component is not a separate force.
items.why: S8 has come up in 17 of 22 sessions; drawing a component of the weight as an extra force is a free-body error named in the examiner reports (Jan2019 Q18(a)).

items.name: Free-body force diagrams; centre of gravity
path: Unit 1 Mechanics and Materials
Mechanics
S8 - draw and interpret free-body force diagrams t
items.question: The diagram shows a uniform ladder leaning against a smooth vertical wall. The foot of the ladder rests on rough horizontal ground. The ladder does not move. Which of the following gives the point at which the weight of the ladder acts and the direction of the frictional force of the ground on the ladder? weight acts at the foot of the ladder; friction acts away from the wall weight acts at the foot of the ladder; friction acts towards the wall weight acts at the midpoint of the ladder; friction acts away from the wall weight acts at the midpoint of the ladder; friction acts towards the wall
items.ms: The ladder is uniform, so its centre of gravity, the point through which its weight acts, is at the midpoint. A smooth wall can only push horizontally, away from the wall, so for zero resultant horizontal force the friction from the ground must act towards the wall. A and B put the weight where the ladder touches the ground; A and C have friction in the same direction as the wall's push, which would leave a resultant horizontal force.
items.why: S8 covers extended bodies through the centre of gravity (Jan2021 Q11(a), Oct2025 Q11(a)); MCQs on where a force acts and which way it points recur (Oct2019 Q6, Oct2024 Q5).

items.name: Free-body force diagrams; centre of gravity
path: Unit 1 Mechanics and Materials

items.question: A garden roller of weight W is pushed at constant velocity across level ground. The push P acts along the handle, at an angle θ below the horizontal. What is the size of the normal contact force of the ground on the roller? W − P sin θ W W + P cos θ W + P sin θ
items.ms: There is no vertical acceleration, so the vertical forces balance: the normal contact force supports W and the downward vertical component of the push, P sin θ. A treats the push as having an upward component (as for a pull above the horizontal). B ignores the vertical component of the push. C uses the horizontal component P cos θ.
items.why: Free-body MCQs with angled forces recur (Oct2021 Q6, Oct2025 Q6, Jun2025 Q5); a push below the horizontal that increases the normal contact force has not been set.

items.question: A uniform scaffold board rests on two trestles, P and Q. A box of tiles is placed on the board, closer to Q than to P, as shown. Add labelled arrows to the diagram to show all the forces acting on the board. A student labels the force that the box exerts on the board as "weight of the box". Explain why this label is not correct.
items.ms: Weight of the board: downward arrow from the midpoint of the board, labelled (W, weight, mg) Upward (normal contact) forces at P and at Q, labelled Downward (contact) force from the box, acting on the board where the box rests, labelled The weight of the box is the (gravitational) force of the Earth on the box, but the force on the board is a (normal) contact force exerted by the box
items.why: Adding the forces on an extended body (plank on supports, pivoted plank) recurs (Jan2021 Q11(a), Oct2025 Q11(a)); the examiner reports stress drawing the weight at the centre of gravity and naming which body exerts each force.

items.question: A child sits on a sledge on level snow. A parent pulls the sledge with a rope at 25° above the horizontal, as shown. The total mass of the child and sledge is 34 kg. The tension in the rope is 85 N and the frictional force of the snow on the sledge is 52 N. The dot below represents the child and sledge. The weight W has been drawn. Complete the free-body force diagram. Explain why the normal contact force on the sledge is less than the weight of the child and sledge. Calculate the acceleration of the sledge.
items.ms: Normal contact force: vertical arrow upwards, labelled (N, R, normal contact force) Tension: arrow at about 25° above the horizontal in the direction of the pull, labelled (T, tension) Friction: horizontal arrow opposite to the direction of motion, labelled (F, friction) The tension has an upward vertical component There is no vertical acceleration, so the vertical forces balance: N + T sin 25° = W Use of T cos 25° for the horizontal component of the tension Use of ΣF = ma with ΣF = T cos 25° − 52 N a = 0.74 m s⁻²
items.why: Completing a free-body diagram with labelled arrows is asked in most sessions (Jan2026 Q11, Oct2022 Q18(a)); a pull at an angle that reduces the normal contact force has not yet been set.

items.question: A kite is held stationary in a steady wind by a string, as shown. The mass of the kite is 0.28 kg. The tension in the string is 6.5 N and the string makes an angle of 35° with the horizontal. Assume that the string is straight. Draw a free-body force diagram for the kite. Use the dot below to represent the kite. State the condition for the kite to remain stationary. Calculate the magnitude and direction of the force of the wind on the kite. The string suddenly breaks. Assume that the force of the wind on the kite does not change at that instant. Determine the magnitude and direction of the initial acceleration of the kite.
items.ms: Weight: vertical arrow downwards, labelled Tension: arrow along the string, towards the person, labelled Force of the wind (air) on the kite: arrow upwards and in the direction the wind blows, labelled The resultant force on the kite is zero Vertical component of the wind force = mg + T sin 35° (= 6.48 N) Horizontal component of the wind force = T cos 35° (= 5.32 N) Force = 8.4 N At 51° above the horizontal, in the direction the wind blows The resultant force is equal in size to the tension (6.5 N) and opposite in direction a = 23 m s⁻² at 35° above the horizontal, away from the person
items.why: S8 asks students to draw **and interpret** free-body diagrams; three-force equilibrium with an angled force has appeared (Jun2023 Q17(a) buoy chain), but reading the motion off a diagram when one force is removed has never been asked.

items.question: A train of mass 4.2 × 10⁵ kg accelerates at 0.35 m s⁻². What is the resultant force on the train? 1.5 × 10⁵ N 1.2 × 10⁶ N 1.5 × 10⁶ N 4.1 × 10⁶ N
items.ms: ΣF = ma = 4.2 × 10⁵ × 0.35 = 1.5 × 10⁵ N. B divides the mass by the acceleration; C is a power-of-ten slip; D is the weight of the train (mg), not the resultant force.
items.why: Direct ΣF = ma comes up in almost every session (Oct2022 Q11(b), Jan2025 Q11, Oct2025 Q11).

items.question: A student stands on bathroom scales in a lift. The lift is moving downwards and slowing down. Which statement about the reading R on the scales and the weight W of the student is correct? R = 0 R is less than W R is equal to W R is greater than W
items.ms: Moving down and slowing down means the acceleration is upwards, so the resultant force on the student is upwards: R − W = ma, so R > W. B applies when the lift speeds up downwards (or slows down while moving up); C applies only at constant velocity; A applies only in free fall.
items.why: Lifts and scale readings were a 6-mark question in Jan2022 Q14 and an MCQ in Jun2019 Q10; the downward-decelerating case, where intuition says 'lighter', has not been asked.

items.question: A car of mass 1200 kg tows a trailer of mass 400 kg along a level road. The driving force on the car is 2400 N. The resistive force on the car is 300 N and the resistive force on the trailer is 100 N. What is the force exerted by the tow bar on the trailer? 500 N 600 N 1500 N 2000 N
items.ms: For the car and trailer together a = (2400 − 300 − 100) ÷ 1600 = 1.25 m s⁻². For the trailer alone T − 100 = 400 × 1.25, so T = 600 N. A leaves out the trailer's resistive force; C is the resultant force on the car (1200 × 1.25); D is the resultant force on the whole system.
items.why: Connected bodies have appeared as MCQs (Oct2025 Q7 pulley, Jan2026 Q10 string breaks); a car towing a trailer is the same idea in a context not yet used.

items.question: A crane lifts a pallet of bricks vertically from rest. The pallet and bricks have a total mass of 1450 kg. The pallet accelerates uniformly and reaches a speed of 0.90 m s⁻¹ after 1.5 s. The crane's cable has a safe working load of 16.0 kN. Calculate the acceleration of the pallet. Deduce whether the tension in the cable stays below its safe working load while the pallet accelerates.

items.question: A student investigates how the acceleration of a trolley depends on the force accelerating it, using the apparatus shown. The string runs over a pulley to a hanger of mass 50 g. For the first run, five 50 g slotted masses are on the trolley and the hanger is empty. Before each later run the student moves one slotted mass from the trolley to the hanger. The trolley is released from rest each time. The accelerating force F is the weight of the hanger and the masses on it. The acceleration a is calculated from the speeds measured by light gates A and B. The table shows the results. Explain why the student moves masses from the trolley to the hanger, rather than adding extra masses to the hanger. In the third run the trolley passed through light gate A at 0.30 m s⁻¹ and through light gate B at 1.07 m s⁻¹. The light gates were 0.500 m apart. Show that the acceleration was about 1.1 m s⁻². Plot a graph of a against F on the grid. Use your graph to determine the total mass being accelerated. The line does not pass through the origin. Explain why, and use your graph to estimate the size of the force that causes this.
items.ms: The total mass being accelerated (trolley, hanger and all the masses) stays the same So the acceleration depends only on the (resultant) force / a ∝ F only when m is constant Use of v² = u² + 2as a = 1.05 m s⁻² Axes labelled with quantities and units, and scales chosen so the points cover more than half of each axis All points plotted correctly (to within half a small square) Best-fit straight line Gradient calculated using a large triangle (more than half the line) Mass = 1 ÷ gradient = 1.25 kg (allow 1.20–1.30 kg) There is a (constant) frictional force on the trolley, so the resultant force is F − friction (the trolley does not accelerate until F exceeds the friction) Friction = intercept on the F axis = 0.15 N (allow 0.10–0.20 N)
items.why: S9's spec wording stresses using ΣF = ma 'where m is constant'; a ΣF = ma experiment with a graph to plot has not been set, while gradient and intercept work appears in most papers.

items.name: Newton's second law, F = ma
path: Unit 1 Mechanics and Materials

items.question: A ball of mass 0.057 kg is launched vertically upwards. Air resistance on the ball is not negligible. The graph shows how the velocity v of the ball varies with time t, from launch until the ball returns to its starting height. Upwards is positive. Determine the magnitude of the acceleration of the ball just after launch. Calculate the air resistance acting on the ball just after launch. Explain, in terms of the forces acting, how the acceleration of the ball changes from launch until it returns to its starting height. Explain, using the graph, why the ball takes longer to fall back to its starting height than to rise to its highest point.
items.ms: Tangent drawn to the curve at t = 0 Gradient calculated using a large triangle a = 18 m s⁻² (allow 16–20 m s⁻²) Use of W = mg mg + D = ma (weight and air resistance both act downwards) D = 0.47 N (0.48 N from a = 18.2 m s⁻²) IC1 On the way up, weight and air resistance both act downwards IC2 So the resultant force is greater than the weight and the deceleration is greater than g IC3 As the ball slows down, air resistance decreases, so the resultant force and the deceleration decrease IC4 At the highest point the velocity is zero, so there is no air resistance and the acceleration is g (only the weight acts) IC5 On the way down, air resistance acts upwards, so the resultant force is less than the weight and the acceleration is less than g IC6 As the ball speeds up, air resistance increases, so the resultant force and the acceleration decrease further The areas between the graph and the time axis above and below the axis are equal (the ball rises and falls the same distance) The speeds on the way down are lower (the curve below the axis stays closer to the time axis; the ball returns at about 15 m s⁻¹ compared with 20 m s⁻¹ at launch), so the same distance takes longer
items.why: 6-mark explanations of how resultant force changes acceleration recur (Oct2020 Q14, Oct2024 Q17(a), Jun2026 Q17(b)); a ball rising and then falling with air resistance, where the drag reverses at the top, has only been an MCQ (Jan2020 Q4).

items.name: Newton's third law
path: Unit 1 Mechanics and Materials
Mechanics
S12 - Newtons third law of motion and know the prop
items.question: An apple hangs at rest from a branch. The weight of the apple is the gravitational pull of the Earth on the apple. Which force forms a Newton's third law pair with the weight of the apple? the pull of the stalk on the apple the pull of the apple on the stalk the gravitational pull of the apple on the Earth the gravitational pull of the Earth on the branch
items.ms: The forces in a third-law pair are the same type, equal in size and opposite in direction, and act on different bodies: the Earth pulls the apple, so the apple pulls the Earth. A acts on the same body (the apple) and is a different type of force; it balances the weight by Newton's first law. B is the third-law partner of A. D is a force on a different object and is not equal in size.
items.why: Identifying a third-law pair is asked in most sessions (Oct2024 Q4, Jan2026 Q7, Jan2026 Q10); the commonest wrong choice is the balancing force on the same body.

items.name: Newton's third law
path: Unit 1 Mechanics and Materials
Mechanics
S12 - Newtons third law of motion and know the prop
items.question: A small car collides head-on with a much heavier lorry. Which statement about the collision is correct? The force on the car is equal to the force on the lorry, and the car's acceleration is greater than the lorry's. The force on the car is equal to the force on the lorry, and the car's acceleration is equal to the lorry's. The force on the car is greater than the force on the lorry, and the car's acceleration is greater than the lorry's. The force on the car is less than the force on the lorry, and the car's acceleration is greater than the lorry's.
items.ms: By Newton's third law the forces that the car and the lorry exert on each other are equal in size (and opposite in direction). Since a = F/m, the car, with the smaller mass, has the greater acceleration. B ignores the different masses; C and D assume the size of the force depends on the masses.
items.why: Third-law forces in collisions recur (Jan2025 Q14(a), May2024 Q15(c), Jun2026 Q13(a)); the belief that the heavier body exerts the bigger force is the misconception these questions target.

items.name: Newton's third law
path: Unit 1 Mechanics and Materials
Mechanics
S12 - Newtons third law of motion and know the prop
items.question: A person stands on the floor of a lift that is accelerating upwards. W is the gravitational pull of the Earth on the person. R is the normal contact force of the floor on the person. P is the push of the person on the floor. Which statement is correct? R and W are a Newton's third law pair, so R = W. P and R are a Newton's third law pair, and R is greater than W. P and R are a Newton's third law pair, and P is greater than R. P and W are a Newton's third law pair, so P = W.
items.ms: P and R are the two forces of the contact between person and floor: same type, equal in size, opposite in direction, on different bodies. The person accelerates upwards, so the resultant force on the person is upwards and R > W. A: R and W act on the same body, are different types and are not equal here. C: third-law forces are always equal in size, even during acceleration. D: P and W are different types of force acting on different bodies, and are not equal while the lift accelerates.
items.why: Jun2026 Q5 and Jun2025 Q4 asked why two forces are not a third-law pair; combining a pair with an accelerating body is the next step.

items.name: Newton's third law
path: Unit 1 Mechanics and Materials
Mechanics
S12 - Newtons third law of motion and know the prop
items.question: A magnet of mass 24 g is held at rest on the vertical steel door of a refrigerator. Four forces act on the magnet: its weight, the magnetic force of the door on the magnet, the normal contact force of the door on the magnet and the frictional force of the door on the magnet. A student says that the weight of the magnet and the frictional force on the magnet form a Newton's third law pair because they are equal in size and opposite in direction. Give two reasons why the student is wrong. Describe fully the force that forms a Newton's third law pair with the frictional force on the magnet.
items.ms: They act on the same body (the magnet); the forces in a third-law pair act on different bodies They are different types of force (gravitational and frictional/contact) They are equal because the magnet is in equilibrium (Newton's first law), not because of Newton's third law The frictional force exerted by the magnet on the door Acting (vertically) downwards Size 0.24 N (equal to the weight of the magnet, mg)
items.why: Explaining why two equal and opposite forces are not a third-law pair recurs (Jun2022 Q11(a), Oct2023 Q16(a), Oct2022 Q18(b)); the examiner reports repeatedly ask students to say which body exerts each force and which body it acts on (Jan2020, Oct2020, Oct2022).

items.name: Newton's third law
path: Unit 1 Mechanics and Materials
Mechanics
S12 - Newtons third law of motion and know the prop
items.question: An airboat is a flat-bottomed boat driven by a large propeller mounted above the back of the boat. The propeller pushes air backwards. The total mass of the airboat and its driver is 520 kg. Explain how the propeller produces a forward force on the airboat. At one instant the forward force on the airboat is 2.3 kN and the total resistive force is 0.90 kN. Calculate the acceleration of the airboat. When the airboat travels at its maximum speed, the forward force is equal in size and opposite in direction to the total resistive force. A student says that these two forces are a Newton's third law pair. Explain why the student is wrong.
items.ms: The propeller exerts a backward force on the air By Newton's third law the air exerts an equal and opposite (forward) force on the propeller (and so on the boat) Resultant force = 2300 − 900 (= 1400 N) Use of ΣF = ma a = 2.7 m s⁻² Both forces act on the same body (the airboat) They are equal because the resultant force is zero at constant velocity (Newton's first law), not because of Newton's third law The third-law partner of the forward force is the backward force of the propeller on the air (or: the partner of the resistive force is the forward force of the boat on the water/air) They are exerted by different bodies (the air pushed backwards by the propeller; the water and air around the hull)
items.why: Third-law propulsion recurs (fireboat pump: Jan2021 Q14(b), Oct2025 Q16(b)); telling balanced forces from a third-law pair was a 5-mark question in Oct2022 Q18(b).

items.question: Which of the following is a condition for the total momentum of a system of colliding objects to be conserved? No external resultant force acts on the system. The objects stick together after the collision. The total kinetic energy of the system is constant. The objects have equal masses.
items.ms: Momentum is conserved in any interaction provided no external (resultant) force acts on the system (a closed system). B, C and D are not required: momentum is conserved whether or not the objects stick together, whether or not kinetic energy is conserved, and for any masses.

The trolleys are on a horizontal track and frictional forces are negligible. The trolleys are released from rest and the plunger pushes them apart. A force sensor on each trolley records the force that the other trolley exerts on it. The graph shows how the two forces vary with time. Forces to the right are positive. Explain how the graph shows that these two forces obey Newton's third law. The mean force on each trolley while the plunger pushes is 1.40 N. items.question: A cargo ship sails from a river into the sea. Seawater is denser than river water. The mass of the ship and its cargo does not change. Which of the following describes the upthrust on the ship and the volume of water it displaces when it floats in the sea, compared with when it floats in the river? upthrust greater, volume displaced smaller upthrust the same, volume displaced smaller upthrust the same, volume displaced the same upthrust smaller, volume displaced greater
items.ms: B is correct: a floating ship has upthrust = weight, and its weight has not changed, so the upthrust is the same. Upthrust = ρVg, so in denser seawater a smaller volume is displaced and the ship floats higher. A: the upthrust on a floating ship cannot be greater than its weight. C ignores the change in density. items.question: A beaker of water stands on a top-pan balance. The balance reads 640 g. A metal block hangs from a newtonmeter, which reads 2.45 N. items.name: Viscous drag, Stokes' law, laminar and turbulent flow

items.question: Two solid spheres P and Q are made of the same material. They fall at terminal velocity through the same liquid, and Stokes' law applies to both. The diameter of Q is twice the diameter of P. What is the value of (terminal velocity of Q) ÷ (terminal velocity of P)? 0.5 2 4 8
items.ms: C is correct: at terminal velocity 6πηrv = W − U = (4/3)πr³(ρsphere − ρliquid)g, so v ∝ r². Doubling the radius gives four times the terminal velocity. A assumes that the larger drag makes Q slower. B takes v ∝ r. D takes v ∝ r³, forgetting that the drag also depends on r.

items.question: A steel sphere of density 7.80 × 10³ kg m⁻³ is released from rest in oil of density 900 kg m⁻³. Stokes' law applies throughout its motion. What is the acceleration of the sphere at the instant its velocity is half its terminal velocity? 4.3 m s⁻² 4.9 m s⁻² 8.7 m s⁻² 9.8 m s⁻²
items.ms: A is correct: at terminal velocity, drag = W − U. Drag ∝ v, so at half the terminal velocity the drag is ½(W − U) and the resultant force is ½(W − U). So a = ½g(1 − ρoil/ρsteel) = ½ × 9.81 × (1 − 900/7800) = 4.3 m s⁻². B leaves out the upthrust. C is the acceleration at release, when there is no drag. D is the acceleration of free fall.
items.why: Accelerating spheres in a liquid are a recurring MCQ (Jan2020 Q10, Jun2022 Q2, Jan2026 Q7); the acceleration at a fraction of terminal velocity has never been asked and joins Stokes' law to ΣF = ma.

items.question: A student uses a falling-ball method to determine the viscosity of a liquid. She uses a stopwatch to time a ball bearing as it falls between two marks on the tube. items.question: Three identical springs, each of stiffness k, are arranged as shown. The two upper springs hang side by side and their lower ends are joined by a light rod. The third spring hangs from the middle of the rod. A weight W hangs from the third spring. Which expression gives the distance the weight moves down as the springs extend? W/(3k) 2W/(3k) 3W/(2k) 3W/k
items.ms: The upper springs share the weight, so each extends W/(2k); the lower spring carries all of W and extends W/k. Total = W/(2k) + W/k = 3W/(2k). A treats all three springs as sharing the weight (stiffness 3k). B inverts the combined stiffness (uses 3k/2 instead of 2k/3). D gives the upper pair a stiffness of k/2 instead of 2k.
items.why: Springs side by side or end to end were MCQs in Jun2022, Jun2023, Jan2025 and Jun2026, but always one arrangement at a time; a mixed arrangement is the natural next step.

items.question: A chest expander is used for strength training. It has four identical springs side by side between two handles, as shown. Each spring has a stiffness of 140 N m⁻¹. When no force is applied, the handles are 0.52 m apart. Explain why the stiffness of the chest expander is four times the stiffness of one spring. An athlete pulls the handles until they are 0.95 m apart. Show that the force applied to each handle is about 240 N. Calculate the elastic strain energy stored in the springs when the handles are 0.95 m apart. The athlete removes two of the springs. She wants to store the same elastic strain energy as in (c). She can pull the handles at most 1.10 m apart. Deduce whether she can store this energy.
items.ms: Each spring has the same extension (the extension of the expander) The force on the handles is shared between the four springs / the total force is four times the force on one spring So four times the force is needed for the same extension, and k = ΔF/Δx is four times as large Use of ΔF = kΔx with k = 4 × 140 N m⁻¹ and Δx = 0.43 m F = 241 N Use of ΔEel = ½FΔx ΔEel = 52 J Use of ΔEel = ½kΔx² (or ½FΔx with ΔF = kΔx) with k = 2 × 140 N m⁻¹ Δx = 0.61 m, so the handles must be 1.13 m apart (or energy stored at 1.10 m apart = 47 J) Comparison of 1.13 m with 1.10 m (or 47 J with 52 J) and conclusion: she cannot store the same energy

items.question: Wires X and Y are made of the same metal. Y has twice the length and twice the diameter of X. The same tensile force is applied to each wire, and both obey Hooke's law. Which gives the stress ratio (stress in Y ÷ stress in X) and the extension ratio (extension of Y ÷ extension of X)? stress ratio ½, extension ratio 1 stress ratio ¼, extension ratio ½ stress ratio ¼, extension ratio ¼ stress ratio 1, extension ratio 2
items.ms: Doubling the diameter makes the area four times larger, so the stress is ¼ as large. The strain (σ/E) is also ¼ as large, and extension = strain × original length, so the extension ratio is ¼ × 2 = ½. A does not square the diameter. C forgets that Y is twice as long. items.question: In a hip replacement, a titanium alloy stem is fixed inside the patient's thigh bone. When the patient walks, the stem is compressed. The stem can be modelled as a solid cylinder of length 0.14 m and diameter 12 mm. Young modulus of titanium alloy = 1.1 × 10¹¹ Pa State what is meant by the Young modulus of a material. The largest compressive force on the stem during walking is 2.4 kN. Calculate the decrease in length of the stem. Bone that carries too little stress gradually becomes weaker. Bone has a Young modulus of about 1.8 × 10¹⁰ Pa. Stainless steel has a Young modulus of about 2.0 × 10¹¹ Pa. The stem and the bone around it are squashed together, so they have the same strain. Suggest why a titanium alloy stem is better for the patient than a stainless steel stem of the same size.
items.ms: Stress ÷ strain (for a material obeying Hooke's law / below the limit of proportionality) Calculates cross-sectional area Use of σ = F/A Use of E = σ/ε and ε = Δx/x Δx = 2.7 × 10⁻⁵ m For the same strain, stress = E × strain, so the stress in the stem is proportional to its Young modulus Titanium alloy has a smaller Young modulus than steel, so the stem takes a smaller share of the force and the bone carries more stress (so the bone does not weaken as much). items.question: A lift car hangs from four identical steel cables, as shown. Each cable has a diameter of 10 mm. When the car is at the lowest floor, the length of each cable is 85 m. The total mass of the car and its passengers is 1200 kg. Ignore the mass of the cables. Young modulus of steel = 2.0 × 10¹¹ Pa The car accelerates upwards from rest at the lowest floor with an acceleration of 1.2 m s⁻². Show that the tension in each cable is about 3300 N. Show that the stiffness of each cable is about 1.8 × 10⁵ N m⁻¹. Calculate the extension of each cable while the car is accelerating. The same group of passengers steps into the car at the lowest floor on one occasion, and at the top floor on another. At the top floor each cable is only 12 m long. Explain why the floor of the car moves down further when they step in at the lowest floor.
items.ms: Use of ΣF = ma Use of W = mg (W = 1.18 × 10⁴ N) Tension in each cable = 3303 N Calculates cross-sectional area Use of k = EA/x (or E = σ/ε with σ = F/A, ε = Δx/x and k = F/Δx) k = 1.85 × 10⁵ N m⁻¹ Use of ΔF = kΔx Δx = 0.018 m The stiffness of a cable is inversely proportional to its length (k = EA/x) At the lowest floor the cables are longer, so their stiffness is smaller The extra force (the passengers' weight) is the same, so by ΔF = kΔx the extra extension is larger Alternative for MP1 and MP2: for the same extra tension each cable has the same extra strain (ε = σ/E), so a longer cable has a larger extra extension (Δx = εx)

items.question: A metal wire is stretched until it breaks. items.question: The graph shows how the force F on a metal wire varies with its extension Δx as the wire is loaded to point Q and then unloaded. Which statement is correct? The wire obeys Hooke's law for all forces up to 52 N. The wire is less stiff while it is unloaded than when it is first loaded. The wire has a permanent extension of 2.4 mm. items.question: The graph shows stress–strain graphs for three materials X, Y and Z. Each sample was stretched until it broke. A cross (×) marks where each sample broke. Which of the following identifies the stiffest material and the material with the greatest breaking stress? stiffest: X; greatest breaking stress: Y stiffest: X; greatest breaking stress: X stiffest: Y; greatest breaking stress: Y stiffest: Z; greatest breaking stress: Y
items.ms: Stiffness is shown by the initial gradient (the Young modulus): X has the steepest line. Breaking stress is the stress where the sample breaks: Y breaks at the highest stress. B: X breaks at a lower stress than Y. C: Y reaches the highest stress but its initial gradient is smaller than X's. D: Z has the largest strain, not the largest gradient.
items.why: Reading stiffness and breaking stress from stress–strain graphs was an MCQ in Jan2024 Q9, Jun2022 Q4 and Jan2026 Q3, and the Jan2020 report says candidates confuse stiffness with strength.

path: Unit 1 Mechanics and Materials
Materials

items.question: The shaft of a thigh bone can be modelled as a hollow cylinder with an outer diameter of 26 mm and an inner diameter of 14 mm. The breaking stress of bone is 130 MPa in tension and 190 MPa in compression. What is the largest compressive force the shaft can withstand? 49 kN 72 kN 100 kN 290 kN
items.ms: Area of bone = π(0.013² − 0.007²) m² = 3.77 × 10⁻⁴ m², F = σA = 190 × 10⁶ Pa × 3.77 × 10⁻⁴ m² = 72 kN. A uses the breaking stress in tension. C treats the shaft as solid. D uses the diameters as radii.
items.why: Breaking force from breaking stress recurs (Oct2019 Q16(b), Jan2021 Q16(b)); a compressive breaking stress and a hollow cross-section have not been asked.

items.name: Stress-strain graphs; brittle, ductile, strong, stiff
path: Unit 1 Mechanics and Materials
Materials
S30 - draw and interpret tensile or compressive str
items.question: Objects made by 3D printing can be made from different plastics. The graph shows stress–strain graphs for samples of two of these plastics, PLA and nylon, each stretched until it broke. A cross (×) marks where each sample broke. State what is meant by breaking stress. Compare the behaviour of the two plastics. Use values from the graph. A 3D-printed phone case must not crack when the phone is dropped. Suggest which plastic is more suitable. Give a reason using the graph.
items.ms: The stress at which a material breaks / the greatest stress a material can withstand before it breaks PLA is stiffer: its initial gradient (Young modulus) is greater, about 3 GPa compared with 1 GPa PLA has a greater breaking stress, about 55 MPa compared with 48 MPa Nylon reaches a much greater strain before breaking, about 0.22 compared with 0.025 Nylon has a large region of plastic deformation (it yields at about 30–40 MPa); PLA breaks after very little plastic deformation Nylon (only with a valid reason) The area under its graph is much larger, so much more energy per unit volume is absorbed before it breaks It deforms plastically instead of breaking, while PLA breaks at a strain of only about 0.025
items.why: Comparing two materials' stress–strain graphs was Jun2026 Q15 (12 marks) and Oct2024 Q18(c); an area-under-the-graph (toughness) argument was last needed in Jan2020 Q14.

items.name: Stress-strain graphs; brittle, ductile, strong, stiff
path: Unit 1 Mechanics and Materials
Materials
S30 - draw and interpret tensile or compressive str
items.question: A synthetic material is being tested as a replacement for damaged tendons. The graph shows stress–strain graphs for samples of a natural tendon and of the synthetic material, each stretched until it broke. A cross (×) marks where each sample broke. Determine the Young modulus of the tendon, using the straight section of its graph. The tendon has a cross-sectional area of 75 mm². Calculate the tension needed to break the tendon. A surgeon considers replacing a damaged tendon with a strip of the synthetic material of the same cross-sectional area. In walking, the stress in the tendon is up to about 30 MPa. In sprinting, it can reach about 70 MPa. Discuss whether the synthetic material would be a suitable replacement. The area under a stress–strain graph is equal to the work done per unit volume in stretching the material. Estimate the elastic strain energy stored per unit volume of the tendon when its strain is 0.040.
items.ms: Uses the gradient of the straight section (Δσ/Δε) Values read correctly from the line, e.g. 16 MPa at a strain of 0.020 and 80 MPa at 0.060 E = 1.6 × 10⁹ Pa Breaking stress read as 96 MPa and use of σ = F/A with A = 75 × 10⁻⁶ m² F = 7.2 × 10³ N IC1 The synthetic material is stiffer: its initial gradient (Young modulus) is greater, about 2.5 GPa compared with 1.6 GPa, so it stretches less for the same stress IC2 The synthetic material's graph is linear only up to about 50 MPa (its limit of proportionality); the tendon's graph stays linear up to about 88 MPa IC3 At 30 MPa (walking) the synthetic material deforms elastically, so it returns to its original length: it is suitable for walking IC4 At 70 MPa (sprinting) it would be beyond its yield point and deform plastically, so it would be permanently lengthened (the joint would become loose) IC5 Its breaking stress is about 68 MPa, less than 70 MPa, so it could break when sprinting (the tendon breaks at about 96 MPa) IC6 A strip with a larger cross-sectional area would have a smaller stress for the same force (σ = F/A); about 1.5 times the area keeps the stress below 50 MPa, so a thicker strip could be suitable Area under the tendon graph up to a strain of 0.040 found, e.g. by counting squares with one small square = 0.004 × 4 × 10⁶ Pa = 1.6 × 10⁴ J m⁻³ Energy per unit volume = 7.5 × 10⁵ J m⁻³
items.why: Stress–strain graphs came up in 15 of 22 sessions, with long comparison questions in Jan2020 Q14 and Jun2026 Q15; a graph whose straight section misses the origin (the Jan2021 report's pitfall) and the spec's 'spare-part surgery' context have not been combined before.

items.name: CORE PRACTICAL 3: Young modulus of a wire
path: Unit 1 Mechanics and Materials
Materials
S31 - CORE PRACTICAL 3 Determine the Young modulus
items.question: A student measures these quantities in an experiment to determine the Young modulus of a metal wire. The uncertainty in each reading is equal to the resolution of the instrument used. Which reading in the table has the largest percentage uncertainty? original length of wire diameter of wire mass on hanger extension of wire
items.ms: Percentage uncertainty = resolution ÷ reading × 100%: length 0.04%, diameter 1.8%, mass 1.3%, extension 3.6%. The extension has the largest. A: a long length makes this tiny. B: the diameter is small, but the micrometer's resolution is ten times finer than the scale used for the extension. C: 1.3% is less than 3.6%.
items.why: Resolution and percentage uncertainty in CP3 were asked in Jan2024 Q17(b) and Jan2026 Q16(b), and the Jan2024 report says candidates use the terms without understanding them.

items.name: CORE PRACTICAL 3: Young modulus of a wire
path: Unit 1 Mechanics and Materials
Materials
S31 - CORE PRACTICAL 3 Determine the Young modulus
items.question: In an experiment to determine the Young modulus of a wire, a student plots a graph of the extension Δx (y-axis) against the mass m hung from the wire (x-axis). The graph is a straight line through the origin with gradient G. The original length of the wire is x and its cross-sectional area is A. Which expression gives the Young modulus of the wire? gGx/A gx/(AG) AG/(gx) x/(AG)
items.ms: E = stress ÷ strain = (mg/A) ÷ (Δx/x) = gx/(A × Δx/m) = gx/(AG), since G = Δx/m. A treats G as mass per unit extension. C inverts the whole expression. D uses the mass instead of the weight (leaves out g).
items.why: CP3 graphs of mass against extension were used in Jan2020 Q18(b) and Oct2025 Q15(b); plotting the axes the other way round tests whether candidates understand what the gradient is.

items.name: CORE PRACTICAL 3: Young modulus of a wire
path: Unit 1 Mechanics and Materials
Materials
S31 - CORE PRACTICAL 3 Determine the Young modulus
items.question: A student writes this plan to determine the Young modulus of copper. 1. Clamp a 0.50 m length of copper wire vertically from a support. Hang a 1.0 kg mass hanger from its lower end. 2. Measure the diameter of the wire once, using vernier calipers. 3. Measure the length of the wire with a metre rule. 4. Add 1.0 kg masses one at a time, up to a total of 10 kg, measuring the length of the wire with the metre rule each time. 5. Calculate the Young modulus using the final length and the final mass only. Discuss the improvements the student should make to the plan. The student improves the plan. She uses a copper wire of diameter 0.27 mm. Copper reaches its limit of proportionality at a stress of about 1.0 × 10⁸ Pa. Calculate the largest mass that can be hung from the wire without the stress exceeding the limit of proportionality. Describe how the student can check that the wire has not been permanently stretched during the experiment.
items.ms: IC1 Use a much longer wire (2 m or more), so the extension is larger and its percentage uncertainty is smaller IC2 Measure the diameter with a micrometer (resolution 0.01 mm), because the resolution of vernier calipers is too coarse for a thin wire IC3 Measure the diameter at several places along the wire and in different orientations, and calculate the mean IC4 Measure the extension directly, from a marker on the wire against a fixed scale with a vernier, instead of measuring the whole length with a metre rule IC5 Use much smaller loads (e.g. 100 g steps), because 10 kg would take the thin wire beyond its limit of proportionality / elastic limit, or break it IC6 Take readings for several loads and plot a graph of force against extension (or stress against strain), and use the gradient of the straight section instead of one pair of values Calculates cross-sectional area Use of σ = F/A Use of W = mg and m = 0.58 kg Remove the masses (back to the initial small load) and check that the marker returns to its original reading / the extension returns to zero
items.why: CP3 has come up in 10 of 22 sessions (May2024 Q16(a) was a 6-mark method); improving a flawed plan has not been asked, and keeping the load below the limit of proportionality links it to S29.

items.name: CORE PRACTICAL 3: Young modulus of a wire
path: Unit 1 Mechanics and Materials
Materials
S31 - CORE PRACTICAL 3 Determine the Young modulus
items.question: A student determines the Young modulus of the metal in a wire using the apparatus shown. The original length of the wire, from the clamp to the marker, is 2.800 m. The student adds masses to the hanger and measures the extension Δx of the wire using a vernier scale. The student measures the diameter d of the wire at five different places along it. The readings are shown in the table. Calculate the cross-sectional area of the wire. The student's results are shown in the table. Plot a graph of m on the y-axis against Δx on the x-axis, on the grid. Determine the Young modulus of the metal, and deduce which metal the wire is made from.
items.ms: Mean diameter = 0.380 mm A = 1.13 × 10⁻⁷ m² Axes labelled with quantities and units: m / kg and Δx / mm Sensible scales: the points cover more than half of the grid in each direction All points plotted correctly (to within half a small square) Single straight line of best fit Gradient found using a large triangle (about 0.42 kg mm⁻¹ = 415 kg m⁻¹) Use of W = mg (gradient × g gives the force per unit extension) Use of σ = F/A and ε = Δx/x with E = σ/ε (or E = gradient × g × x/A) E = 1.0 × 10¹¹ Pa Comparison with the table and conclusion: brass
items.why: CP3 data processing is the commonest core-practical question (Jan2020 Q18(b), Oct2021 Q14(b), Oct2025 Q15(b)); a full plot followed by identifying the metal from a table (Jan2024 Q17(c)) has not been set.

items.name: Elastic strain energy ΔEel = ½FΔx
path: Unit 1 Mechanics and Materials
Materials
S32 - calculate the elastic strain energy Eel in a
items.question: The spring in a toy dart gun has a stiffness of 250 N m⁻¹. It is compressed by 4.0 cm. How much elastic strain energy is stored in the spring? 0.20 J 0.40 J 5.0 J 2.0 × 10³ J
items.ms: F = kΔx = 250 × 0.040 = 10 N, ΔEel = ½FΔx = ½ × 10 N × 0.040 m = 0.20 J. B leaves out the ½. C uses ½kΔx without squaring. D leaves the compression in cm.
items.why: S32 has come up in 15 of 22 sessions; Jun2026 Q12 set the same calculation from a force and a stiffness, and the reports say the ½ and the cm-to-m conversion are often missed.

items.name: Elastic strain energy ΔEel = ½FΔx
path: Unit 1 Mechanics and Materials
Materials
S32 - calculate the elastic strain energy Eel in a
items.question: A steel wire of original length 2.0 m and cross-sectional area 1.5 × 10⁻⁷ m² is stretched by 1.2 mm. The wire obeys Hooke's law. Young modulus of steel = 2.0 × 10¹¹ Pa How much elastic strain energy is stored in the wire? 1.1 × 10⁻² J 2.2 × 10⁻² J 4.3 × 10⁻² J 1.1 × 10⁴ J
items.ms: Strain = 1.2 × 10⁻³ m ÷ 2.0 m = 6.0 × 10⁻⁴, stress = Eε = 1.2 × 10⁸ Pa, F = σA = 18 N, ΔEel = ½FΔx = ½ × 18 N × 1.2 × 10⁻³ m = 1.1 × 10⁻² J. B leaves out the ½. C multiplies by the length instead of dividing (k = EAx). D uses the extension in mm.
items.why: Linking the Young modulus to the energy stored (via k = EA/x) appears in long questions (Jun2021 Q17(b), Oct2023 Q16(b)) but has not been set as an MCQ.

items.name: Elastic strain energy ΔEel = ½FΔx
path: Unit 1 Mechanics and Materials
Materials
S32 - calculate the elastic strain energy Eel in a
items.question: A spring in a car's suspension has a stiffness of 4.2 × 10⁴ N m⁻¹. When the car is empty, the compressive force on the spring is 3.1 kN. When passengers get in, the force increases to 4.0 kN. The spring obeys Hooke's law. Calculate the increase in the elastic strain energy stored in the spring.
items.ms: Use of ΔF = kΔx to find a compression (0.0738 m or 0.0952 m) Use of ΔEel = ½FΔx Subtracts the energy stored at 3.1 kN from the energy stored at 4.0 kN (190 J − 114 J) Increase in energy = 76 J
items.why: S32 came up in 15 of 22 sessions; the change in energy between two loaded states (Jun2025 Q15(a), Jan2026 Q9) catches candidates who use ½ΔFΔx.

items.name: Elastic strain energy ΔEel = ½FΔx
path: Unit 1 Mechanics and Materials
Materials
S32 - calculate the elastic strain energy Eel in a
items.question: An archer pulls back the string of a bow and then releases it to fire an arrow. The graph shows how the force F needed to hold the string varies with the distance x the string is pulled back. Estimate the elastic strain energy stored in the bow when the string is pulled back 0.50 m. The arrow has a mass of 25 g. 75% of the stored elastic strain energy is transferred to the kinetic energy of the arrow. Calculate the speed of the arrow as it leaves the bow. A second bow also needs a force of 300 N when the string is pulled back 0.50 m, but its force–distance graph is a straight line through the origin. The same percentage of the stored energy is transferred to the arrow. Explain why the same arrow leaves the second bow with a smaller speed.
items.ms: Uses the area under the graph (counting squares, or strips / trapezia) Energy represented by one square stated or used correctly, e.g. one large square = 0.10 m × 50 N = 5.0 J Energy = 88 J Use of efficiency: kinetic energy = 0.75 × energy from (a) Use of Ek = ½mv² with m = 0.025 kg v = 73 m s⁻¹ The area under a straight-line graph is smaller: energy stored = ½ × 300 N × 0.50 m = 75 J, less than 88 J So less kinetic energy is transferred to the arrow, and since Ek = ½mv² its speed is smaller
items.why: The spec expects area estimates for non-linear force–extension graphs, but only Jan2019 Q17(b) and Jan2024 Q11(b) have asked one; turning stored energy into a launch speed (Jan2020 Q17, Jan2022 Q16) is the usual synoptic step.

items.name: Work done ΔW = FΔs, including a force not along the line of motion
path: Unit 1 Mechanics and Materials
Mechanics
S17 - use the equation for work W  Fs, including ca
items.question: A traveller pulls a wheeled suitcase at constant speed along a level floor. She exerts a force of 45 N on the suitcase along its handle, which is at 55° to the horizontal. The suitcase moves 80 m. What is the work done on the suitcase by the force from the traveller? 2.1 kJ 2.9 kJ 3.6 kJ 6.3 kJ
items.ms: ΔW = FΔs cos θ = 45 N × 80 m × cos 55° = 2.06 × 10³ J ≈ 2.1 kJ: only the horizontal component of the force is along the displacement. B uses sin 55°, the vertical component, which does no work here. C ignores the angle. D divides by cos 55° instead of multiplying.
items.why: S17 has come up in 11 of 22 sessions, most often as an MCQ on a force at an angle to the motion (Oct2023 Q10, Jun2023 Q2, Jun2026 Q7); a steep handle angle, where the sin and cos answers are far apart, is the likely next form.

items.name: Work done ΔW = FΔs, including a force not along the line of motion
path: Unit 1 Mechanics and Materials
Mechanics
S17 - use the equation for work W  Fs, including ca
items.question: A child slides down a straight playground slide. Which force does no work on the child? normal contact force from the slide friction from the slide air resistance weight of the child
items.ms: The normal contact force acts at 90° to the surface of the slide, so at 90° to the displacement: work done = FΔs cos 90° = 0. B and C act opposite to the motion, so work is done against them and energy is dissipated. D has a component down the slide, so the weight does work on the child (its Egrav decreases).
items.why: Every past S17 question had a force with a component along the motion; a force at 90° to the displacement doing no work is the obvious untested case of 'a force not along the line of motion'.

items.name: Work done ΔW = FΔs, including a force not along the line of motion
path: Unit 1 Mechanics and Materials
Mechanics
S17 - use the equation for work W  Fs, including ca
items.question: Narrowboats on canals used to be pulled by horses walking along a towpath beside the canal. The diagram shows a view from above. The tow rope is at 20° to the direction in which the boat moves. The tension in the rope is a constant 450 N. Calculate the work done on the boat by the tension as the boat moves 250 m along the canal. Suggest why a long tow rope was used. When the boat starts from rest, the tension in the rope is larger. The graph shows how the tension T in the rope varies with the distance s moved by the boat during the first 40 m. The rope stays at 20° to the direction of motion. Determine the work done on the boat by the tension during the first 40 m.
items.ms: Use of ΔW = FΔs with the component of the tension along the canal, 450 N × cos 20° ΔW = 1.06 × 10⁵ J With a long rope, the angle between the rope and the direction of motion is smaller So the component of the tension along the canal is larger / more of the tension does work on the boat (for the same tension) The sideways component of the tension, pulling the boat towards the bank, is smaller Area under the graph used (area = 2.93 × 10⁴ J) Area multiplied by cos 20° ΔW = 2.75 × 10⁴ J
items.why: S17 is warm (11 of 22 sessions, last asked Jun2026) and the force-at-an-angle calculation is its core; work as the area under a force–distance graph has appeared only once, as an MCQ (Oct2019 Q4).

items.name: Kinetic energy ½mv²
path: Unit 1 Mechanics and Materials
Mechanics

items.question: A cricket ball of mass 160 g is bowled at a speed of 36 m s⁻¹. What is the kinetic energy of the ball? 2.9 J 5.8 J 10.4 J 104 J
items.ms: Ek = ½mv² = ½ × 0.160 kg × (36 m s⁻¹)² = 104 J. A does not square the speed (½mv). B is mv, the momentum, given in joules. C converts 160 g to 0.016 kg (a power-of-ten slip).
items.why: S18 has come up in 9 of 22 sessions, usually as a one-step ½mv² (Jun2026 Q11, Jun2023 Q13(a)); the examiners report slips in squaring v and in converting the mass to kg.

path: Unit 1 Mechanics and Materials
Mechanics
S18 - use the equation Ek  12 mv 2 for the kinetic
items.question: The speed of a car increases from 20 m s⁻¹ to 30 m s⁻¹. What is the percentage increase in the kinetic energy of the car? 50% 125% 150% 225%
items.ms: Ek ∝ v², so the new Ek is (30 ÷ 20)² = 2.25 times the old value: an increase of 125%. A is the percentage increase in speed. C treats Ek as proportional to v and quotes the ratio as the increase. D is the ratio of the kinetic energies, not the increase.
items.why: Ratio MCQs on ½mv² recur (Oct2023 Q6: E_{k} doubled; Oct2022 Q9: equal E_{k}); a percentage change is the variant not yet set.

items.name: Kinetic energy ½mv²
path: Unit 1 Mechanics and Materials
Mechanics

items.question: An ice hockey puck slides across level ice. The momentum of the puck is 6.5 kg m s⁻¹ and its kinetic energy is 123 J. Calculate the mass of the puck.
items.ms: Use of p = mv Use of Ek = ½mv² m = 0.17 kg
items.why: S18 is warm (9 of 22 sessions) and every past question gave m and v directly; pairing ½mv² with p = mv, so that neither is given, is the likeliest short variant.

items.name: Gravitational potential energy ΔEgrav = mgΔh
path: Unit 1 Mechanics and Materials
Mechanics
S19 - use the equation Egrav  mgh for the differenc
items.question: A uniform ladder of mass 14 kg and length 3.2 m lies flat on level ground. It is lifted until it stands vertically on one end. What is the increase in the gravitational potential energy of the ladder? 22 J 45 J 220 J 440 J
items.ms: The centre of gravity of a uniform ladder is at its middle, so it rises by 3.2 m ÷ 2 = 1.6 m (the thickness of the ladder is negligible). ΔEgrav = mgΔh = 14 kg × 9.81 N kg⁻¹ × 1.6 m = 220 J. A leaves out g. B leaves out g and uses the full length. D uses the full length, 3.2 m, as Δh.
items.why: S19 is cool (5 of 22 sessions) and has only ever used point objects; the rise of the centre of gravity of an extended object links S19 with S16 and has not been asked.

items.name: Gravitational potential energy ΔEgrav = mgΔh
path: Unit 1 Mechanics and Materials
Mechanics
S19 - use the equation Egrav  mgh for the differenc
items.question: The graph shows the height above sea level of a road against the distance along the road, for part of a cycle race. A cyclist rides from A to B. The total mass of the cyclist and bicycle is 74 kg. Show that the gain in gravitational potential energy of the cyclist and bicycle between A and B is about 9 × 10⁵ J. The cyclist takes 75 minutes to ride from A to B. Calculate the average rate at which the gravitational potential energy of the cyclist and bicycle increases. Give one reason why the average useful power output of the cyclist must be greater than your answer to (b).
items.ms: Δh = 1650 m − 450 m = 1200 m (read from the graph) Use of ΔEgrav = mgΔh ΔEgrav = 8.7 × 10⁵ J Use of P = E/t with t = 4500 s P = 194 W Work is done against air resistance / rolling resistance / friction (in the bicycle) Energy is dissipated by braking on the descent (between 9 km and 15 km), so the height lost must be climbed again
items.why: S19 is cool (5 of 22 sessions, last asked Jan2025) and GPE on its own is the thinnest-examined part of the topic; reading Δh from a race profile tests the most reported error, using a distance along the route instead of the vertical height (Jan2021, Jan2025, Oct2022).

items.name: Conservation of energy
path: Unit 1 Mechanics and Materials
Mechanics
S20 - apply, the principle of conservation of energ
items.question: A cyclist freewheels over the top of a hill at a speed of 4.0 m s⁻¹. The road then descends through a vertical height of 6.5 m. Resistive forces are negligible. What is the speed of the cyclist at the bottom of the hill? 10.6 m s⁻¹ 11.3 m s⁻¹ 12.0 m s⁻¹ 15.3 m s⁻¹
items.ms: ½mv² = ½mu² + mgΔh, so v = √(u² + 2gΔh) = √((4.0 m s⁻¹)² + 2 × 9.81 m s⁻² × 6.5 m) = 12.0 m s⁻¹. A subtracts the initial kinetic energy. B ignores the initial kinetic energy. D adds 4.0 m s⁻¹ to 11.3 m s⁻¹: energies add, speeds do not.
items.why: Speed-from-height MCQs recur (Oct2020 Q3, Jun2023 Q8, Oct2025 Q10), always starting from rest; a start with kinetic energy already is the obvious twist.

items.name: Conservation of energy
path: Unit 1 Mechanics and Materials
Mechanics
S20 - apply, the principle of conservation of energ
items.question: A pendulum consists of a small bob on a string of length 0.80 m. The bob is released from rest with the string taut at 50° to the vertical, as shown. Air resistance is negligible. What is the speed of the bob at its lowest point? 1.92 m s⁻¹ 2.37 m s⁻¹ 3.18 m s⁻¹ 3.47 m s⁻¹
items.ms: The bob falls through Δh = L − L cos 50° = 0.80 m × (1 − cos 50°) = 0.286 m. mgΔh = ½mv² gives v = √(2gΔh) = 2.37 m s⁻¹. A uses Δh = L(1 − sin 50°). C uses Δh = L cos 50°, the depth of the starting point below the pivot. D uses Δh = L sin 50°, the horizontal distance of the bob from the vertical.
items.why: S20 is hot (18 of 22 sessions), but a pendulum, where the fall in height must be found from an angle, has not been set; it suits a late MCQ.

items.name: Conservation of energy
path: Unit 1 Mechanics and Materials
Mechanics
S20 - apply, the principle of conservation of energ
items.question: A ball is thrown from the flat roof of a tall building to the level ground below. It could be thrown with the same speed horizontally, at an angle above the horizontal, or vertically downwards. Air resistance is negligible. Which statement about the speed of the ball as it reaches the ground is correct? It is greatest when the ball is thrown at an angle above the horizontal. It is greatest when the ball is thrown horizontally. It is greatest when the ball is thrown vertically downwards. It is the same whichever way the ball is thrown.
items.ms: In every case the ball starts with the same kinetic energy and falls through the same height, so ½mv² = ½mu² + mgΔh gives the same final speed: energy is a scalar, so the direction of the throw does not matter. A, B and C confuse the speed with the time of flight or with the direction of the final velocity, which do depend on the direction of the throw.
items.why: Using energy (a scalar) to compare landing speeds of projectiles links S20 with S7; energy steps appear in recent projectile questions (Oct2024 Q15(b)) but this comparison has not been asked.

items.name: Conservation of energy
path: Unit 1 Mechanics and Materials
Mechanics
S20 - apply, the principle of conservation of energ
items.question: A fairground 'drop tower' ride lifts a car carrying riders to the top of a tall tower and releases it from rest. The car falls freely through 42 m. Magnetic brakes then exert a constant upward force on the car, which brings it to rest after falling a further 20 m, as shown in the diagram. mass of car and riders = 2600 kg Calculate the speed of the car when the brakes start to act. Calculate the size of the braking force. On the axes, sketch a graph to show how the kinetic energy Ek of the car varies with the distance fallen, from release until the car stops.
items.ms: Use of mgΔh = ½mv² v = 28.7 m s⁻¹ Energy transferred by the brakes = Ek + loss of Egrav during braking = mg × (42 m + 20 m) (1.58 × 10⁶ J) Use of ΔW = FΔs with Δs = 20 m F = 7.9 × 10⁴ N Straight line from the origin rising to a maximum at 42 m Straight line falling from the maximum to zero at 62 m
items.why: S20 is hot; Jan2025 Q13(a) used the work done by a stopping force on level ground, but a vertical stop, where the weight still does work during braking, and a sketch of E_{k} against distance have not been asked.

items.name: Conservation of energy
path: Unit 1 Mechanics and Materials
Mechanics
S20 - apply, the principle of conservation of energ
items.question: In ski jumping, a skier starts from rest at the top of a steep track called the in-run and leaves the take-off point at high speed. The diagram shows the in-run (not to scale). The vertical drop from the start to the take-off point is 38 m and the length of the track is 98 m. mass of skier and skis = 64 kg Show that the speed of the skier at the take-off point would be about 27 m s⁻¹ if there were no resistive forces. The speed of the skier at the take-off point is measured as 25.1 m s⁻¹. Calculate the average resistive force on the skier along the in-run. A heavier skier crouches in the same position. At any given speed, the air resistance on the heavier skier is the same as on the first skier. Friction between the skis and the track is negligible. Explain why the heavier skier would reach a greater speed at the take-off point.
items.ms: Use of ΔEgrav = mgΔh Use of Ek = ½mv² with Ek = ΔEgrav v = 27.3 m s⁻¹ Use of ΔEgrav = mgΔh (2.39 × 10⁴ J) Use of Ek = ½mv² (2.02 × 10⁴ J) Use of ΔW = FΔs with work done against resistive forces = ΔEgrav − Ek and Δs = 98 m F = 38 N The gravitational potential energy transferred is proportional to the mass (as is the kinetic energy needed for a given speed) Air resistance does not depend on mass, so the work done against air resistance is a smaller fraction of the energy transferred / less energy is dissipated per kilogram Alternative: the component of the weight along the track is larger but air resistance is the same, so the resultant force per unit mass (the acceleration) is greater at every speed
items.why: S20 is hot; speed at the bottom of a slope (Jun2021 Q12, Jan2026 Q11 and Q17) and an average resistive force from missing energy (Oct2020 and Oct2025 Q18(b), Oct2022 Q19(b)) recur, and the effect of mass when air resistance acts is the untested follow-up to May2024 Q19(c) and Jan2024 Q14(b).

items.name: Conservation of energy
path: Unit 1 Mechanics and Materials
Mechanics
S20 - apply, the principle of conservation of energ
items.question: A pole vaulter runs along a runway, plants the end of a flexible pole in a box in the ground and is lifted over a bar. The diagram shows the path of the vaulter's centre of gravity (not to scale). mass of vaulter = 68 kg The vaulter's speed at take-off is 9.4 m s⁻¹. Show that, if all of the vaulter's kinetic energy at take-off were transferred to gravitational potential energy, his centre of gravity would rise by about 4.5 m. At take-off, the vaulter's centre of gravity is 1.10 m above the ground. At the top of the vault his centre of gravity is 5.95 m above the ground and he is moving horizontally at 1.2 m s⁻¹. Deduce whether the vaulter's kinetic energy at take-off is enough to provide both his gain in gravitational potential energy and his kinetic energy at the top of the vault. Explain the energy transfers that take place from the moment the pole is planted in the box until the vaulter comes to rest on the landing mat. Your answer should refer to work done.
items.ms: Use of Ek = ½mv² Use of ΔEgrav = mgΔh Δh = 4.50 m Δh = 5.95 m − 1.10 m = 4.85 m Use of ΔEgrav = mgΔh (ΔEgrav = 3.24 × 10³ J) Use of Ek = ½mv² for the speed at the top (49 J), so the energy needed = 3.28 × 10³ J Compares 3.28 × 10³ J with 3.00 × 10³ J and concludes that the kinetic energy at take-off is not enough: the vaulter must do about 280 J of extra work (e.g. pushing on the pole with his arms) IC1 As the pole bends, the vaulter does work on the pole: his kinetic energy decreases and elastic strain energy is stored in the pole IC2 As the vaulter rises, work is done against his weight and his gravitational potential energy increases IC3 As the pole straightens, it does work on the vaulter: its elastic strain energy is transferred to his gravitational potential energy IC4 The vaulter also does work by pushing / pulling on the pole with his arms, so his gain in Egrav is greater than his Ek at take-off IC5 After clearing the bar his weight does work on him: Egrav is transferred to Ek as he falls (he keeps some Ek at the top because he is still moving horizontally) IC6 The mat exerts an upward force on him over the distance it is compressed: the work done by the mat reduces his Ek to zero (energy is transferred to the mat as elastic strain energy and is dissipated as thermal energy)
items.why: S20 is the hottest point in this topic (18 of 22 sessions, 5.1% of the unit's marks); its long questions pair an energy calculation with an extended explanation in terms of work done (Jan2021 Q15 bungee, Oct2025 Q18(b)), and an athlete who must supply extra work is a fresh 'deduce whether'.

path: Unit 1 Mechanics and Materials
Mechanics

items.question: A builder's hoist raises a pallet of roof tiles of total mass 620 kg through a vertical height of 18 m at constant speed in 25 s. What is the useful power output of the hoist? 0.45 kW 4.4 kW 43 kW 110 kW
items.ms: P = ΔEgrav ÷ t = mgΔh ÷ t = 620 kg × 9.81 N kg⁻¹ × 18 m ÷ 25 s = 4.4 × 10³ W. A leaves out g. C multiplies by g twice (treats the weight as a mass). D is the energy transferred, 1.1 × 10⁵ J, not divided by the time.
items.why: S21 is hot (18 of 22 sessions); P = W/t for a lifted load is its most common one-step form (Jan2023 Q8, Jun2022 Q1, Jan2022 Q12(b)).

items.question: A car of mass 1200 kg travels at a constant speed of 20 m s⁻¹ up a straight road inclined at 3.0° to the horizontal. The total resistive force on the car is 650 N. What is the useful power output of the car's engine? 12 kW 13 kW 25 kW 250 kW
items.ms: At constant speed, driving force = resistive force + component of weight down the slope = 650 N + 1200 kg × 9.81 N kg⁻¹ × sin 3.0° = 1.27 × 10³ N. The car moves 20 m each second, so P = W/t = FΔs/t = 1.27 × 10³ N × 20 m s⁻¹ = 2.5 × 10⁴ W. A includes only the component of the weight. B includes only the resistive force. D uses cos 3.0° instead of sin 3.0°.
items.why: Power from a force and a speed is examined although only P = W/t is in the spec (Oct2021 Q18(a), Jun2021 Q16(c)); a car climbing at constant speed (Jan2024 Q4 as a graph) combines it with resolving the weight.

items.question: A pump in a garden pond drives water up a vertical pipe. The water leaves a nozzle at the top of the pipe vertically upwards, as shown. The nozzle is 0.85 m above the surface of the water in the pond. The water leaves the nozzle at a speed of 6.3 m s⁻¹. Show that the water rises about 2 m above the nozzle. Ignore air resistance. The volume of water leaving the nozzle is 18 litres every minute. density of water = 1000 kg m⁻³ 1 litre = 1.0 × 10⁻³ m³ Show that the mass of water leaving the nozzle each second is about 0.3 kg. items.question: The engine of a boat has an efficiency of 0.40. The useful output power of the engine is 18 kW. What is the total input power to the engine? 7.2 kW 11 kW 30 kW 45 kW
items.ms: total power input = useful power output ÷ efficiency = 18 kW ÷ 0.40 = 45 kW. A multiplies by the efficiency. B multiplies by (1 − 0.40). C divides by (1 − 0.40).
items.why: Finding the input from the efficiency is the commonest S22 MCQ (Jan2020 Q8, Oct2020 Q6, Jun2021 Q4, Oct2024 Q6), and multiplying instead of dividing is the error the examiners report most.

items.question: A motor drives a gearbox, which turns the drum of a winch. The efficiency of the motor is 0.80, the efficiency of the gearbox is 0.90 and the efficiency of the winch drum is 0.70. What is the efficiency of the whole system? 0.50 0.70 0.80 0.90
items.ms: Each stage passes on that fraction of the energy it receives, so the overall efficiency = 0.80 × 0.90 × 0.70 = 0.50. B is the efficiency of the least efficient stage. C is the mean of the three efficiencies. D is the efficiency of the most efficient stage.

items.question: A trolley of mass 0.80 kg is released from rest at the top of a ramp 1.20 m long. The top of the ramp is 0.35 m higher than the bottom. The trolley reaches the bottom of the ramp at a speed of 2.2 m s⁻¹. What is the efficiency of the transfer of gravitational potential energy to kinetic energy? 0.21 0.30 0.70 1.4
items.ms: Useful energy output Ek = ½ × 0.80 kg × (2.2 m s⁻¹)² = 1.94 J; energy input ΔEgrav = 0.80 kg × 9.81 N kg⁻¹ × 0.35 m = 2.75 J; efficiency = 1.94 J ÷ 2.75 J = 0.70. items.why: Efficiency with E_{grav} or E_{k} as the input appeared in Jun2025 Q14 and Jun2022 Q14(a), and Jan2019 Q4 used a ramp; using the ramp length as Δh is the most reported S19 error.

items.question: A student investigates the efficiency of the pulley system shown in the diagram. The load is lifted by pulling down on the free end of the rope with a force F, called the effort. When the effort moves down 0.40 m, the load rises 0.20 m. The student uses a newtonmeter to measure the effort F needed to raise loads of different weight W slowly at a steady speed. The results are shown in the table. Calculate the efficiency of the pulley system when W = 10.0 N. Plot a graph of F against W on the grid. Explain why the efficiency of the pulley system increases as the load increases. You should refer to your graph.
items.ms: Use of efficiency = useful work output ÷ total work input, with work done = FΔs for both efficiency = 0.82 Axes labelled with quantities and units: F / N (vertical) and W / N (horizontal) Sensible scales chosen, so that the points cover more than half of the grid in each direction All six points plotted correctly (to within half a small square) Straight line of best fit drawn The line has an intercept on the F axis (about 0.8 N): an effort is needed even with no load, to lift the moving pulley and to do work against friction This part of the work input is about the same for every load, so it becomes a smaller fraction of the total work input as W increases (so the efficiency increases)

items.question: A wind turbine has three blades. Each blade is 42 m long, so the blades sweep out a circle of radius 42 m as they turn. The wind blows directly towards the turbine at a speed of 12 m s⁻¹. density of air = 1.2 kg m⁻³ Show that the mass of air passing through the circle swept out by the blades each second is about 8 × 10⁴ kg. The useful output power of the turbine at this wind speed is 2.3 MW. Calculate the efficiency of the turbine. Assume that the total input power is the kinetic energy of the air passing through the circle each second. Explain why a wind turbine cannot transfer all of the kinetic energy of the air passing through its blades to useful energy. On another day the wind speed is 7.0 m s⁻¹. The efficiency of the turbine is unchanged. Deduce whether the useful output power of the turbine is more than 0.50 MW.
items.ms: Use of A = πr² (5.54 × 10³ m²) Volume passing each second = A × 12 m (6.65 × 10⁴ m³) Use of ρ = m/V giving m = 7.98 × 10⁴ kg Use of Ek = ½mv² (5.75 × 10⁶ J each second) Use of efficiency = useful power output ÷ total power input efficiency = 0.40 The air must keep moving after it has passed the blades (so that more air can pass through) So the air still has kinetic energy after passing the turbine Work is done against friction in the moving parts (bearings, gearbox), so some energy is dissipated Mass of air each second = 4.66 × 10⁴ kg, or input power scaled by (7.0 ÷ 12)³ Useful output power = 0.40 × 1.14 MW = 0.46 MW Compares 0.46 MW with 0.50 MW and concludes that the output power is not more than 0.50 MW
items.why: S22 is hot (19 of 22 sessions); efficiency questions so far use lifts, cranes and vehicles, and a turbine whose input is the kinetic energy of the air (linking S18 and S23) has not been asked.

items.name: Moment of a force
path: Unit 1 Mechanics and Materials

items.question: A person opens a door by pulling on the handle with a horizontal force of 24 N. The handle is 0.78 m from the line of the hinges. The force acts at 40° to the surface of the door. What is the moment of the force about the hinges? 12 N m 14 N m 19 N m 31 N m
items.ms: The perpendicular distance from the hinges to the line of action of the force is 0.78 sin 40°, so moment = 24 × 0.78 × sin 40° = 12 N m. B uses cos 40° (the component along the door); C ignores the angle; D divides the force by the distance.
items.why: S15 has come up in 8 of 22 sessions, and its commonest form is a force at an angle to a lever (Oct2024 Q13(a), a pedal at 24°); MCQs on moments recur (Oct2019, Oct2021, Jan2022, Oct2024).

items.question: Looking down at a mobile phone for long periods can cause neck pain. The diagram shows a simple model of a person's head tilted forward. The head pivots about point P at the top of the spine. The weight W of the head acts at its centre of gravity G, which is 8.0 cm from P. The line PG makes an angle θ with the vertical. When the head is upright, G is vertically above P. The neck muscles exert a force M on the head. In this model, M always acts vertically downwards at a perpendicular distance of 5.0 cm from P. The mass of the head is 5.0 kg. Calculate the moment of W about P when θ = 50°. Calculate M when θ = 50°. Sketch a graph on the axes to show how the moment of W about P varies as θ increases from 0 to 90°. Add the maximum value of the moment to the vertical axis. Explain why the force exerted on the head by the spine at P increases as θ increases.
items.ms: Use of W = mg Use of perpendicular distance = 8.0 cm × sin 50° (= 6.1 cm) Moment = 3.0 N m Use of principle of moments about P: M × 0.050 m = moment of W M = 60 N Curve from the origin, increasing with a decreasing gradient (gradient zero at 90°) Maximum value of 3.9 N m marked at θ = 90° The moment of W about P increases (perpendicular distance 8.0 sin θ increases), so M must increase to keep the moments about P balanced The resultant force on the head is zero, so the upward force from the spine = W + M, which increases
items.why: Body-lever models appeared in Jun2019 Q15 (forearm and biceps); how a moment changes with angle has been asked only in words (Oct2024 Q13(b)), never as a sketch graph.

items.name: Centre of gravity; principle of moments; equilibrium
path: Unit 1 Mechanics and Materials
Mechanics

items.question: A uniform plank of weight 250 N is lifted by two people. Each pulls vertically upwards on one end of the plank with a force of 150 N. Which of the following describes the resultant force on the plank and the resultant moment on the plank about its centre? resultant force zero and resultant moment zero resultant force zero and resultant moment not zero resultant force 50 N upwards and resultant moment zero resultant force 50 N upwards and resultant moment not zero
items.ms: The upward forces total 2 × 150 = 300 N and the weight is 250 N, so the resultant force is 50 N upwards. About the centre the weight has no moment, and the two 150 N forces act at equal distances on opposite sides, so their moments are equal and opposite: the resultant moment is zero. A and B assume the plank is in equilibrium although the forces do not balance; B and D do not recognise that the moments of the two equal forces cancel.
items.why: The conditions for equilibrium are asked in most sessions (Jan2024, Jan2025, Oct2025, Jan2026) and Jun2025 Q2 used this table form for a balanced see-saw; a body with a resultant force but no resultant moment has not yet been asked.

items.question: A window cleaner of weight 720 N stands on a uniform plank of length 3.6 m and weight 200 N. The plank is horizontal and rests on two trestles, one at each end, A and B. The window cleaner stands 0.90 m from end A. What is the force exerted on the plank by the trestle at A? 280 N 460 N 540 N 640 N
items.ms: Moments about B: FA × 3.6 = 200 × 1.8 + 720 × 2.70, so FA = 640 N. A is the force at B (920 − 640); B shares the total weight of 920 N equally between the trestles; C omits the weight of the plank.
items.why: Support forces on a loaded beam recur (Jun2021 Q16(a), Jan2022 Q9, May2024 Q18(a)); omitting the moment of the beam's own weight is a pitfall named in the examiner reports (Jan2019, Jun2023).

items.question: A tall uniform cabinet stands on a horizontal floor. Viewed from the side it is a rectangle 0.40 m wide and 1.20 m high. The cabinet is tilted about one bottom edge and then released. What is the largest angle through which it can be tilted from the upright position and still fall back to the upright position? 9.5° 18° 34° 72°

A uses the full height (0.20 / 1.20); C uses the full width with half the height (0.40 / 0.60); D is the angle between the line from the edge to G and the floor.

items.question: A steelyard is a type of balance. The diagram shows a steelyard being used in a market to weigh a fish. The beam of the steelyard hangs from a pivot P. The fish hangs from a hook 6.0 cm to the left of P. The combined weight of the beam and hook is 2.4 N and acts 3.0 cm to the left of P. A 5.0 N weight can slide along the beam to the right of P. items.question: The diagram shows a diving board at a swimming pool. The board is uniform, 4.80 m long and has a weight of 410 N. End A is bolted to a concrete block, and the board rests on a fulcrum F, 1.50 m from A. A diver of mass 66 kg stands at end B. The board is horizontal and in equilibrium. Explain why the force exerted on the board by the bolt must act downwards. Calculate the magnitude of the force exerted on the board by the bolt. Calculate the magnitude of the force exerted on the board by the fulcrum.

items.question: The diagram shows a forklift truck at rest on level ground. The mass of the truck is 3200 kg and its centre of gravity G is 0.85 m behind the front axle. The front and rear axles are 1.45 m apart. When the truck carries a crate on its forks, the centre of gravity X of the crate is 0.95 m in front of the front axle. State the two conditions needed for the truck to be in equilibrium. The truck is not carrying a crate. Show that the force exerted by the ground on the rear wheels is about 18 kN. Calculate the maximum mass of crate that the truck can carry without tipping forwards. The truck lifts a crate of mass 1200 kg vertically through 2.5 m at constant speed. This takes 4.0 s. Calculate the useful power output of the lifting mechanism.
items.ms: The resultant force (on the truck) is zero The resultant moment (about any point) is zero Use of W = mg Use of principle of moments about the front axle Force = 18.4 kN When the truck is about to tip, the force on the rear wheels is zero Use of principle of moments about the front axle: m × g × 0.95 = 3200 × g × 0.85 Maximum mass = 2860 kg Use of ΔEgrav = mgΔh and P = E/t P = 7.4 kW

path: Unit 1 Mechanics and Materials

items.question: A student is asked to determine the weight of a non-uniform wooden rod about 1 m long. She has a knife-edge pivot, a 200 g mass, some thread and a metre rule. State what is meant by the principle of moments. Describe how the student could locate the centre of gravity of the rod and then use the principle of moments to determine the weight of the rod. In one trial, the rod balanced horizontally with the 200 g mass hung 34.5 cm from the knife edge, as shown. The centre of gravity G of the rod was 21.0 cm from the knife edge, on the other side. Calculate the weight of the rod. Each distance was measured with an uncertainty of ±0.3 cm. The uncertainty in the mass is negligible. Determine the percentage uncertainty in the student's value for the weight of the rod.
items.ms: For a body in equilibrium, the sum of the clockwise moments about any point equals the sum of the anticlockwise moments about the same point IC1 Balance the rod (on its own) on the knife edge, adjusting its position until it is horizontal IC2 The centre of gravity is then directly above the knife edge: mark this point on the rod IC3 Hang the 200 g mass from the rod with a loop of thread and move the rod on the knife edge (or move the mass) until it balances horizontally again IC4 Use the metre rule to measure the distance d₁ from the knife edge to the thread and the distance d₂ from the knife edge to the centre of gravity mark IC5 Principle of moments: mgd₁ = Wd₂, so W = mgd₁ / d₂ with m = 0.200 kg IC6 Repeat with the mass at different positions and calculate a mean W (or plot d₁ against d₂: W = mg × gradient) Use of principle of moments: 0.200 × 9.81 × 0.345 = W × 0.210 W = 3.2 N Percentage uncertainty in either distance (0.87% or 1.4%) Percentage uncertainties of the two distances added Percentage uncertainty = 2.3%
items.why: The principle of moments was defined in Jun2025 and Oct2025, but the spec's suggested experiment to find the centre of gravity of an irregular rod has never been examined; 6-mark method questions are set (Jun2019 Q16(c), Jun2024 Q16(a)), and combining uncertainties is a unit skill.

items.question: A salt solution conducts electricity by the movement of ions. In 0.50 s, 2.5 × 10¹⁸ positive ions, each with a charge of +1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, cross a plane in the solution from left to right. In the same time, 2.5 × 10¹⁸ negative ions, each with a charge of −1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, cross the same plane from right to left. What is the current in the solution? 0 A 0.40 A 0.80 A 1.6 A
items.ms: Negative charge moving to the left has the same effect as positive charge moving to the right, so the two flows add: ΔQ = 2 × 2.5 × 10¹⁸ × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C = 0.80 C and I = ΔQ/Δt = 0.80 C ÷ 0.50 s = 1.6 A. A assumes the opposite charges cancel; B multiplies the charge by the time instead of dividing; C counts only one type of ion.
items.why: Every past S64 question used electrons in a metal; the spec says 'rate of flow of charged particles', so a current carried by ions of both signs is the likeliest untested angle.
