S64 - that electric current is the rate of flow of
items.question: A heart pacemaker sends short pulses of current to the heart. It is powered by a battery with a capacity of 1.8 A h. This means that the battery can deliver the same total charge as a current of 1.8 A for 1.0 hour. Show that the battery can deliver a total charge of about 6500 C. Each pulse is a current of 5.0 mA lasting 0.50 ms. Calculate the number of electrons that pass a point in the circuit during one pulse. The pacemaker produces 70 pulses every minute. Between pulses, its electronic circuit draws a constant current of 12 μA. Calculate the time for which the battery can operate the pacemaker. Give your answer in years. 1 year = 3.15 × 10⁷ s
items.ms: Use of ΔQ = IΔt with Δt = 3600 s ΔQ = 6480 C Use of ΔQ = IΔt (ΔQ = 2.5 × 10⁻⁶ C) and N = ΔQ/e N = 1.6 × 10¹³ Charge per minute from the pulses = 70 × 2.5 × 10⁻⁶ C = 1.75 × 10⁻⁴ C, or average current of the pulses = 2.9 × 10⁻⁶ A Total average current = 1.49 × 10⁻⁵ A (or total charge per minute = 8.95 × 10⁻⁴ C) used in Δt = ΔQ/I Δt = 4.3 × 10⁸ s = 14 years
items.why: S64 has come up in 11 of 21 sessions, with electron counts in structured parts (Jun2023 Q11a, Jun2021 Q18c, Oct2019 Q13b); a battery rated in ampere-hours and an average current from pulses have not yet been used.

path: Unit 2 Waves and Electricity
Electric Circuits
S65 - how to use the equation V  Q V
items.question: When a car engine is started, the p.d. across the starter motor is 12 V and 4.8 kJ of energy is transferred to the motor. How much charge flows through the starter motor? 2.5 × 10⁻³ C 0.40 C 400 C 5.8 × 10⁴ C
items.ms: V = W/Q, so Q = W/V = 4800 J ÷ 12 V = 400 C. A is V/W; B leaves the energy in kJ; D multiplies the energy by the p.d.
items.why: S65 MCQs ask for energy or charge from V = W/Q (Jun2025 Q8, Jan2023 Q9); one needing the rearrangement and a prefix conversion is the likely next form.

path: Unit 2 Waves and Electricity
Electric Circuits
S65 - how to use the equation V  Q V
items.question: In a spacecraft's ion engine, xenon ions are accelerated from rest through a potential difference of 3.0 kV. Each ion has a charge of +2e. What is the kinetic energy gained by each ion? 4.8 × 10⁻¹⁹ J 9.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J 4.8 × 10⁻¹⁶ J 9.6 × 10⁻¹⁶ J
items.ms: W = QV = 2 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C × 3.0 × 10³ V = 9.6 × 10⁻¹⁶ J, and all of this becomes kinetic energy. A uses a charge of e and the p.d. in kV; B uses 2e but leaves the p.d. in kV; C uses a charge of e.
items.why: Energy gained by a charge accelerated through a p.d. recurs in structured parts (Jan2026 Q14a, Oct2024 Q19d, Oct2023 Q15b), always for an electron; an ion of charge 2e in the spec's space-technology setting is untested.

path: Unit 2 Waves and Electricity
Electric Circuits
S65 - how to use the equation V  Q V
items.question: An electric eel stuns its prey by producing a potential difference of 650 V between its head and its tail. During one pulse, a charge of 1.4 × 10⁻³ C flows through the water around the eel. Calculate the energy transferred by the charge during the pulse.
items.ms: Use of V = W/Q W = 0.91 J
items.why: S65 structured parts are short energy-from-charge calculations (Jun2021 Q12c, Jun2023 Q11b, Oct2019 Q13a); an animal source of p.d. is the kind of unfamiliar context the Oct2022 examiners' report describes.

path: Unit 2 Waves and Electricity
Electric Circuits
S66 - that resistance is defined by R  and that Ohm
items.question: A student measures the current I in a component X for different potential differences V across it. The table shows her results. State Ohm's law. Deduce whether X obeys Ohm's law over the whole range of these readings.
items.ms: The current in a conductor is (directly) proportional to the potential difference across it, provided the temperature (and other physical conditions) stays constant Calculates V/I for at least two readings including one above 2.00 V, e.g. 5.00 Ω at 1.00 V and 6.80 Ω at 5.00 V; or shows that doubling V from 2.00 V to 4.00 V does not double I The resistance increases above 2.00 V (I is not proportional to V), so X does not obey Ohm's law over the whole range (only up to about 2 V)
items.why: S66 has been asked once in 21 sessions (Jun2021 Q11a) and Ohm's law has never been asked as a statement; a data test of whether a component is ohmic is its likeliest form.

path: Unit 2 Waves and Electricity
Electric Circuits
S67 - (a) understand how the distribution of curren
items.question: Four wires meet at a junction. The currents in three of the wires are: 0.45 A towards the junction 0.30 A away from the junction 0.12 A away from the junction. What is the current in the fourth wire? 0.03 A away from the junction 0.03 A towards the junction 0.27 A away from the junction 0.87 A away from the junction
items.ms: Charge is conserved, so the total current in equals the total current out: 0.45 A = 0.30 A + 0.12 A + I, so I = 0.03 A. It flows away from the junction because 0.45 A flows in but only 0.42 A flows out along the other two wires. B has the right size but the wrong direction; C treats the 0.12 A as flowing into the junction; D adds all three currents.
items.why: S67 MCQs (Jun2026 Q6, May2024 Q9) have used series p.d.s or one branch current; a junction with currents in both directions tests charge conservation itself.

path: Unit 2 Waves and Electricity
Electric Circuits
S67 - (a) understand how the distribution of curren
items.question: A student sets up the circuit shown. The battery has an e.m.f. of 6.0 V and negligible internal resistance. The table shows the readings on the meters. Explain how these readings are consistent with the conservation of charge and the conservation of energy.
items.ms: IC1 Current is the rate of flow of charge IC2 Charge is conserved, so the charge flowing into a junction each second equals the charge flowing out IC3 So the reading on A₁ equals the sum of the readings on A₂ and A₃: 0.20 A + 0.40 A = 0.60 A IC4 Potential difference is the energy transferred per unit charge (the e.m.f. is the energy given to each unit of charge by the battery) IC5 Energy is conserved, so the energy given to each coulomb by the battery equals the energy it transfers in the resistors round the circuit: 3.6 V + 2.4 V = 6.0 V IC6 Each coulomb passes through only one of R₂ and R₃, so (by energy conservation round each loop) the p.d. across R₃ is also 2.4 V / components in parallel have the same p.d.
items.why: Jun2022 Q15a set a 6-mark question on showing charge and energy conservation from measurements; giving the readings makes candidates use numbers, and the unit always has one 6-mark linkage question (Jun2023, Jun2024 ERs).

path: Unit 2 Waves and Electricity
Electric Circuits
S68 - derive the equations for combining resistance
items.question: A student has three identical resistors, each of resistance R. How should she connect all three resistors to make a combination of resistance 1.5R? two in parallel, with this pair in series with the third two in series, with this pair in parallel with the third all three in parallel all three in series
items.ms: Two in parallel give R/2; adding the third in series gives R/2 + R = 1.5R. B gives (2R × R)/(2R + R) = 2R/3; C gives R/3; D gives 3R.
items.why: S68 has come up in 17 of 21 sessions and MCQs on networks of identical resistors recur (Jan2025 Q6); choosing an arrangement for a target value has not been asked.

path: Unit 2 Waves and Electricity
Electric Circuits
S68 - derive the equations for combining resistance
items.question: Three resistors, each of resistance 6.0 Ω, are connected in a triangle as shown. What is the resistance between X and Y? 2.0 Ω 4.0 Ω 9.0 Ω 18 Ω
items.ms: Between X and Y there are two paths in parallel: the single 6.0 Ω resistor, and the other two in series (12 Ω). R = (6.0 × 12)/(6.0 + 12) = 4.0 Ω. A treats all three as in parallel; C puts two in parallel and adds the third; D adds all three.
items.why: Network MCQs ask for the resistance between two terminals (Oct2024 Q8, May2024 Q7); a triangle, where the candidate must first see which resistors are in series, is a plausible next layout.

path: Unit 2 Waves and Electricity
Electric Circuits
S68 - derive the equations for combining resistance
items.question: A 100 Ω resistor is connected in parallel with a resistor of unknown resistance. Which statement about the resistance of the combination must be correct? It is less than 50 Ω. It is less than 100 Ω. It is between 50 Ω and 100 Ω. It is greater than 100 Ω.
items.ms: A parallel path always lowers the resistance below that of each branch, so the combination is less than 100 Ω whatever the other resistor is. A is true only if the unknown resistance is less than 100 Ω; C only if it is greater than 100 Ω; D would need a parallel combination to exceed one of its branches, which never happens.
items.why: Oct2021 Q15b(ii) rewarded 'a parallel combination is always less than the smallest resistor'; a reasoning MCQ on that rule is a likely S68 variation.

path: Unit 2 Waves and Electricity
Electric Circuits
S68 - derive the equations for combining resistance
items.question: Resistors can be combined in series and in parallel. Two resistors, of resistance R₁ and R₂, are connected in series with a battery. Use the conservation of charge and the conservation of energy to derive the formula for their total resistance R. A uniform resistance wire of resistance 16.0 Ω is bent into a circle and its ends are joined. Connections are made to the ring at points P and Q. The shorter arc between P and Q is one quarter of the circumference, as shown. Calculate the resistance between P and Q. Q is moved around the ring. The resistance between P and Q is greatest when PQ is a diameter of the ring. Deduce whether the resistance between P and Q could be 5.0 Ω.
items.ms: Charge is conserved, so the current I is the same in both resistors Energy is conserved, so the total p.d. V = V₁ + V₂ IR = IR₁ + IR₂, and dividing by I gives R = R₁ + R₂ Resistances of the two arcs: 4.0 Ω and 12.0 Ω (resistance proportional to length) R = 3.0 Ω Greatest resistance = 8.0 Ω in parallel with 8.0 Ω = 4.0 Ω 4.0 Ω is less than 5.0 Ω, so the resistance can never be 5.0 Ω
items.why: Derivations of the combination formulae have been set three times (Jun2019 Q15a, Oct2021 Q15a, Oct2023 Q12), the series one only in 2019; the ring of wire joins S68 to resistance ∝ length in a layout not yet used.

path: Unit 2 Waves and Electricity
Electric Circuits
S68 - derive the equations for combining resistance
items.question: A student connects two resistors, R₁ and R₂, each of resistance 220 kΩ, in series with a 6.0 V battery of negligible internal resistance. She calculates that the p.d. across R₂ is 3.0 V. She then connects a voltmeter of resistance 680 kΩ across R₂, as shown. Show that the resistance of R₂ and the voltmeter together is about 170 kΩ. Calculate the reading on the voltmeter. Explain why connecting the voltmeter reduces the p.d. across R₂ below 3.0 V. The student replaces the voltmeter with a digital voltmeter of resistance 10 MΩ. She wants the reading to be within 2% of 3.0 V. Deduce whether this voltmeter is suitable.
items.ms: Use of 1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ R = 166 kΩ Total resistance = 220 kΩ + 166 kΩ = 386 kΩ Use of I = V/R (I = 1.55 × 10⁻⁵ A) and V = IR, or of the ratio VR2/V = R/Rtotal V = 2.58 V The voltmeter is in parallel with R₂, so the resistance of that section of the circuit decreases So the current in the circuit increases and the p.d. across R₁ increases The p.d.s across R₁ and across the parallel section still add up to 6.0 V (energy conservation), so the p.d. across R₂ decreases Combined resistance of R₂ and the voltmeter = 215 kΩ V = 2.97 V Percentage difference = (3.0 − 2.97)/3.0 × 100% = 1.1%, which is less than 2%, so the voltmeter is suitable
items.why: Series–parallel calculations are in almost every paper (Jun2026 Q12, Jun2025 Q16b, Oct2022 Q13a); the effect of a voltmeter's own resistance has only appeared as an evaluation point (Oct2020 Q12b), so a calculation on it is a likely surprise.

path: Unit 2 Waves and Electricity
Electric Circuits
S68 - derive the equations for combining resistance
items.question: A heated jacket contains two identical heating pads, A and B. Each pad has a resistance of 4.0 Ω. The pads are powered by a 7.4 V battery of negligible internal resistance. The diagram shows how the pads are connected for the three settings X, Y and Z. Show that the power output on setting Z is about 27 W. Explain why the power output on setting X is one quarter of the power output on setting Z. The fully charged battery can deliver a total charge of 1.8 × 10⁴ C. Calculate the maximum time for which the jacket can run on setting Z. Each pad is a strip of carbon-fibre fabric 1.20 m long, 15 mm wide and 0.30 mm thick. The current flows along the length of the strip. Calculate the resistivity of the material of the pad. The battery has a safety circuit that switches it off if the current exceeds 5.0 A. The manufacturer considers adding a third identical pad in parallel with A and B on setting Z. Deduce whether the jacket would still work on setting Z.
items.ms: Use of 1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ (R = 2.0 Ω) Use of P = V²/R (or I = V/R and P = VI) P = 27.4 W On X the resistance is 2R (8.0 Ω) and on Z it is R/2 (2.0 Ω), so the resistance on X is four times the resistance on Z The p.d. across the combination of pads is 7.4 V (the battery p.d.) on both settings P = V²/R, so with V constant, P is inversely proportional to R (four times the resistance gives one quarter of the power) Use of I = V/R or I = P/V (I = 3.7 A) Use of ΔQ = IΔt Δt = 4.9 × 10³ s A = 15 × 10⁻³ m × 0.30 × 10⁻³ m = 4.5 × 10⁻⁶ m² Use of R = ρl/A ρ = 1.5 × 10⁻⁵ Ω m Use of the parallel formula: R = 1.33 Ω (or current in each pad = 1.85 A) I = 5.55 A 5.6 A is greater than 5.0 A, so the safety circuit would switch the battery off: the jacket would not work
items.why: S68 is the most examined point in the topic (17 of 21 sessions, 5.3% of marks), usually as a long series–parallel question with power (Oct2025 Q18, Jan2026 Q14b, Jun2025 Q16b); a switchable heater with a current limit adds the 'deduce whether' ending the mark schemes reward.

path: Unit 2 Waves and Electricity
Electric Circuits
S69 - use the equations P  VI, W  VIt and be able t
items.question: Resistors of resistance R and 2R are connected in parallel across a cell of negligible internal resistance. Which row gives (current in R) : (current in 2R) and (power in R) : (power in 2R)? currents 2 : 1; powers 2 : 1 currents 2 : 1; powers 4 : 1 currents 1 : 2; powers 1 : 2 currents 1 : 2; powers 1 : 4
items.ms: The p.d. V is the same across both, so I = V/R gives currents 2 : 1 and P = V²/R gives powers 2 : 1 (check: P = I²R gives 4R : 1 × 2R = 2 : 1). B squares the current ratio but forgets that the resistances differ; C and D use the series idea that the larger resistor takes the larger share.
items.why: S69 MCQs compare powers in two resistors (Oct2024 Q10, in series); the parallel case, where the smaller resistor dissipates more, is the natural pair to it.

path: Unit 2 Waves and Electricity
Electric Circuits
S69 - use the equations P  VI, W  VIt and be able t
items.question: A filament lamp is rated 12 V, 36 W. It is connected to a 6.0 V supply. Which statement about the power of the lamp is correct? It is less than 9.0 W. It is 9.0 W. It is between 9.0 W and 18 W. It is 18 W.
items.ms: At 12 V, R = V²/P = 4.0 Ω and I = 3.0 A. At 6.0 V the filament is cooler, so its resistance is less than 4.0 Ω and P = V²/R is more than 6.0²/4.0 = 9.0 W. The current at 6.0 V is less than 3.0 A, so P = VI is less than 18 W. B assumes constant resistance; A assumes the resistance increases at lower p.d.; D assumes the current stays 3.0 A.
items.why: Oct2019 Q8 used P ∝ V² at constant resistance; combining it with the lower resistance of a cooler filament (S70) is the obvious harder version.

path: Unit 2 Waves and Electricity
Electric Circuits
S69 - use the equations P  VI, W  VIt and be able t
items.question: An electric car is charged at home from a 230 V supply. The charger takes a power of 7.4 kW. Calculate the current in the cable to the charger. The cable contains two copper conductors, each 18 m long with a cross-sectional area of 6.0 mm². The current flows to the charger along one conductor and back along the other. resistivity of copper = 1.7 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m Calculate the power dissipated in the cable. Explain why it is better to supply a given power at a higher p.d.
items.ms: Use of P = VI I = 32 A A = 6.0 × 10⁻⁶ m² Use of R = ρl/A (R = 0.102 Ω with l = 36 m) Use of P = I²R P = 106 W For the same power, a higher p.d. means a smaller current (P = VI) The power dissipated in the cables is I²R, so less energy is wasted (for the same cable resistance)
items.why: S69 comes up in about half of sessions, mostly as power or energy from VI, I²R or V²/R (Jun2026 Q11, Oct2025 Q12a); power wasted in connecting cables, which needs R = ρl/A first, is a likely synoptic version.

path: Unit 2 Waves and Electricity
Electric Circuits
S70 - how to sketch, recognise and interpret curren
items.question: The graph shows how the potential difference V across a component varies with the current I in it. Which component is it? diode filament lamp ohmic conductor thermistor
items.ms: Here V is on the vertical axis. V/I increases as I increases (the graph gets steeper), so the resistance rises with current, in both directions: a filament lamp. D comes from reading the graph as if I were on the vertical axis (a thermistor's I–V graph has this shape); C would be a straight line; A would show almost no current for one polarity.
items.why: Identifying a component from its graph is the commonest S70 MCQ (Jan2026 Q1, Oct2025 Q1, Jan2023 Q1, Jan2022 Q8); every past version put I on the vertical axis, so swapped axes are the likeliest twist.

path: Unit 2 Waves and Electricity
Electric Circuits
S70 - how to sketch, recognise and interpret curren
items.question: Which row describes how the resistance of each component changes as the current in it increases? filament lamp: increases; NTC thermistor: increases filament lamp: decreases; NTC thermistor: decreases filament lamp: increases; NTC thermistor: decreases filament lamp: decreases; NTC thermistor: increases
items.ms: A larger current heats both components. In the metal filament the ions vibrate more, so electrons collide with them more often and the resistance increases. In an NTC thermistor more conduction electrons are released as the temperature rises, so the resistance decreases. A, B and D get one or both of these wrong.
items.why: S70 has come up in 16 of 21 sessions; the Oct2019 examiners' report notes candidates swapping lamp and thermistor behaviour, so a two-column row MCQ on both is likely.

path: Unit 2 Waves and Electricity
Electric Circuits
S70 - how to sketch, recognise and interpret curren
items.question: The graph shows the current–potential difference characteristic of a filament lamp. The lamp is connected in parallel with a 15 Ω resistor across a 6.0 V supply of negligible internal resistance. What is the current from the supply? 0.10 A 0.40 A 0.50 A 0.90 A
items.ms: Both have 6.0 V across them. From the graph the lamp current at 6.0 V is 0.50 A; the resistor current is 6.0 V ÷ 15 Ω = 0.40 A. Charge conservation at the junction gives 0.50 A + 0.40 A = 0.90 A. A subtracts the currents; B is the resistor alone; C is the lamp alone.
items.why: Reading an I–V graph and using it in a circuit is set in structured parts (Oct2024 Q14b, Jun2023 Q16); an MCQ joining it to a parallel resistor is a likely compact version.

path: Unit 2 Waves and Electricity
Electric Circuits
S70 - how to sketch, recognise and interpret curren
items.question: A student investigates how the current I in a filament lamp varies with the potential difference V across it. The table shows her results. Plot a graph of I against V on the grid. Use your graph to determine the resistance of the lamp when the p.d. across it is 2.5 V. Explain the shape of the graph.
items.ms: Axes labelled with quantities and units, with a sensible scale (points cover more than half the grid) All points plotted accurately (to within half a small square) Smooth curve of best fit through the origin Current read from the graph at 2.5 V (0.37–0.39 A) R = V/I = 6.5 Ω IC1 As the p.d. increases the current increases, but by smaller amounts for equal increases in p.d. (the gradient decreases) IC2 So V/I, the resistance of the filament, increases IC3 A larger current transfers more energy per second in the filament (P = VI), so its temperature rises IC4 The metal ions (the lattice) vibrate with greater amplitude IC5 The conduction electrons collide with the ions more often IC6 n is constant in a metal, so by I = nqvA the lower drift velocity gives less current than if the resistance had stayed constant
items.why: S70 has come up in 16 of 21 sessions, mostly as MCQs; the filament explanation was the Jan2021 Q16 6-marker and the sketch Jun2022 Q13a, while plotting I–V data and reading R = V/I from the curve has not been set.

items.name: Resistivity, R = ρl/A
path: Unit 2 Waves and Electricity
Electric Circuits
S71 - use the equation R  A
items.question: Wire X and wire Y are made of the same metal. Y is twice as long as X and has half the diameter of X. What is (resistance of Y) ÷ (resistance of X)? 1 2 4 8
items.ms: R = ρl/A with A = πd²/4. Halving d makes A one quarter, so R is 4 times larger; doubling l doubles R: 2 × 4 = 8. A treats R as proportional to l × d; B allows for the length only; C halves the area instead of quartering it.
items.why: Ratio questions on R = ρl/A recur in MCQs (Jun2026 Q9, Jan2025 Q8); halving the diameter tests the d² dependence, the error the Jun2019 examiners' report describes.

items.name: Resistivity, R = ρl/A
path: Unit 2 Waves and Electricity
Electric Circuits
S71 - use the equation R  A
items.question: Which unit is equivalent to the unit of resistivity? V m A⁻¹ V A⁻¹ m⁻¹ W m A⁻¹ J m C⁻¹
items.ms: ρ = RA/l, so its unit is Ω m² m⁻¹ = Ω m, and Ω = V A⁻¹, giving V m A⁻¹. B is the unit of resistance per unit length (Ω m⁻¹); C and D are both equivalent to V m, because W A⁻¹ and J C⁻¹ are both the volt.
items.why: 'Which unit is equivalent to …' MCQs appear most years (Jan2026 Q1, Jun2025 Q3, Oct2022 Q10, Jan2022 Q1) but have only used the volt and the coulomb; the unit of resistivity, often confused with Ω m⁻¹, is next in line.

items.name: Resistivity, R = ρl/A
path: Unit 2 Waves and Electricity
Electric Circuits
S71 - use the equation R  A
items.question: A rectangular block of conducting rubber has sides of length a, 2a and 4a. The resistance between each pair of opposite faces is measured. What is (largest resistance) ÷ (smallest resistance)? 2 4 8 16
items.ms: Largest: current along the 4a side, through a cross-section a × 2a: R = ρ × 4a/(2a²) = 2ρ/a. Smallest: current along the a side, through 2a × 4a: R = ρa/(8a²) = ρ/(8a). Ratio = 16. B uses only the ratio of the lengths (or only of the areas); A and C pair a length with the wrong face.
items.why: Oct2025 Q6 asked for the resistivity of a cube; a block with unequal sides, where both length and area change with the direction of the current, is the natural harder version.

items.name: Resistivity, R = ρl/A
path: Unit 2 Waves and Electricity
Electric Circuits
S71 - use the equation R  A
items.question: On a printed circuit board, components are connected by thin tracks of copper on an insulating board. The diagram shows one track (not to scale). resistivity of copper = 1.7 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m Calculate the resistance of the track. Another track of the same length and thickness must carry a current of 3.0 A with a p.d. across it of no more than 0.18 V. Determine the minimum width of this track. Some circuit boards use copper 70 μm thick. Suggest an advantage of using thicker copper.
items.ms: A = 0.40 × 10⁻³ m × 35 × 10⁻⁶ m = 1.4 × 10⁻⁸ m² Use of R = ρl/A R = 0.146 Ω R = V/I = 0.060 Ω Use of R = ρl/A to find A (3.4 × 10⁻⁸ m²) width = 9.7 × 10⁻⁴ m (0.97 mm) Doubling the thickness doubles the cross-sectional area, so (for the same width) the resistance halves So tracks can be narrower for the same resistance or current, and more tracks fit on the board Less power is dissipated in each track (P = I²R), so it heats up less
items.why: Rectangular cross-sections (width × thickness) have appeared in five recent S71 questions (Oct2023, Oct2024, Jun2024, Jan2026, Jun2026), and the reports flag area errors each time; a design calculation for a minimum width has not been set.

items.name: Resistivity, R = ρl/A
path: Unit 2 Waves and Electricity
Electric Circuits
S71 - use the equation R  A
items.question: An overhead power cable is made of strands of aluminium and steel twisted together. The diagram shows a cross-section of the cable, which has 26 aluminium strands and 7 steel strands. Each strand has a diameter of 3.0 mm. Treat each strand as a straight wire and assume that all the strands are connected in parallel. resistivity of aluminium = 2.8 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m resistivity of steel = 1.8 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m Show that the resistance of a 1.0 km length of one aluminium strand is about 4 Ω. Calculate the resistance of a 1.0 km length of the whole cable. Explain why the steel strands make very little difference to the resistance of the cable. The cable carries a current of 650 A. Calculate the power dissipated in a 1.0 km length of the cable. On a hot day the temperature of the cable is higher. Explain why more power is dissipated in the cable for the same current.
items.ms: Use of A = πd²/4 (A = 7.07 × 10⁻⁶ m²) Use of R = ρl/A with l = 1000 m R = 3.96 Ω Resistance of one steel strand = 25.5 Ω Use of R/n for n identical strands in parallel (0.152 Ω and 3.64 Ω), or of 1/R = Σ1/R Use of the parallel formula to combine the aluminium and the steel R = 0.146 Ω The steel strands together have a much greater resistance (3.6 Ω) than the aluminium strands together (0.15 Ω), because steel has a greater resistivity and there are fewer steel strands In parallel the combined resistance is close to the smaller resistance / almost all the current flows in the aluminium Use of P = I²R P = 6.2 × 10⁴ W At a higher temperature the metal ions vibrate with greater amplitude, so the electrons collide with them more often and the resistance increases P = I²R with I unchanged, so the power dissipated increases
items.why: S71 has come up in 16 of 21 sessions, often with an unusual cross-section (Oct2024 Q15a, Jan2026 Q15a, Jun2026 Q17a); a multi-strand cable joins R = ρl/A to the parallel formula, the pairing in the Jun2026 Q17 long question.

path: Unit 2 Waves and Electricity

items.question: In an experiment to determine the resistivity ρ of a metal, a student measures the resistance R of different lengths l of a wire of cross-sectional area A. Which graph would be a straight line with a gradient equal to ρ? R against l R against 1/A RA against l l against RA
items.ms: R = ρl/A gives RA = ρl, so a graph of RA against l is a straight line through the origin with gradient ρ. A has gradient ρ/A; B would need wires of different areas, and its gradient would be ρl; D has gradient 1/ρ.
items.why: CP7 graph questions accept several choices of axes (Oct2019 Q15b) but each needs the gradient identified; no MCQ has yet tested this, and CP7 has not been examined since Jan2021.

path: Unit 2 Waves and Electricity
Electric Circuits
S72 - CORE PRACTICAL 7 Determine the electrical res
items.question: A student determines the resistivity of constantan. She connects a constantan wire to an ohmmeter using two leads with crocodile clips, and measures the resistance R between the clips for different lengths l of the wire. Describe how she should measure the diameter of the wire to obtain an accurate value. The mean diameter of the wire is 0.28 mm. The graph shows her results. Use the graph to determine the resistivity of constantan. The line of best fit does not pass through the origin. Explain the cause of this, and why it does not affect the value of resistivity she found.
items.ms: Use a micrometer screw gauge (or digital callipers) Take readings at several places along the wire, and in different directions, and calculate a mean Check for, and correct, any zero error Gradient found using a large triangle (8.0 Ω m⁻¹) A = πd²/4 = 6.16 × 10⁻⁸ m² ρ = gradient × A ρ = 4.9 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m The intercept is due to the resistance of the leads and crocodile clips (contact resistance) or a zero error on the ohmmeter This adds the same resistance to every reading (a systematic error) So the gradient is unchanged, and ρ is found from the gradient A single value of R/l would give a value of ρ that is too large
items.why: CP7 has been examined in only 2 of 21 sessions, last in Jan2021, although a core practical appears in almost every paper; the method (Oct2019 Q15a, Jun2024 Q14a) and the gradient (Jan2021 Q19b) recur, while the meaning of the intercept has not been asked.

S73 - use I  nqvA to explain the large range of res
items.question: A copper wire of diameter 0.80 mm carries a current of 2.0 A. The number of conduction electrons per unit volume in copper is 8.5 × 10²⁸ m⁻³. What is the drift velocity of the electrons? 7.3 × 10⁻⁵ m s⁻¹ 2.3 × 10⁻⁴ m s⁻¹ 2.9 × 10⁻⁴ m s⁻¹ 9.2 × 10⁻⁴ m s⁻¹
items.ms: A = π(0.40 × 10⁻³ m)² = 5.0 × 10⁻⁷ m²; v = I/(nqA) = 2.0/(8.5 × 10²⁸ × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 5.0 × 10⁻⁷) = 2.9 × 10⁻⁴ m s⁻¹. A uses the diameter as the radius; B uses A = d² (no π/4); D uses A = r² (no π).
items.why: Drift-velocity calculations have come up in 8 sessions (Jan2026 Q11, Oct2025 Q11, Jun2019 Q12b); the Jan2021 examiners' report lists using the diameter as the radius and forgetting π as the main errors.

path: Unit 2 Waves and Electricity
Electric Circuits
S73 - use I  nqvA to explain the large range of res
items.question: Which statement best explains why the resistivity of a polymer insulator is very much greater than the resistivity of copper? The number of charge carriers per unit volume is very much smaller in the insulator. The drift velocity of the charge carriers is very much greater in the insulator. The ions in the insulator vibrate with a much larger amplitude. The insulator has a much smaller cross-sectional area.
items.ms: By I = nqvA, for a given drift velocity and area the current is proportional to n. An insulator has very few free charge carriers per unit volume, so for the same p.d. its current is tiny and its resistivity is huge. B would make the current larger; C is a small effect that also happens in metals and cannot explain a factor of more than 10²⁰; D: resistivity does not depend on the size of the sample.
items.why: The S73 spec asks candidates to 'explain the large range of resistivities', but past questions have compared only metals (Oct2024 Q12, Jan2024 Q16c); the insulator–metal comparison is the untested half.

S73 - use I  nqvA to explain the large range of res
items.question: Wire X is connected across a cell of negligible internal resistance. It is then replaced by wire Y, made of the same metal. Y is twice as long as X and has twice the diameter of X. What is (drift velocity of electrons in Y) ÷ (drift velocity of electrons in X)? 0.25 0.5 1 2
items.ms: Y has resistance ρ(2l)/(4A), half that of X, so with the same p.d. the current in Y is twice that in X. v = I/(nqA) with n and q unchanged: v(Y)/v(X) = 2/4 = 0.5. A allows for the larger area but not the larger current; C assumes the drift velocity depends only on the metal; D allows for the larger current but not the larger area.
items.why: Jun2026 Q7 and Jun2025 Q10 compared drift velocities in wires in series; with the same p.d. across one wire, as in Jan2022 Q11c, v depends only on the length, a result no MCQ has yet tested.

path: Unit 2 Waves and Electricity
Electric Circuits
S73 - use I  nqvA to explain the large range of res
items.question: A car's brake lamp is connected to the 12 V battery by a copper cable 4.5 m long. The copper conductor in the cable has a cross-sectional area of 1.0 mm². The lamp is rated 12 V, 21 W. number of conduction electrons per unit volume in copper = 8.5 × 10²⁸ m⁻³ Calculate the drift velocity of the conduction electrons in the cable when the lamp is working normally. When the driver presses the brake pedal, a switch closes and the lamp lights almost at once. A student says that the lamp should not light until about 10 hours after the switch closes, because electrons must travel 4.5 m along the cable. Show how the student obtained this time. Explain why the lamp lights almost as soon as the switch closes. The tungsten filament of the lamp has a much smaller cross-sectional area than the cable. The number of conduction electrons per unit volume in tungsten is similar to that in copper. Explain why the drift velocity in the filament is much greater than in the cable. Silicon is a semiconductor. Its resistivity is very much greater than that of copper. Explain, using I = nqvA, why the resistivity of silicon is very much greater.
items.ms: Use of P = VI (I = 1.75 A) Use of I = nqvA with A = 1.0 × 10⁻⁶ m² v = 1.3 × 10⁻⁴ m s⁻¹ Use of time = distance ÷ drift velocity with 4.5 m t = 3.5 × 10⁴ s = 9.7 hours The cable and the filament are already full of free (conduction) electrons When the switch closes, electrons all round the circuit, including those in the filament, start to drift at (almost) the same time So no electron needs to travel from the switch to the lamp before the lamp lights The current in the filament is the same as the current in the cable (they are in series / charge is conserved) I = nqvA with n and q about the same, so a much smaller A means a much greater v The number of charge carriers per unit volume, n, is very much smaller in silicon So for the same p.d. and dimensions (similar drift velocity), the current is very much smaller, so the resistance and therefore the resistivity are very much greater
items.why: S73 has come up in 20 of 21 sessions, usually as a drift-velocity calculation (Jan2026 Q11, Oct2025 Q11) or a wire comparison (Oct2024 Q12); the slow drift against the instant lamp (an Oct2019 report note) and the semiconductor half of the spec statement have not been asked.

S33 - the terms amplitude, frequency, period, speed
items.question: The diagram shows the trace on an oscilloscope screen when a microphone detects the sound from a loudspeaker. The time-base is set to 2.0 ms div⁻¹ and the Y-gain is set to 0.50 V div⁻¹. Which of the following gives the amplitude of the voltage signal and the frequency of the sound? amplitude 1.5 V; frequency 250 Hz amplitude 3.0 V; frequency 125 Hz amplitude 3.0 V; frequency 250 Hz amplitude 1.5 V; frequency 125 Hz
items.ms: Amplitude = 3.0 div × 0.50 V div⁻¹ = 1.5 V (centre line to peak). One cycle occupies 4.0 div, so T = 4.0 × 2.0 ms = 8.0 ms and f = 1/T = 125 Hz. B and C use the peak-to-peak height (6.0 div) as the amplitude; A and C take half a cycle (peak to trough, 2.0 div) as the period.
items.why: S33 MCQs that read the period from an oscilloscope trace recur (Oct2025 Q3, Jan2024 Q7); reading the amplitude from the Y-gain alongside it has not been asked.

S33 - the terms amplitude, frequency, period, speed
items.question: A fishing float bobs up and down as water waves pass it. The float moves through a vertical distance of 0.24 m between its highest and lowest positions. It makes 18 complete oscillations in 45 s. State the amplitude of the oscillation of the float. Calculate the frequency of the waves.
items.ms: Amplitude = 0.12 m f = 18 ÷ 45 s = 0.40 Hz
items.why: S33 has come up in 8 of 21 sessions, mostly as short items; Oct2024 and Oct2025 both open the structured section with a 2-mark question, and amplitude as half the peak-to-peak movement has not been asked directly.

path: Unit 2 Waves and Electricity
Waves and Particle Nature of Light
S34 - use the wave equation v  f
items.question: A sound wave of wavelength 0.85 m in air passes into water. The speed of sound is 330 m s⁻¹ in air and 1480 m s⁻¹ in water. What is the wavelength of the sound in the water? 0.19 m 0.85 m 3.8 m 4.5 m
items.ms: The frequency does not change when the wave enters the water: f = 330/0.85 = 388 Hz, so λ = 1480/388 = 3.8 m. A uses the ratio of the speeds the wrong way up (0.85 × 330/1480); B assumes the wavelength does not change; D is just the ratio of the speeds (1480/330), not a wavelength.
items.why: S34 has come up in 6 of 21 sessions; Jun2023 Q3 tested only as a statement that frequency is unchanged in a new medium, and the Jan2020 report found candidates lose marks on exactly this point.

path: Unit 2 Waves and Electricity
Waves and Particle Nature of Light
S34 - use the wave equation v  f
items.question: A tsunami is a water wave produced by an undersea earthquake. In water of depth d, a tsunami travels with speed v given by v = √(gd) A tsunami crosses an ocean where the depth of the water is 4000 m. The period of the tsunami is 12 minutes. Show that the speed of the tsunami in the ocean is about 200 m s⁻¹. Calculate the wavelength of the tsunami in the ocean. As the tsunami approaches the coast, the depth of the water decreases. Explain why the wavelength of the tsunami decreases.
items.ms: Use of v = √(gd) v = 198 m s⁻¹ Use of v = fλ with f = 1/T (or λ = vT) and T = 720 s λ = 1.43 × 10⁵ m The frequency (and period) of the wave does not change, because it is set by the source (the earthquake) The speed decreases as the depth decreases (v = √(gd)), and λ = v/f, so the wavelength decreases
items.why: S34 has come up in 6 of 21 sessions and Jan2020 Q15 gave water-wave speed formulas in the stem; the unchanged frequency on entering a new medium is the error the Jan2020 report highlights.

Waves and Particle Nature of Light
S35 - describe longitudinal waves in terms of press
items.question: A loudspeaker produces a sound of frequency 425 Hz in air. The speed of sound in air is 340 m s⁻¹. What is the distance between the centre of a compression and the centre of the nearest rarefaction? 0.20 m 0.40 m 0.80 m 1.6 m
items.ms: λ = v/f = 340/425 = 0.80 m. A compression and the nearest rarefaction are half a wavelength apart, 0.40 m. A is a quarter of a wavelength (the distance from a compression to a point of maximum displacement); C is the distance between neighbouring compressions; D is two wavelengths.
items.why: S35 has come up in 8 of 21 sessions, almost always as an MCQ (Jun2026 Q3, Jan2026 Q10, Oct2025 Q2 and Q4); Oct2021 Q10 used the spacing of compressions, but the compression-to-rarefaction spacing has not been asked.

S35 - describe longitudinal waves in terms of press
items.question: A loudspeaker sends a sound wave along a tube of air. The diagram shows the positions of layers of air molecules in the tube at one instant. Before the sound arrived, the layers were evenly spaced. P, Q and R are positions along the tube. Describe how the air molecules in the tube move as the sound wave passes. State which of P, Q and R is at the centre of a rarefaction. State the displacement of the layer of air molecules at P at this instant. Use the diagram to determine the frequency of the sound. speed of sound in air = 340 m s⁻¹
items.ms: The molecules oscillate (vibrate) about their equilibrium (undisturbed) positions The oscillations are parallel to the direction in which the wave travels (energy is transferred) R Zero (the layer at the centre of a compression is at its undisturbed position) λ read from the diagram as the distance between the centres of two compressions (or two rarefactions): λ = 0.50 m Use of v = fλ f = 680 Hz
items.why: S35 has come up in 8 of 21 sessions but only once as a structured question (Oct2019 Q19a, a diagram of displaced molecules); a layer diagram with pressure, displacement and wavelength questions is the likeliest longer form.

path: Unit 2 Waves and Electricity
Waves and Particle Nature of Light
S36 - describe transverse waves
items.question: A transverse wave travels from left to right along a stretched rope. At one instant, point P on the rope is at a crest. Point Q is a quarter of a wavelength to the right of P and is at its equilibrium position. Which of the following describes the motion of P and Q at this instant? P is momentarily at rest; Q is moving upwards P is momentarily at rest; Q is moving downwards P is moving upwards; Q is momentarily at rest P is moving downwards; Q is momentarily at rest
items.ms: At a crest the displacement is a maximum, so P is momentarily at rest. The crest at P is moving to the right towards Q, so Q is about to rise: it is moving upwards (at its maximum speed). B gives Q's motion for a wave travelling to the left; C and D treat the point at maximum displacement as moving and the point at equilibrium as stationary, which is the wrong way round.
items.why: S36 has come up in 7 of 21 sessions; Oct2024 Q9 asked about the motion of two points as a transverse wave passes, and comparing a point at a crest with one at equilibrium has not been asked.

path: Unit 2 Waves and Electricity
Waves and Particle Nature of Light
S36 - describe transverse waves
items.question: A student holds one end of a long spring (a 'slinky') stretched along a smooth bench. The other end of the spring is fixed. State what is meant by a transverse wave. Describe how the student could use the spring to show the difference between a transverse wave and a longitudinal wave.
items.ms: The oscillations (vibrations) are perpendicular to the direction of wave travel (energy transfer) Transverse: move the end of the spring from side to side (perpendicular to its length), so the coils oscillate perpendicular to the direction the wave travels along the spring Longitudinal: move the end of the spring backwards and forwards along its length, so the coils oscillate parallel to the direction the wave travels (forming compressions and rarefactions) In both cases the coils return to their original positions; only energy travels along the spring
items.why: 'State what is meant by a transverse wave' was asked in four of the last eight sessions (Jan2024, Oct2024, Jan2025, Jan2026); the contrast with longitudinal waves was last asked in Jan2022 Q16a.

path: Unit 2 Waves and Electricity

S37 - draw and interpret graphs representing transv
items.question: An athlete trains by moving one end of a long heavy rope up and down. A transverse wave travels along the rope, away from the athlete. The displacement–distance graph shows the displacement y of the rope against the distance x from the athlete's hand at time t = 0. The wave travels in the direction of increasing x. The displacement–time graph shows how the displacement of point P on the rope varies with time, starting at t = 0. Determine the speed of the wave. On the displacement–distance graph, draw the shape of the rope at t = 0.10 s. The far end of the rope is then tied to a post. A stationary wave forms on the rope. State two differences between the motion of points on the rope in the stationary wave and in the progressive wave.
items.ms: λ = 2.8 m (read from the displacement–distance graph) T = 0.40 s (read from the displacement–time graph) Use of v = fλ with f = 1/T (or v = λ/T) v = 7.0 m s⁻¹ Sinusoidal curve with the same amplitude (15 cm) and wavelength (2.8 m) Curve shifted by 0.70 m (a quarter of a wavelength) in the direction of increasing x: crests at x = 1.4 m and 4.2 m (troughs at 2.8 m and 5.6 m) In the stationary wave the amplitude varies along the rope (zero at nodes, maximum at antinodes); in the progressive wave all points oscillate with the same amplitude In the stationary wave all points between two adjacent nodes oscillate in phase (and in antiphase with the next section); in the progressive wave the phase changes continuously along the rope
items.why: S37 has only been asked as MCQs (Jun2026 Q1, Oct2023 Q5, Oct2020 Q1) on which graph gives which quantity; a structured question that combines both graphs to find a speed and asks for a drawn shift is the likeliest new form.

path: Unit 2 Waves and Electricity
Waves and Particle Nature of Light
S38 - CORE PRACTICAL 4 Determine the speed of sound
items.question: A student determines the speed of sound in air using a loudspeaker, a microphone, a signal generator and a two-beam oscilloscope. She moves the microphone away from the loudspeaker and measures the distance between positions at which the two traces are in phase. Which change would reduce the percentage uncertainty in her value for the wavelength? Increase the frequency of the sound. Increase the amplitude of the sound. Start with the microphone closer to the loudspeaker. Measure the distance moved while the traces come back into phase ten times, and divide by ten.
items.ms: The distance moved over ten wavelengths is ten times longer but has the same absolute uncertainty in the positions, so the percentage uncertainty is ten times smaller. A makes the wavelength shorter, so the same uncertainty in position is a larger percentage of it; B changes the height of the traces but not the distance measured; C does not change the distance moved between in-phase positions or its uncertainty.
items.why: Core Practical 4 was asked in Jun2021 and Oct2019; the Oct2019 mark scheme turned on the same length uncertainty being a larger percentage of a shorter wavelength.

path: Unit 2 Waves and Electricity
Waves and Particle Nature of Light
S38 - CORE PRACTICAL 4 Determine the speed of sound
items.question: A student uses the apparatus shown to determine the speed of sound in air. The loudspeaker is connected to a signal generator. The loudspeaker signal and the microphone signal are both displayed on a two-beam oscilloscope. The microphone can be moved along a tape measure fixed to the bench in line with the loudspeaker. Describe how the student should use the apparatus to obtain an accurate value for the wavelength of the sound. The student does not rely on the frequency scale of the signal generator. The diagram shows the oscilloscope screen when the two traces are in phase. The time-base is set to 0.25 ms div⁻¹. Determine the frequency of the sound. The student records the position of the microphone when the traces are in phase. She then moves the microphone away from the loudspeaker until the traces have come back into phase five times. The two readings of the microphone position are 11.8 cm and 149.0 cm. Calculate the speed of sound in air. Each reading of the microphone position has an uncertainty of ±0.5 cm. Calculate the percentage uncertainty in the student's value for the wavelength.
items.ms: Place the microphone near the loudspeaker and adjust its position until the two traces are in phase Move the microphone away from the loudspeaker until the traces are next in phase Measure the distance moved by the microphone using the tape measure: this distance is one wavelength Move the microphone through several (n) wavelengths, counting the in-phase positions, and divide the distance by n (or repeat and calculate a mean) Keep the microphone on the line from the loudspeaker and read the tape at eye level (avoid parallax) Period read from the trace (e.g. 3 cycles occupy 9.6 div), T = 9.6 × 0.25 ms ÷ 3 = 0.80 ms f = 1/T = 1250 Hz λ = (149.0 − 11.8) cm ÷ 5 = 27.44 cm v = fλ = 343 m s⁻¹ Uncertainty in the distance moved = 2 × 0.5 cm = 1.0 cm Percentage uncertainty = 1.0 cm ÷ 137.2 cm × 100% = 0.73%
items.why: Core Practical 4 has been examined twice (Oct2019 Q19b, Jun2021 Q17), each time with a method description, and was last asked in Jun2021, so a full CP4 question with trace reading and uncertainty is due.

items.name: Coherence, path difference, superposition, interference
path: Unit 2 Waves and Electricity
Waves and Particle Nature of Light
S39 - what is meant by wavefront, coherence, path d
items.question: Two pulses travel towards each other along a stretched string. One pulse has a maximum displacement of +3.0 cm. The other pulse has a maximum displacement of −1.0 cm. The pulses have the same shape and width. What is the displacement of the string at the centre of the pulses at the instant they exactly overlap? 0 cm 1.0 cm 2.0 cm 4.0 cm
items.ms: By the principle of superposition the displacements add: +3.0 cm + (−1.0 cm) = +2.0 cm. A assumes that overlapping pulses cancel; B averages the two displacements; D adds the sizes and ignores the sign of the second pulse.
items.why: S39 is hot (18 of 21 sessions) and superposition of pulses on a string was the MCQ in Jun2026 Q10 and Jan2025 Q4; pulses of opposite sign and unequal size are the next variation.

items.name: Coherence, path difference, superposition, interference
path: Unit 2 Waves and Electricity
Waves and Particle Nature of Light
S39 - what is meant by wavefront, coherence, path d
items.question: Which of the following pairs of sources would produce coherent waves? two loudspeakers connected to the same signal generator two identical filament lamps two loudspeakers connected to separate signal generators set to 500 Hz and 502 Hz two sodium lamps emitting light of the same wavelength
items.ms: Coherent sources have a constant phase difference, which needs the same frequency. Two loudspeakers driven by one signal generator vibrate at the same frequency with a fixed phase relationship. B: lamps emit light in random bursts (and many wavelengths), so the phase difference keeps changing; C: the frequencies differ, so the phase difference changes continuously; D: the wavelength is the same but each lamp emits randomly, so there is no constant phase difference.
items.why: Coherence comes up nearly every year (Oct2025 Q16a, Jan2024 Q11a, Jun2023 Q7, Jan2023 Q15b), and the Jan2024 report notes candidates write 'same phase' instead of 'constant phase difference'.

items.name: Coherence, path difference, superposition, interference
path: Unit 2 Waves and Electricity
Waves and Particle Nature of Light
S39 - what is meant by wavefront, coherence, path d
items.question: Straight water waves travel across a ripple tank. Which statement about two points on the same wavefront is correct? They are one wavelength apart. They oscillate in phase. They have a phase difference of π rad. They lie on a line parallel to the direction in which the wave travels.
items.ms: A wavefront is a line joining points that are in phase, so B. A describes points on adjacent wavefronts (e.g. neighbouring crests); C describes points half a wavelength apart along the direction of travel; D is wrong because a wavefront is perpendicular to the direction of travel.
items.why: S39 includes wavefronts, defined as 'a line on which all points are in phase' in Oct2023 Q18a; no MCQ has yet tested the idea.

items.name: Coherence, path difference, superposition, interference
path: Unit 2 Waves and Electricity
Waves and Particle Nature of Light
S39 - what is meant by wavefront, coherence, path d
items.question: Two dippers S₁ and S₂ are attached to the same vibrating bar in a ripple tank. The dippers are 8.0 cm apart. The diagram shows the crests of the circular waves from S₁ and S₂ at one instant. Explain why the dippers are attached to the same vibrating bar. Explain why there are places in the tank where the water surface is almost still, and other places where it oscillates with a large amplitude. Point P is 15.0 cm from S₁ and 10.0 cm from S₂. The frequency of the vibrating bar is 12 Hz and the speed of the waves is 0.24 m s⁻¹. Deduce whether the water at P is almost still or oscillates with a large amplitude.
items.ms: So that the two sources have the same frequency and a constant phase difference (they are coherent) So that the interference pattern is stable: the places of large and small disturbance stay in the same positions IC1 The waves from S₁ and S₂ overlap and superpose: the resultant displacement is the sum of the individual displacements IC2 At each point there is a path difference between the waves from the two dippers IC3 Where the path difference is a whole number of wavelengths (nλ), the waves arrive in phase IC4 So constructive interference occurs (crest meets crest, trough meets trough) and the water oscillates with a large amplitude IC5 Where the path difference is an odd number of half wavelengths ((n + ½)λ), the waves arrive in antiphase (phase difference π rad or 180°) IC6 So destructive interference occurs (crest meets trough) and the water is almost still; it is not completely still because the two waves have slightly different amplitudes there Use of v = fλ: λ = 0.24/12 = 0.020 m (2.0 cm) Path difference = 15.0 cm − 10.0 cm = 5.0 cm = 2.5λ The waves arrive in antiphase, so destructive interference: the water at P is almost still
items.why: S39 has come up in 18 of 21 sessions and its 6-mark questions (Oct2020 Q13b, Oct2022 Q15a, Jan2023 Q15a, Jan2024 Q17b) all ask why some places are loud or calm; a two-dipper ripple tank drawn with wavefronts and a path-difference deduction has not been set.

path: Unit 2 Waves and Electricity
Waves and Particle Nature of Light
S40 - use the relationship between phase difference
items.question: A loudspeaker emits sound of frequency 850 Hz. The speed of sound in air is 340 m s⁻¹. Points X and Y are 0.30 m apart on a line along which the sound travels. What is the phase difference between the oscillations of the air molecules at X and Y? 135° 240° 270° 480°
items.ms: λ = v/f = 340/850 = 0.40 m. X and Y are 0.30/0.40 = ¾ of a wavelength apart, so the phase difference is ¾ × 360° = 270°. A multiplies the fraction by 180° instead of 360°; B uses λ/x (0.40/0.30) multiplied by 180°; D uses λ/x multiplied by 360°.
items.why: S40 MCQs appear most years (Jan2026 Q5, Oct2025 Q5 and Q7, Jun2025 Q7), all with waves from two sources; the phase difference between two points on one progressive wave has not been asked.

path: Unit 2 Waves and Electricity
Waves and Particle Nature of Light
S40 - use the relationship between phase difference
items.question: Two loudspeakers A and B are connected to the same signal generator so that they vibrate in phase with a frequency of 1360 Hz. A microphone is placed at point M, which is 3.200 m from A and 3.825 m from B, as shown. speed of sound in air = 340 m s⁻¹ Calculate the phase difference between the waves from A and B when they arrive at M. Explain whether the microphone at M detects a maximum or a minimum of sound intensity. The connections to loudspeaker B are now reversed, so that A and B vibrate in antiphase. Explain what the microphone now detects at M.
items.ms: Use of v = fλ: λ = 0.250 m Path difference = 3.825 m − 3.200 m = 0.625 m Use of phase difference = (path difference ÷ λ) × 360° (or × 2π rad) Phase difference = 900° (5π rad), equivalent to 180° (π rad) The waves arrive at M in antiphase (path difference 2.5λ, an odd number of half wavelengths) So destructive interference occurs and M is a minimum The waves from B now have an extra phase difference of 180° (π rad), so the waves arrive at M in phase (total phase difference 360°) So constructive interference occurs and M is now a maximum (loud)
items.why: S40 has come up in 8 of 21 sessions, almost all as MCQs (Jan2026 Q5, Oct2025 Q7); a structured two-loudspeaker calculation, with sources switched to antiphase so that the usual conditions reverse, has not been asked.

items.name: Standing waves, nodes and antinodes
path: Unit 2 Waves and Electricity
Waves and Particle Nature of Light
S41 - what is meant by a standingstationary wave an
items.question: A tube is closed at one end. The lowest frequency at which the air in the tube resonates is 125 Hz. At which of the following frequencies would the air in the tube not resonate? 250 Hz 375 Hz 625 Hz 875 Hz
items.ms: A tube closed at one end has a node at the closed end and an antinode at the open end, so its length is an odd number of quarter wavelengths (λ/4, 3λ/4, 5λ/4 …). The resonant frequencies are odd multiples of 125 Hz: 375 Hz (3×), 625 Hz (5×) and 875 Hz (7×) all resonate. 250 Hz (2×) would need the length to be half a wavelength, which would put a node, not an antinode, at the open end.
items.why: S41 is hot (19 of 21 sessions) and closed-tube resonance recurs (Jun2026 Q8, Jun2025 Q17b, Jun2024 Q15d, Oct2021 Q12); that a closed tube has only odd multiples of its lowest frequency has not been tested directly.

S41 - what is meant by a standingstationary wave an
items.question: Which statement about a stationary wave on a stretched string is correct? Adjacent nodes are one wavelength apart. Energy is transferred along the string from one end to the other. All points on the string oscillate with the same amplitude. All points between two adjacent nodes oscillate in phase.
items.ms: Between two adjacent nodes every point moves up and down together, so they are in phase (points in neighbouring loops are in antiphase). A: adjacent nodes are half a wavelength apart; B: a stationary wave does not transfer energy along the string; C: the amplitude varies from zero at a node to a maximum at an antinode.
items.why: S41 has come up in 19 of 21 sessions; the Jan2022 report found candidates think points in different loops are in phase, and MCQs on the phase and amplitude of points on a stationary wave recur (Jan2025 Q7, Jan2022 Q7).

items.question: Microwaves from a transmitter are reflected by a metal plate, and a stationary wave forms between the transmitter and the plate. A detector is moved along the line between them. Adjacent positions of minimum signal are 1.4 cm apart. speed of microwaves = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ What is the frequency of the microwaves? 2.1 × 10⁸ Hz 5.4 × 10⁹ Hz 1.1 × 10¹⁰ Hz 2.1 × 10¹⁰ Hz
items.ms: Adjacent minima (nodes) are half a wavelength apart, so λ = 2 × 1.4 cm = 2.8 cm = 0.028 m and f = c/λ = 3.00 × 10⁸/0.028 = 1.1 × 10¹⁰ Hz. A uses 1.4 (cm not converted to m) as the wavelength; B takes the spacing as a quarter of a wavelength (λ = 5.6 cm); D takes the spacing as a whole wavelength.
items.why: Jan2026 Q18 used radio waves reflected from a metal plate to give a stationary wave and a wave speed; the same set-up with microwaves and a frequency to find is a likely MCQ.

items.question: A guitar string is fixed at the nut and at the bridge, 0.65 m apart. When the string is plucked, it vibrates at its lowest frequency, as shown. Label each node with N and each antinode with A on the diagram. State the wavelength of the stationary wave. The guitarist lightly touches the midpoint of the string with a finger and plucks the string again. The point she touches cannot move. Draw the new stationary wave on the diagram below. Explain why the frequency of the note is now twice the frequency of the note in the first diagram. P and Q are points on the string 0.15 m from the nut and 0.15 m from the bridge, as shown on the diagram in (c)(i). State the phase difference between the oscillations of P and Q when the string vibrates as in (c).
items.ms: Nodes (N) at the nut and at the bridge, and one antinode (A) at the midpoint λ = 2 × 0.65 m = 1.30 m Two loops: nodes at both ends and at the midpoint, with an antinode midway between each pair of nodes There is now a node at the midpoint, so the string forms two loops and the wavelength is halved (λ = 0.65 m) The speed of the wave is unchanged because the tension and the mass per unit length are unchanged (v = √(T/μ)) f = v/λ, so the frequency doubles 180° (π rad) / antiphase: P and Q are in adjacent loops
items.why: Labelling or drawing a stationary wave on a string recurs (Jan2026 Q15b, Jan2025 Q17a, Jan2024 Q15b) and the Jan2022 report flags points in adjacent loops being in antiphase; making a harmonic by touching the midpoint has not been asked.

items.question: In an acoustic levitator, an ultrasound transducer sends a sound wave of frequency 40.0 kHz upwards towards a flat reflector. A stationary wave forms between the transducer and the reflector. Small polystyrene beads can be held in the air by the stationary wave, as shown. Explain how the stationary wave is formed. Each bead is held at a point where the amplitude of the pressure variation is zero (a pressure node). Use the diagram to calculate the speed of sound in the air. Describe how the amplitude and the phase of the oscillations of the air molecules vary between two adjacent points where the molecules do not move.
items.ms: The ultrasound is reflected by the reflector So two waves of the same frequency travel in opposite directions between the transducer and the reflector The two waves superpose (interfere) Nodes form where the waves always interfere destructively and antinodes where they interfere constructively Distance between adjacent beads = 21.5 mm ÷ 5 = 4.30 mm λ = 2 × 4.30 mm = 8.60 mm v = fλ = 40.0 × 10³ Hz × 8.60 × 10⁻³ m = 344 m s⁻¹ The amplitude is zero at each of these points (displacement nodes) It increases to a maximum midway between them (antinode) and then decreases to zero again All the molecules between the two points oscillate in phase They are in antiphase with the molecules beyond either of these points (the next section)
items.why: Stationary-wave formation is asked in almost every session (Jan2026 Q18a, Oct2025 Q17a, Jan2025 Q17b) and the Oct2021 report says marks go to naming the reflector in an unfamiliar context; counting the gaps between nodes to find λ (Jan2026 Q18b) recurs.

items.question: A student uses a glass tube that is open at both ends. The tube stands vertically in a tall cylinder of water, as shown. She holds a vibrating tuning fork above the top of the tube and slowly raises the tube until the sound is loudest for the first time. She then measures the length L of the air column from the water surface to the top of the tube. Explain how a stationary wave is formed in the air column, and why the sound is loudest at this length. The antinode is a small distance e above the top of the tube. Show that L = v/(4f) − e where f is the frequency of the fork and v is the speed of sound in air. The student repeats the experiment with tuning forks of different frequencies. Her results are shown in the table. Plot a graph of L against 1/f on the grid. Use the extra column of the table for your processed data. Use your graph to determine a value for the speed of sound in air. Use your graph to determine e.
items.ms: IC1 Sound waves from the tuning fork travel down the tube and are reflected at the water surface IC2 The incident and reflected waves have the same frequency and travel in opposite directions IC3 The two waves superpose (interfere) to form a stationary wave IC4 There is a node at the water surface because the air there cannot move IC5 There is an antinode at (just above) the open end, where the air oscillates with maximum amplitude IC6 At this length the stationary wave fits the air column with a node at the water surface and an antinode at the top, so the reflected waves reinforce each other: the air column resonates, the amplitude is a maximum and the sound is loudest The distance from the node at the water surface to the antinode is a quarter of a wavelength: L + e = λ/4 Use of v = fλ to replace λ with v/f, giving L = v/(4f) − e 1/f values correct (3.91, 3.47, 3.12, 2.60, 2.35, 1.95, in units of 10⁻³ s) Axes labelled with quantity and unit (e.g. L / m and (1/f) / 10⁻³ s) and sensible scales (points cover more than half the grid) All points plotted accurately (to within half a small square) Best-fit straight line drawn Gradient determined from a large triangle on the best-fit line (about 86 m s⁻¹) v = 4 × gradient v = 343 m s⁻¹ e = magnitude of the intercept on the L axis (or e = v/(4f) − L for a point on the line): e = 0.012 m
items.why: S41 is hot (19 of 21 sessions); closed-tube resonance and the end correction recur (Jun2025 Q17, Oct2021 Q12, Jun2024 Q15d) and Jun2025 Q17a made the formation of the stationary wave in a tube a 6-mark question; finding v and the end correction from a graph has not been asked.

S42 - use the equation for the speed of a transvers
items.question: A string passes over a pulley and supports a mass of 0.25 kg. The mass per unit length of the string is 6.0 × 10⁻⁴ kg m⁻¹. What is the speed of transverse waves on the string? 20 m s⁻¹ 64 m s⁻¹ 2.0 × 10² m s⁻¹ 4.1 × 10³ m s⁻¹
items.ms: T = mg = 0.25 × 9.81 = 2.45 N; v = √(T/μ) = √(2.45/6.0 × 10⁻⁴) = 64 m s⁻¹. A uses the mass (0.25) as the tension; C uses μ = 6.0 × 10⁻⁵ kg m⁻¹ (a power-of-ten slip); D leaves out the square root.
items.why: S42 is hot (16 of 21 sessions); T = mg followed by v = √(T/μ) is the standard set-up (Jan2020 Q11b, Jan2026 Q6).

S42 - use the equation for the speed of a transvers
items.question: A stretched wire vibrates at its fundamental frequency f. It is replaced by a wire of the same material and length but twice the diameter, under the same tension. What is the fundamental frequency of the new wire? f/4 f/2 f/√2 2f
items.ms: Doubling the diameter makes the cross-sectional area, and so the mass per unit length μ, four times bigger. v = √(T/μ) halves; the length is the same, so λ = 2L is unchanged and f = v/λ halves. A leaves out the square root; C treats μ as doubling (proportional to the diameter); D reverses the effect of a larger μ.
items.why: MCQs that change one property of the string recur (Oct2025 Q7 doubled the tension, May2024 Q8 doubled the length, Oct2023 Q8); changing the diameter, which changes μ as its square, has not been asked.

items.question: A guitar string has a vibrating length of 0.65 m and the mass of this length of string is 0.26 g. The string vibrates at its fundamental frequency of 330 Hz. What is the tension in the string? 0.17 N 18 N 48 N 74 N
items.ms: μ = 0.26 × 10⁻³ kg ÷ 0.65 m = 4.0 × 10⁻⁴ kg m⁻¹. For the fundamental λ = 2L = 1.30 m, so v = fλ = 429 m s⁻¹ and T = μv² = 74 N. A leaves out the square (μv); B takes λ = L; C uses the mass of the string instead of the mass per unit length.
items.why: S42 has come up in 16 of 21 sessions; finding μ from a string's mass and length and then a tension (Jun2026 Q12, Jan2024 Q15c) is its most common calculation.

items.question: A piano string is made of steel wire. The vibrating length of the string is 0.620 m. The string is tuned so that its fundamental frequency is 262 Hz. A 1.50 m sample of the same wire has a mass of 9.25 g. Show that the mass per unit length of the wire is about 6 × 10⁻³ kg m⁻¹. Calculate the tension in the string when it is correctly tuned. Some weeks later the fundamental frequency of the string has fallen to 258 Hz. Calculate the percentage increase in tension needed to return the frequency to 262 Hz. The lowest string on the piano has a vibrating length of 2.00 m and a fundamental frequency of 27.5 Hz. The tension in it is 650 N. Deduce whether the steel wire in (a) could be used for this string. Suggest how the piano maker could make a string that sounds this note with the same length and tension.
items.ms: Use of μ = m/l with the mass in kg μ = 6.17 × 10⁻³ kg m⁻¹ λ = 2L = 1.24 m and use of v = fλ (v = 325 m s⁻¹) Use of v = √(T/μ) T = 651 N Recognises that f ∝ √T because λ and μ are unchanged, so T ∝ f² T(new)/T(old) = (262/258)² = 1.0312 Percentage increase = 3.1% v = 2Lf = 2 × 2.00 m × 27.5 Hz = 110 m s⁻¹ μ needed = T/v² = 650/110² = 0.0537 kg m⁻¹ This is about 9 times the μ of the steel wire, so the steel wire cannot be used Increase the mass per unit length, e.g. by winding (copper) wire around the steel core or using a much thicker wire
items.why: S42 is hot (16 of 21 sessions) and its long questions ask for μ, a tension or a frequency and end with a deduction (Jun2026 Q12, Oct2025 Q17c, Jan2026 Q15c); retuning through f ∝ √T was last asked in Oct2022 Q15b.

items.question: A student investigates a vibrating wire. The tension and the mass per unit length of the wire are kept constant, and the length l of wire between the bridges is varied. The frequency f of the fundamental is measured for each length. Which graph would be a straight line through the origin? f against 1/l f against l f² against l f against l²
items.ms: f = (1/2l)√(T/μ), so with T and μ constant f ∝ 1/l and a graph of f against 1/l is a straight line through the origin. B gives a curve with f decreasing as l increases; C and D also give curves (f² ∝ 1/l²).
items.why: Core Practical 5 is examined through graphs of f against a variable (Jan2025 Q17c, Oct2020 Q17b, Jan2022 Q15b), always with the tension varied; varying the length has not been asked.

S43 - CORE PRACTICAL 5 Investigate the effects of l
items.question: A student investigates how the frequency of the fundamental of a stretched wire depends on the tension in the wire. The wire passes over two bridges 0.600 m apart and over a pulley to slotted masses, as shown. A vibration generator connected to a signal generator makes the wire vibrate. Describe how the student should find the frequency of the fundamental for each tension. Show that f² = T/(4l²μ) where T is the tension, l is the distance between the bridges and μ is the mass per unit length of the wire. The student's results are shown in the table. Plot a graph of f² against T on the grid. Use the extra column of the table for your processed data. Use your graph to determine the mass per unit length of the wire. To check her value, the student measures the mass of a 2.00 m length of the same wire using a balance that reads to 0.01 g. Explain why she uses a 2.00 m length of wire rather than a 0.600 m length.
items.ms: Increase the frequency of the signal generator slowly from a low value until the wire vibrates with a single loop between the bridges Adjust the frequency until the amplitude of the loop is a maximum and read f from the signal generator (or from an oscilloscope, f = 1/T) Repeat, approaching the maximum from a higher frequency, and take the mean For the fundamental λ = 2l, and use of v = fλ (v = 2lf) Equates 2lf with √(T/μ) and squares: 4l²f² = T/μ, so f² = T/(4l²μ) f² values correct (4.90, 9.60, 14.6, 19.6, 24.0, 29.2, in units of 10³ Hz²) Axes labelled with quantity and unit (f² / 10³ Hz² and T / N) and sensible scales (points cover more than half the grid) All points plotted accurately (to within half a small square) Best-fit straight line drawn (passing close to the origin) Gradient determined from a large triangle on the best-fit line (about 991 Hz² N⁻¹) Use of gradient = 1/(4l²μ) μ = 7.0 × 10⁻⁴ kg m⁻¹ A longer length of wire has a larger mass (about 1.4 g rather than 0.42 g) So the resolution of the balance (0.01 g) is a smaller percentage of the mass, giving a smaller percentage uncertainty in μ (about 0.7% rather than 2.4%)
items.why: Core Practical 5 was last asked in Jun2025, with f² against T and the gradient 1/(4l²μ) in Jan2025 Q17c; a full investigation with a plotted graph and a value of μ, as in Jan2022 Q15b, is the likeliest CP5 question.

items.question: Over time, scientists have described the behaviour of light using a wave model and a photon model. Each model was developed to explain experimental observations. Complete the table by putting a tick (✓) in the correct column to show which model explains each observation. When the photon model was introduced, scientists did not abandon the wave model of light. Explain why.
items.ms: Two or three rows correct All four rows correct The wave model (still) explains observations such as interference, diffraction and polarisation The photon model cannot explain these observations (and the wave model cannot explain the photoelectric effect or line spectra) So both models are needed to describe the behaviour of electromagnetic radiation / each model applies to different observations
items.why: S57 has only been examined as MCQs on which phenomena each model explains (Jan2021 Q4, Jun2026 Q5); the 'how these models developed over time' half of the spec point has never been asked, so a short structured question on keeping both models is the likeliest surprise.

items.question: A microwave oven produces electromagnetic radiation of frequency 2.45 GHz. What is the energy of one photon of this radiation? 8.1 × 10⁻³⁵ J 1.6 × 10⁻²⁷ J 1.6 × 10⁻²⁴ J 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ J
items.ms: E = hf = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s × 2.45 × 10⁹ Hz = 1.6 × 10⁻²⁴ J. A uses hc/f, treating the frequency as if it were a wavelength. B takes the prefix giga as 10⁶. D is the photon energy in electronvolts (1.0 × 10⁻⁵ eV) given the unit J.
items.why: S58 photon energies appear in nearly every paper, mostly inside longer questions; a low-energy photon (asked once, Jan2021 Q20b, a 902 MHz router) suits a one-step opening MCQ.

items.question: Plant growers use LED grow-lights. The graph shows the spectrum of the light emitted by one of the blue LEDs in a grow-light. Use the graph to show that the energy of a photon at the peak wavelength is about 4.4 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. When the LED is working normally, the potential difference across it is 3.10 V and the current in it is 0.350 A. It emits light with a total power of 0.480 W. Calculate the efficiency of the LED. Calculate the number of photons emitted by the LED each second. Assume that every photon has the energy at the peak wavelength. In the LED, each photon is produced when one electron passing through the LED loses energy. Calculate the percentage of the electrons passing through the LED that produce a photon.
items.ms: Use of E = hf and v = fλ (or E = hc/λ) with λ = 450 nm E = 4.42 × 10⁻¹⁹ J Use of P = VI (input power = 1.08 W) Efficiency = 0.44 (44%) Use of N = P/E (number per second = power ÷ photon energy) N = 1.09 × 10¹⁸ s⁻¹ Use of I = ΔQ/Δt with ΔQ = Ne Number of electrons per second = 2.19 × 10¹⁸ Percentage = 49.6%
items.why: S58 is asked in nearly every paper and photon counting from a power recurs (Oct2022 Q17 LED, Jan2026 Q21 CCD, Oct2025 Q15b); comparing photons per second with electrons per second (I/e), here for an LED, is the synoptic twist the examiners used in Jun2024 Q18c and Jan2026 Q21.

path: Unit 2 Waves and Electricity
Waves and Particle Nature of Light
S59 - that the absorption of a photon can result in
items.question: Monochromatic ultraviolet radiation falls on a clean zinc surface and photoelectrons are emitted. Which statement is correct? Each electron that is emitted has absorbed the energy of one photon. An electron can absorb energy from several photons until it has enough energy to escape. All of the emitted electrons have the same kinetic energy. Photons are emitted from the zinc surface with a range of energies.
items.ms: Absorption is a one-to-one interaction: one photon gives all its energy to one electron. B is the wave-model idea of energy building up; an electron cannot collect energy from several photons. C: every photon has the same energy, but electrons from below the surface lose energy getting out, so the kinetic energies range up to a maximum. D confuses photons with electrons: it is electrons that are emitted.
items.why: S59 MCQs test the one-to-one photon–electron interaction (Jun2022 Q7, Jun2024 Q6), and the Oct2020 examiners' report notes candidates confusing photons and electrons.

path: Unit 2 Waves and Electricity

S59 - that the absorption of a photon can result in
items.question: A vacuum photocell is used to detect boxes on a conveyor belt in a factory. A light beam crosses the belt and falls on the photocell. The diagram shows the photocell in a circuit. The anode is positive with respect to the cathode. Explain how light falling on the cathode produces a current in the microammeter. When the light beam is not blocked, the current in the microammeter is 0.36 μA. Calculate the number of photoelectrons that reach the anode each second. The lamp is replaced by one that delivers the same power of light to the cathode, but at a shorter wavelength. Assume that the same fraction of the photons release electrons. Explain how the current changes.
items.ms: A photon is absorbed by a (single) electron in the cathode / one photon interacts with one electron The electron gains all the energy of the photon (E = hf) If the photon energy is greater than the work function, the electron is released from the surface (as a photoelectron) The photoelectrons are attracted to the (positive) anode / move across the vacuum to the anode Electrons flow round the circuit (back to the cathode) through the microammeter, so there is a current Use of I = ΔQ/Δt with ΔQ = Ne N = 2.25 × 10¹² s⁻¹ Shorter wavelength, so higher frequency, so each photon has more energy (E = hf) Same power, so fewer photons per second, so fewer electrons are released per second and the current decreases
items.why: S59 has been asked in 5 of 21 sessions, always as an explanation of how photoelectrons are released (Oct2024 Q19a, Oct2025 Q15a 4 marks); linking the release to the current in a circuit follows Oct2023 Q17 and Oct2025 Q15c.

items.question: The work function of caesium is 2.14 eV. What is the longest wavelength of electromagnetic radiation that can release photoelectrons from caesium? 9.3 × 10⁻²⁶ m 5.8 × 10⁻⁷ m 9.3 × 10⁻⁷ m 1.7 × 10⁶ m
items.ms: λ₀ = hc/φ = (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s × 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹) ÷ (2.14 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J) = 5.8 × 10⁻⁷ m. A leaves the work function in eV. C takes 2.14 eV as 2.14 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. D divides the threshold frequency φ/h by c instead of dividing c by the threshold frequency.
items.why: Threshold frequency or wavelength from a work function recurs (Jan2024 Q19a, Oct2024 Q19c, Jun2026 Q2); the eV-to-J conversion is the marking point candidates most often miss.

items.name: Photoelectric equation, work function, threshold frequency
path: Unit 2 Waves and Electricity

items.question: Graphs of the maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons against the frequency of the incident radiation are plotted for two metals, P and Q. Metal Q has a greater work function than metal P. Compared with the line for P, which of the following describes the line for Q? gradient: the same; intercept on the frequency axis: greater gradient: the same; intercept on the frequency axis: smaller gradient: greater; intercept on the frequency axis: greater gradient: greater; intercept on the frequency axis: the same
items.ms: Ek max = hf − φ, so the gradient is h for every metal, and the line meets the frequency axis at the threshold frequency f₀ = φ/h, which is greater for the greater work function. B would be a metal with a smaller work function. C and D make the gradient depend on the metal; D also keeps the same threshold frequency.
items.why: The E_{k}–f graph (gradient h, frequency intercept f₀) was asked in Jun2022 Q17c, May2024 Q10 and Oct2025 Q10, but comparing the lines for two metals has not been asked.

items.name: Photoelectric equation, work function, threshold frequency
path: Unit 2 Waves and Electricity
Waves and Particle Nature of Light
S60 - the terms threshold frequency and work functi
items.question: Electromagnetic radiation of frequency f releases photoelectrons from a metal surface. The maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons is E. The frequency of the radiation is doubled. What is the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons now? E more than E but less than 2E 2E more than 2E
items.ms: hf = φ + E, so 2hf = 2φ + 2E = φ + (2E + φ). The new maximum kinetic energy is 2E + φ, which is more than 2E. A treats the kinetic energy as independent of frequency. B wrongly thinks the work function takes a larger share of the bigger photon energy; the work function is the same, so all of the extra energy hf goes to the electron. C treats the kinetic energy as proportional to frequency, ignoring the work function.
items.why: Candidates treat the kinetic energy as proportional to frequency (Jan2021 Q17(b) asked them to judge a student's wrong claim); S60 is hot (15 of 21 sessions), and a proportional-reasoning MCQ on hf = φ + ½mv²_{max} is a likely late MCQ.

items.name: Photoelectric equation, work function, threshold frequency
