items.question: A hospital uses lamps that emit ultraviolet radiation of wavelength 254 nm to disinfect rooms. A photoelectric sensor is used to check that a lamp is working. The sensor must respond to the 254 nm radiation. It must not respond to visible light or to the ultraviolet in daylight that passes through window glass, which has wavelengths of 320 nm and longer. State what is meant by the work function of a metal. Explain why a photoelectric sensor does not respond to radiation below a certain frequency, however intense the radiation is. The table gives the work functions of some metals. Deduce which of these metals would be suitable for the sensor.
items.ms: The minimum energy needed to release an electron from the surface of the metal Photon energy depends on frequency (E = hf), so below the threshold frequency the photon energy is less than the work function One photon interacts with one electron, so an electron cannot gain enough energy to escape Increasing the intensity only increases the number of photons (per second), not the energy of each photon Use of E = hc/λ (or E = hf with v = fλ) Photon energy at 254 nm = 4.89 eV (7.83 × 10⁻¹⁹ J) Photon energy at 320 nm = 3.88 eV (6.22 × 10⁻¹⁹ J) Only zinc: its work function is less than 4.89 eV but greater than 3.88 eV
items.why: Choosing a photocathode by comparing photon energies with work functions recurs as a 'deduce whether' (Oct2024 Q19c, Jan2025 Q19c, Oct2023 Q17b(ii)), and why there is a threshold frequency was asked in Oct2024 Q19b and Jun2026 Q19b; a sensor that must ignore longer wavelengths as well is a fresh two-sided version.

items.question: Ultraviolet radiation from the Sun releases photoelectrons from the aluminium surface of a satellite in orbit. Much of this radiation is emitted when electrons in hydrogen atoms in the Sun move from the −3.40 eV energy level to the −13.6 eV energy level. Show that the wavelength of this radiation is about 120 nm. The work function of aluminium is 4.08 eV. Calculate the maximum speed of the photoelectrons released from the aluminium. Calculate the de Broglie wavelength of the fastest photoelectrons. Give one reason why most of the photoelectrons leave the surface with less than this maximum speed.
items.ms: ΔE = 10.2 eV, converted to J (1.63 × 10⁻¹⁸ J) Use of E = hf and v = fλ (or λ = hc/E) λ = 1.22 × 10⁻⁷ m (122 nm) Conversion of eV to J (work function 6.53 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, or Ek max = 6.12 eV converted) Use of hf = φ + ½mv²max Ek max = 9.79 × 10⁻¹⁹ J vmax = 1.47 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ Use of λ = h/p with p = mv λ = 4.96 × 10⁻¹⁰ m Electrons from below the surface lose energy (in collisions) before they escape / some electrons need more energy than the work function to escape
items.why: Calculating v_{max} from hf = φ + ½mv²_{max} and then a de Broglie wavelength is the commonest S60 calculation (Jan2021 Q17a, Oct2021 Q14b, May2024 Q17b, Jun2026 Q19a); taking the photon energy from a hydrogen transition makes it synoptic with S63.

items.question: A student investigates the photoelectric effect. Light from a mercury lamp passes through a filter, so that radiation of only one frequency f falls on a metal surface in a vacuum photocell. The collecting electrode is made negative with respect to the metal surface, and the potential difference between them is increased until the current just falls to zero. This potential difference is called the stopping potential Vs. The student repeats this for several filters. When the collecting electrode is first made negative, the current decreases, but it only becomes zero when the potential difference reaches Vs. Explain why. Explain why a graph of Vs against f should be a straight line with a gradient equal to h/e. The table shows the student's results. Plot a graph of Vs against f on the grid. Use your graph to determine a value for the Planck constant h. The table gives the work functions of some metals. Use your graph to deduce which metal the student used.
items.ms: The photoelectrons are released with a range of kinetic energies (up to a maximum) As the potential difference increases, electrons with less kinetic energy are stopped first / no longer reach the collecting electrode The current is zero only when the electrons with the maximum kinetic energy are stopped, so eVs = maximum kinetic energy The work done stopping the fastest electrons is eVs, so hf = φ + eVs Vs = (h/e)f − φ/e, which has the form y = mx + c, with gradient h/e (φ/e and h/e are constants) Axes labelled with quantities and units Sensible scales, with the plotted points covering at least half of the grid in each direction All points plotted accurately (to within half a small square) Best-fit straight line Gradient calculated using a large triangle (at least half the length of the line) Use of h = gradient × e h = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ J s (range 6.4 to 6.9 × 10⁻³⁴ J s) Threshold frequency read from the intercept on the f axis (about 6.9 × 10¹⁴ Hz) Use of φ = hf₀ and conversion of J to eV φ = 2.9 eV, so the metal is calcium
items.why: S60 is the hottest photon point (15 of 21 sessions, 5.7% of the marks); the E_{k}–f graph (Jun2022 Q17c) and the stopping potential (Jan2020 Q14c, Jan2025 Q19c) have each been asked, but never a plotted graph of stopping potential against frequency that gives h and identifies the metal, as Oct2020 Q14b and Jan2023 Q18a did from φ.

path: Unit 2 Waves and Electricity
Waves and Particle Nature of Light
S61 - use the electronvolt (eV) to express small en
items.question: Energies on the scale of atoms and electrons are often given in electronvolts (eV). State what is meant by an energy of 1 eV. In an electron microscope, electrons are accelerated from rest through a potential difference of 2.40 kV. State the kinetic energy of each electron, in eV. Calculate this energy in joules.
items.ms: The energy transferred to an electron when it moves through a potential difference of 1 V 2400 eV (2.40 keV) E = 2400 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J = 3.84 × 10⁻¹⁶ J
items.why: S61 has been tested directly only by one MCQ (Jan2024 Q4), although eV–J conversions earn a mark in most photon calculations (Jun2019 Q16b, Jun2021 Q15a, Jun2026 Q13b); a short opening question on what an electronvolt means is the likeliest new form.

path: Unit 2 Waves and Electricity
Waves and Particle Nature of Light
S62 - how the photoelectric effect provides evidenc
items.question: A wave model of electromagnetic radiation can be used to make predictions about the photoelectric effect. Which of the following is predicted by the wave model but is not observed? Increasing the intensity increases the rate at which electrons are emitted. Ultraviolet radiation releases electrons from a zinc surface. The maximum kinetic energy of the emitted electrons increases when the frequency increases. Radiation of any frequency releases electrons if it is intense enough.
items.ms: In a wave model, energy is delivered continuously, so radiation of any frequency should release electrons if it is intense enough (or after long enough); in fact there is a threshold frequency. A and B are observed. C is observed but is not predicted by the wave model, in which the kinetic energy would depend on intensity.
items.why: MCQs on what the photoelectric effect shows recur (Jan2020 Q6, Jan2021 Q4, Jun2025 Q9); asking which wave-model prediction fails reverses the usual form and tests the indicative content of the 6-mark (Jun2019 Q14).

path: Unit 2 Waves and Electricity
Waves and Particle Nature of Light
S62 - how the photoelectric effect provides evidenc
items.question: A clean zinc plate is placed on a gold-leaf electroscope and given a negative charge, so that the leaf rises. The work function of zinc is 4.3 eV. Which radiation, shone on the plate, would make the leaf fall straight away? very bright red light, photon energy 1.9 eV very bright violet light, photon energy 3.1 eV dim ultraviolet radiation, photon energy 4.9 eV dim ultraviolet radiation, photon energy 3.9 eV
items.ms: Only photons with more energy than the work function (4.3 eV) can release electrons; the plate then loses negative charge and the leaf falls at once, however dim the radiation. A and B: however bright, each photon has too little energy, and brightness only changes the number of photons per second. D is ultraviolet, but its photons still have less energy than the work function.
items.why: The gold-leaf electroscope (Oct2021 Q14a) is the classic demonstration of the photon model; an MCQ combining the threshold with the irrelevance of intensity matches the S62 MCQs of Jan2020 Q6 and Jun2025 Q9.

path: Unit 2 Waves and Electricity
Waves and Particle Nature of Light
S62 - how the photoelectric effect provides evidenc
items.question: A photomultiplier on a telescope detects light from a faint star. Light falling on the photocathode of the photomultiplier releases electrons. The work function of the photocathode is 1.90 eV. The intensity of the starlight at the photocathode is 2.5 × 10⁻⁹ W m⁻². In a wave model, the energy of the light is spread evenly over the photocathode. Assume that each electron at the surface can only absorb the energy falling on an area of 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁹ m². Calculate the time it would take, according to the wave model, for an electron to absorb enough energy to be released. In fact, electrons are released as soon as the starlight falls on the photocathode. Explain how the photon model accounts for this. The frequency of the starlight stays the same, but its intensity changes. Sketch graphs on the axes to show how the number of electrons released per second varies with intensity, the maximum kinetic energy of the released electrons varies with intensity.
items.ms: Conversion of work function to J (3.04 × 10⁻¹⁹ J) Use of I = P/A (power absorbed = 2.5 × 10⁻²⁸ W) t = 1.2 × 10⁹ s Light arrives as photons, each with energy E = hf (which does not depend on intensity) One photon gives all its energy to one electron, at once If hf is greater than the work function, the electron is released immediately; no build-up of energy is needed Low intensity means few photons per second, so few electrons per second, but no delay Straight line through the origin Horizontal straight line above the intensity axis
items.why: The wave-model time-delay estimate has been asked only once (Oct2020 Q14c) and the intensity dependence only as an MCQ (Oct2019 Q4), so both are likely surprises in a structured S62 question; a faint star gives a striking time.

path: Unit 2 Waves and Electricity
Waves and Particle Nature of Light
S62 - how the photoelectric effect provides evidenc
items.question: A student investigates the photoelectric effect using a vacuum photocell with a potassium cathode. The work function of potassium is 2.30 eV. She shines light from LEDs of different colours onto the cathode, one at a time, and measures the current. The table shows her results. With the green LED, the current started as soon as the LED was switched on, even at the lowest power. Show that the energy of a photon of the green light is about 2.4 eV. Explain why the current with the green LED is ten times greater when the power is ten times greater. Explain how these results provide evidence for the photon (particle) model of electromagnetic radiation rather than the wave model. Your answer should refer to the results for both LEDs.
items.ms: Use of E = hf and v = fλ (or E = hc/λ) Conversion to eV: E = 2.39 eV The photon energy is unchanged (same frequency), so ten times the power means ten times as many photons per second One photon is absorbed by one electron / each photon can release (at most) one electron So ten times as many electrons are released per second, and current is the rate of flow of charge IC1 The energy of a photon depends on frequency (E = hf), so red photons (lower frequency) have less energy than green photons IC2 One photon interacts with one electron, so an electron can only gain the energy of a single photon IC3 A red photon has 1.97 eV, less than the work function of 2.30 eV, so no electrons are released at any power; a green photon (2.39 eV) has more than the work function IC4 In the wave model, the energy delivered depends on intensity, so ten times the power of red light (or a longer time) should release electrons, but it does not IC5 In the photon model, an electron receives a photon's energy all at once, so electrons are released as soon as the light is switched on, even at low power IC6 In the wave model, at low intensity energy would have to build up over time, so there would be a delay before electrons are released; none is seen
items.why: S62 has come up in 12 of 21 sessions, and an extended answer on why the photoelectric effect supports the photon model has been set four times (Jun2019 Q14, Jun2021 Q15b, Jan2022 Q13, Oct2023 Q17a); reasoning from a table of results, as in Jan2025 Q19b, is the likeliest next form.

items.name: Line spectra and energy levels
path: Unit 2 Waves and Electricity
Waves and Particle Nature of Light
S63 - atomic line spectra in terms of transitions b
items.question: The diagram shows some of the energy levels of a hydrogen atom and four transitions, A, B, C and D. Which transition emits the photon with the longest wavelength? transition A transition B transition C transition D
items.ms: λ = hc/ΔE, so the longest wavelength comes from the smallest energy difference: B, 0.31 eV. A has the largest energy difference (10.2 eV), so it gives the shortest wavelength; choosing it links a bigger jump with a longer wavelength. C (2.55 eV) and D (1.89 eV) have larger energy differences than B.
items.why: Choosing a transition from an energy-level diagram is a near-annual MCQ (Oct2022 Q2, Jun2025 Q5, Jan2026 Q2); the Oct2022 examiners' report says many candidates thought a larger jump means a longer wavelength.

items.name: Line spectra and energy levels
path: Unit 2 Waves and Electricity
Waves and Particle Nature of Light
S63 - atomic line spectra in terms of transitions b
items.question: Radiation with a continuous spectrum passes through a cool gas. All the atoms of the gas are in their ground state. The spectrum of the radiation that has passed through the gas has dark lines. Which photon energies are missing at the dark lines? the energy differences between the ground state and each higher energy level the energy differences between every pair of energy levels the energies of each of the energy levels all energies less than the energy difference between the ground state and the first excited state
items.ms: A photon is absorbed only if its energy exactly matches a transition, and atoms in the ground state can only make transitions up from the ground state, so only those photon energies are removed. B lists the possible emission lines, which need atoms in excited states. C: the value of an energy level is not a transition energy. D: photons with less energy than any transition cannot be absorbed, so they pass straight through.
items.why: S63 asks about emission or absorption between levels in every session; an absorption spectrum from ground-state atoms has not been asked and is the next variation of the 'which photon can be absorbed' MCQs (Jan2026 Q3).

items.name: Line spectra and energy levels
path: Unit 2 Waves and Electricity
Waves and Particle Nature of Light
S63 - atomic line spectra in terms of transitions b
items.question: A hydrogen atom is in its ground state, at −13.6 eV. The next two energy levels are at −3.40 eV and −1.51 eV. Which of the following could raise the atom from the ground state to the −3.40 eV level? 1 a photon of energy 10.2 eV 2 a photon of energy 11.0 eV 3 an electron with kinetic energy 11.0 eV that collides with the atom 1 only 1 and 3 only 2 and 3 only 1, 2 and 3
items.ms: A photon is absorbed only if its whole energy matches a level difference: 10.2 eV matches −13.6 eV to −3.40 eV, but 11.0 eV matches no transition (−13.6 eV to −1.51 eV needs 12.1 eV), so photon 2 is not absorbed. A colliding electron can give up part of its kinetic energy (10.2 eV) and keep the rest (0.8 eV), so 3 can excite the atom. A ignores excitation by collision. C and D wrongly let a photon give up part of its energy.
items.why: Excitation by electron collisions drives the lamp questions (Jun2024 Q17a, Jun2025 Q18a), and the Jan2021 Q14 examiners' report found candidates confused about a photon of the wrong energy; contrasting the two is a likely late MCQ.

items.name: Line spectra and energy levels
path: Unit 2 Waves and Electricity
Waves and Particle Nature of Light
S63 - atomic line spectra in terms of transitions b
items.question: The energy of the ground state of a hydrogen atom is −13.6 eV. Explain why the energy levels of an atom have negative values. Calculate the minimum frequency of electromagnetic radiation that can ionise a hydrogen atom in its ground state. A photon of energy 15.0 eV is absorbed by a hydrogen atom in its ground state, and the electron is released. Calculate the kinetic energy of the released electron, in joules.
items.ms: Zero energy is when the electron is (just) free of the atom / the atom is ionised Energy must be supplied to remove an electron from the atom, so a bound electron has less than zero energy Conversion of 13.6 eV to J and use of E = hf f = 3.28 × 10¹⁵ Hz Energy left after ionisation = 15.0 eV − 13.6 eV = 1.4 eV Ek = 2.2 × 10⁻¹⁹ J
items.why: Negative energy levels with ionisation at 0 eV appear in every S63 diagram (beyond spec but examined) yet have never been asked about directly; ionisation followed by kinetic energy mirrors hf = φ + ½mv²_{max}, and S63 has come up in all 21 sessions.

items.name: Line spectra and energy levels
path: Unit 2 Waves and Electricity
Waves and Particle Nature of Light
S63 - atomic line spectra in terms of transitions b
items.question: A fluorescent lamp is a glass tube that contains mercury vapour. Electrons passing through the vapour excite the mercury atoms, which then emit ultraviolet radiation. A coating on the inside of the glass absorbs the ultraviolet radiation and emits visible light. The diagram shows some of the energy levels of a mercury atom. Electrons in mercury atoms are excited to the −2.7 eV level. Determine the number of different photon energies that could be emitted as the electrons return to the ground state. Calculate the wavelength of the radiation emitted when an electron moves from the −5.5 eV level to the −10.4 eV level. Explain how the coating can emit visible light when it absorbs ultraviolet radiation. Each ultraviolet photon absorbed by the coating produces no more than one visible photon. Assume that all the ultraviolet photons absorbed by the coating have the wavelength calculated in (b), and that all the visible photons have a wavelength of 545 nm. The manufacturer claims that the coating transfers 80% of the energy of the ultraviolet radiation it absorbs to visible light. Deduce whether the manufacturer's claim could be correct.
items.ms: Possible transitions between the −2.7, −3.7, −5.5 and −10.4 eV levels identified (e.g. drawn on the diagram) 6 ΔE = 4.9 eV, converted to J (7.84 × 10⁻¹⁹ J) Use of E = hf and v = fλ (or λ = hc/E) λ = 2.54 × 10⁻⁷ m An ultraviolet photon is absorbed by an electron in the coating, which is raised to a much higher energy level The electron returns to lower levels in several smaller steps (through intermediate levels) / some of the energy is transferred as thermal energy A smaller energy difference means a photon of lower energy, so lower frequency / longer wavelength So photons in the visible range can be emitted Use of E = hc/λ for a visible photon (3.65 × 10⁻¹⁹ J or 2.28 eV) Greatest fraction = visible photon energy ÷ ultraviolet photon energy = 0.47 (47%) 47% is less than 80%, so the claim cannot be correct
items.why: S63 is asked every session and lamp contexts recur (Jun2024 Q17 discharge tube, Jun2025 Q18 mercury lamp, Jun2026 Q13 neon); fluorescence, absorbing one high-energy photon and emitting lower-energy ones, has never been asked, and the efficiency claim is a compare-and-conclude in Edexcel's style.

items.name: Line spectra and energy levels
path: Unit 2 Waves and Electricity
Waves and Particle Nature of Light
S63 - atomic line spectra in terms of transitions b
items.question: In 1868, astronomers observed a bright yellow line in the spectrum of light from the Sun that did not match the line spectrum of any element known on Earth. The line was later shown to be produced by helium. State why a line spectrum can be used to identify an element. Helium gas in a discharge tube on Earth emits the same yellow line. There is a large potential difference across the tube. Explain how the helium in the tube emits light that has a line spectrum. The light from the discharge tube passes through a diffraction grating that has 300 lines per mm. The first-order maximum for the yellow line is at an angle of 10.2° to the straight-through direction. Show that the wavelength of the yellow light is about 5.9 × 10⁻⁷ m. The diagram shows some of the energy levels of a helium atom. Determine which transition produces the yellow line.
items.ms: Each element has its own (unique) set of energy levels, so it emits (or absorbs) its own set of frequencies / wavelengths IC1 The potential difference accelerates (free) electrons through the gas / there is a current in the gas IC2 These electrons collide with helium atoms and transfer energy to them IC3 Electrons in the helium atoms are raised (excited) to higher energy levels IC4 The atomic electrons fall back (de-excite) to lower energy levels, emitting a photon IC5 The photon energy equals the difference between the two energy levels: ΔE = hf IC6 The energy levels are discrete, so only certain energy differences, and so only certain frequencies / wavelengths, are emitted d = 1 ÷ (3.00 × 10⁵ m⁻¹) = 3.33 × 10⁻⁶ m Use of nλ = d sin θ with n = 1 λ = 5.90 × 10⁻⁷ m Use of E = hf and v = fλ (or E = hc/λ): E = 3.37 × 10⁻¹⁹ J Conversion to eV: E = 2.11 eV Transition from −1.51 eV down to −3.62 eV
items.why: S63 has come up in all 21 sessions; explaining a discharge-tube line spectrum is its most frequent 6-mark (Oct2021 Q16a, Jun2024 Q17a(ii)), and identifying a measured line on a level diagram (Oct2019 Q11, Oct2025 Q11) after a grating measurement makes a typical late long question.

path: Unit 2 Waves and Electricity
Waves and Particle Nature of Light
S44 - use the equation for the intensity of radiati
items.question: A navigation lamp on top of a mast emits light with a power of 12 W uniformly in all directions. What is the intensity of the light at a distance of 2.0 m from the lamp? 0.24 W m⁻² 0.48 W m⁻² 0.95 W m⁻² 3.0 W m⁻²
items.ms: I = P/4πr² = 12 W ÷ (4π × (2.0 m)²) = 0.24 W m⁻². B uses 4πr instead of 4πr²; C uses the area of a circle, πr², instead of the area of a sphere; D divides the power by r² only.
items.why: S44 has come up in 19 of 21 sessions; light spreading from a point source over 4πr² is the commonest set-up (Jan2024 Q8, Oct2022 Q17c), and the digest notes candidates using πr² for a sphere.

path: Unit 2 Waves and Electricity
Waves and Particle Nature of Light
S44 - use the equation for the intensity of radiati
items.question: A laser pointer emits a parallel beam of light with a power of 5.0 mW. The beam has a circular cross-section of diameter 2.0 mm. What is the intensity of the beam? 1.6 W m⁻² 4.0 × 10² W m⁻² 1.6 × 10³ W m⁻² 1.6 × 10⁶ W m⁻²
items.ms: The beam does not spread out, so A is its cross-sectional area: A = π × (1.0 × 10⁻³ m)² = 3.14 × 10⁻⁶ m², and I = 5.0 × 10⁻³ W ÷ 3.14 × 10⁻⁶ m² = 1.6 × 10³ W m⁻². A does not square the radius; B uses the diameter as the radius (the same value as using 4πr²); D leaves the power in mW.
items.why: Intensity questions nearly always use a point source or a solar panel (Jun2026 Q18, Jan2025 Q12); the intensity of a parallel beam, where A is the beam's cross-section, has not been asked and is a likely variation.

path: Unit 2 Waves and Electricity
Waves and Particle Nature of Light
S44 - use the equation for the intensity of radiati
items.question: A space probe has solar panels that always face the Sun. Near the Earth the panels supply 2.4 kW of electrical power. The probe then moves into orbit around Venus, which is 0.72 times as far from the Sun as the Earth is. The efficiency of the panels does not change. What power do the panels supply near Venus? 1.2 kW 1.7 kW 3.3 kW 4.6 kW
items.ms: The Sun's power spreads over a sphere, so I ∝ 1/r² and the panels' output is proportional to I: 2.4 kW ÷ 0.72² = 4.6 kW. A multiplies by 0.72² instead of dividing; B multiplies by 0.72; C divides by 0.72 (inverse instead of inverse square).
items.why: Comparing the intensity of sunlight at two planets was asked in Jun2023 Q9 (an expression MCQ) and Jun2019 Q13; here it is numerical, with the probe moving closer to the Sun.

path: Unit 2 Waves and Electricity
Waves and Particle Nature of Light
S44 - use the equation for the intensity of radiati
items.question: A radio beacon left on the surface of the Moon transmits radio waves with a power of 5.0 W. Assume that the beacon emits uniformly in all directions. A radio telescope on the Earth, 3.84 × 10⁸ m from the beacon, has a circular dish of diameter 25 m facing the Moon. Calculate the power of the radio waves received by the dish.
items.ms: Use of A = 4πr² Use of I = P/A (I = 2.7 × 10⁻¹⁸ W m⁻²) Area of dish = π × (12.5 m)² (= 491 m²) P = 1.3 × 10⁻¹⁵ W
items.why: S44 has come up in 19 of 21 sessions; spreading over 4πr² (Jan2024 Q8) and the power collected by a dish of given area (Jan2026 Q11(b)) are joined here, with two different areas to keep apart.

path: Unit 2 Waves and Electricity
Waves and Particle Nature of Light
S44 - use the equation for the intensity of radiati
items.question: A student investigates how the intensity I of the light from a small lamp varies with the distance d from the lamp. She uses a light sensor that measures intensity in W m⁻². Her results are shown in the table. The student predicts that a graph of I against d⁻² will be a straight line. Explain why she makes this prediction. Complete the table. Plot a graph of I against d⁻² on the grid. Use your graph to determine the power of the light emitted by the lamp. The line of best fit does not pass through the origin. Suggest why.
items.ms: The light (power) from the lamp spreads out over the surface of a sphere of area 4πd² So I = P/4πd²; P is constant, so I is proportional to d⁻² (a straight line through the origin) d⁻² = 44.4 m⁻² Axes labelled with quantities and units, with sensible scales (plotted points cover at least half of the grid in each direction) All points plotted accurately (to within half a small square) Straight line of best fit Gradient determined using a large triangle Gradient = P/4π (or use of I = P/4πd² with the gradient) P = 0.88 W The sensor also detects light from other sources (e.g. a window, a screen, or light reflected from walls), which adds a constant intensity to every reading
items.why: S44 is hot (19 of 21 sessions) but is nearly always set as a calculation; the digest's graph skills (linearise, then use the gradient) have not yet been applied to the inverse-square law, so a practical-style question is a likely surprise.

path: Unit 2 Waves and Electricity
Waves and Particle Nature of Light
S44 - use the equation for the intensity of radiati
items.question: Some drones can be powered in flight by an infrared laser on the ground. The laser beam has a power of 2.0 kW and a wavelength of 1.06 μm. The beam is aimed vertically upwards at a circular panel of photovoltaic cells, of diameter 0.30 m, under a drone hovering at a height of 120 m. At this height the beam is a circle of diameter 0.24 m, so all of the beam falls on the panel. Assume that the intensity is uniform across the beam and that no energy is absorbed by the air. Calculate the intensity of the beam at the panel. Show that about 1 × 10²² photons reach the panel each second. The panel converts the infrared to electrical energy with an efficiency of 42%. The drone's motors work at a potential difference of 48 V. Calculate the current in the motors. The beam spreads out so that its diameter is proportional to its distance from the laser. The drone needs at least 600 W of electrical power to hover. The drone rises to a height of 180 m. Deduce whether the drone can still hover at this height. Suggest why the drone might not be able to hover at 120 m on a foggy day.
items.ms: Use of I = P/A with A = π × (0.12 m)² I = 4.4 × 10⁴ W m⁻² Use of c = fλ (f = 2.83 × 10¹⁴ Hz) Use of E = hf (E = 1.88 × 10⁻¹⁹ J) Number per second = P/E = 1.07 × 10²² Use of efficiency = useful power output ÷ total power input (electrical power = 840 W) Use of P = VI I = 17.5 A Beam diameter at 180 m = 0.36 m (or intensity at 180 m = 1.96 × 10⁴ W m⁻², or intensity reduced by a factor of (120/180)²) Power reaching the panel = I × area of panel = 1.39 kW (or fraction of beam on panel = (0.30/0.36)² = 0.69) Electrical power = 0.42 × 1.39 kW = 583 W 583 W is less than 600 W, so the drone cannot hover at 180 m Water droplets absorb or scatter some of the infrared, so less power (a lower intensity) reaches the panel
items.why: Photon rates from a beam (Jun2025 Q18(b), Jan2026 Q21(a)) and the efficiency of a panel (Jun2026 Q18) recur; a laser beam whose intensity falls as it widens is a new set-up that tests what A means in I = P/A.

items.name: Refraction and refractive index
path: Unit 2 Waves and Electricity
Waves and Particle Nature of Light
S45 - that at the interface between medium 1 and me
items.question: Light passes from air into glass. Which row describes what happens to the speed, the frequency and the wavelength of the light? speed: decreases; frequency: unchanged; wavelength: decreases speed: decreases; frequency: decreases; wavelength: unchanged speed: increases; frequency: unchanged; wavelength: increases speed: unchanged; frequency: decreases; wavelength: decreases
items.ms: Glass has a greater refractive index than air, so the speed v = c/n is smaller. The frequency is set by the source and does not change at the boundary, so the wavelength λ = v/f decreases. B changes the frequency instead of the wavelength; C has the light speeding up in glass; D keeps the speed constant.
items.why: S45 has come up in all 21 sessions; the speed in a medium is asked in most of them (Jun2025 Q1, Oct2024 Q17(a)), and linking it to v = fλ checks that students know the frequency does not change.

items.name: Refraction and refractive index
path: Unit 2 Waves and Electricity
Waves and Particle Nature of Light
S45 - that at the interface between medium 1 and me
items.question: A ray of light in water meets the flat top surface of a glass block lying on the bottom of a tank. The angle of incidence is 40°. refractive index of water = 1.33 refractive index of glass = 1.52 What is the angle of refraction in the glass? 25° 34° 47° 61°
items.ms: 1.33 sin 40° = 1.52 sin θ, so sin θ = 0.562 and θ = 34°. A ignores the water (sin 40° ÷ 1.52, as if from air); C puts the refractive indices the wrong way round; D is the critical angle for the glass–water boundary (sin C = 1.33/1.52).
items.why: Refraction between two media that are not air (Oct2023 Q18b, Jun2026 Q14(a)) is a regular variation; the Jun2021 mark scheme notes candidates who put the refractive indices the wrong way round.

items.name: Refraction and refractive index
path: Unit 2 Waves and Electricity
Waves and Particle Nature of Light
S45 - that at the interface between medium 1 and me
items.question: Light travels from vegetable oil into water. The speed of light is 2.05 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ in the oil and 2.25 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ in the water. A ray in the oil makes an angle of 38° with the boundary. What happens to the ray at the boundary? It refracts, with an angle of refraction of 43°. It refracts, with an angle of refraction of 46°. It refracts, with an angle of refraction of 60°. It is totally internally reflected.
items.ms: The angle of incidence is measured from the normal: 90° − 38° = 52°. With n = c/v, noil sin 52° = nwater sin θ, so sin θ = sin 52° × 2.25/2.05 = 0.865 and θ = 60°. A uses 38° as the angle of incidence; B puts the speeds in place of the refractive indices; D: the critical angle is sin⁻¹(2.05/2.25) = 66°, which is larger than 52°, so there is no total internal reflection.
items.why: Oct2021 Q11a and Jun2026 Q10 gave speeds instead of refractive indices, and the Oct2021 report says substituting speeds as n scored 0; the Jan2023 report adds that candidates used angles that were not to the normal.

items.name: Refraction and refractive index

items.question: A laser beam is directed at the glass wall of an aquarium full of water. The diagram shows the beam meeting the glass at an angle of incidence of 35°. refractive index of glass = 1.52 refractive index of water = 1.33 Calculate the angle of refraction in the glass. Calculate the angle between the beam in the water and the normal. The laser light has a wavelength of 532 nm in air. Calculate the wavelength of the light in the water.
items.ms: Use of n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂ with 1.00 and 1.52 θ = 22.2° Use of 1.52 sin θglass = 1.33 sin θwater with the angle from (a) (or 1.00 sin 35° = 1.33 sin θwater) θ = 25.5° Use of n = c/v (v = 2.26 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹) Use of v = fλ with the frequency unchanged (f = 5.64 × 10¹⁴ Hz) λ = 400 nm
items.why: S45 has been asked in all 21 sessions; a ray crossing two boundaries (air–glass–water) and the wavelength in the second medium combine the calculations of Jun2025 Q12(a) and Oct2024 Q17(a) with v = fλ.

items.name: Refraction and refractive index
path: Unit 2 Waves and Electricity
Waves and Particle Nature of Light
S45 - that at the interface between medium 1 and me
items.question: On a hot, still day a driver sees what looks like a pool of water on the road far ahead. The air just above the road surface is much hotter than the air higher up. The diagram shows the path of a ray of light from the sky that reaches the driver's eye. The diagram is not to scale. refractive index of air at 20 °C = 1.000 27 refractive index of air at 60 °C = 1.000 24 Calculate the critical angle for light travelling from air at 20 °C into air at 60 °C. Explain why light from the sky follows the path shown, and why the driver sees what looks like a pool of water on the road. Use your answer to (a) to explain why the 'pool of water' is seen only on the road far ahead of the car and not close to it.
items.ms: Use of n₁ sin C = n₂ sin 90° with both values (sin C = 1.000 24 ÷ 1.000 27) C = 89.6° IC1 The air nearer the road is hotter (less dense), so it has a lower refractive index and light travels faster in it IC2 As the ray travels down into warmer air it refracts away from the normal IC3 So the angle of incidence at each layer increases and the path curves (becomes more nearly horizontal) IC4 When the angle of incidence exceeds the critical angle the light is totally internally reflected and travels back upwards IC5 Going up into cooler air the ray refracts towards the normal and reaches the driver's eye from below the horizontal IC6 The eye/brain assumes light travels in straight lines, so the light appears to come from the road surface ahead: an image of the sky on the road, which looks like light reflected from water The angle of incidence must be greater than about 89.6°, so the ray must travel almost parallel to the road (within about 0.4°); only light reaching the eye from points far along the road arrives this close to horizontal
items.why: Oct2024 Q17b set a 6-mark question on refraction and total internal reflection at a water surface, and Jan2026 Q18(a) asked why a wave's path curves as its speed changes; a mirage applies both ideas to light in air.

items.name: Refraction and refractive index
path: Unit 2 Waves and Electricity
Waves and Particle Nature of Light
S45 - that at the interface between medium 1 and me
items.question: Rainbows are formed when sunlight passes through raindrops. The diagram shows the path of a ray of red light through a spherical raindrop with centre O. The ray enters the drop at A, is reflected at B and leaves the drop at C. The angle of incidence at A is 59.0°. refractive index of water for red light = 1.331 refractive index of water for violet light = 1.343 Explain why the light changes direction at A. Show that the angle of refraction of the red light at A is about 40°. Sunlight also contains violet light. Calculate the angle between the red ray and the violet ray inside the drop just after they enter at A. The angle of incidence at B is equal to the angle of refraction at A. Deduce whether the red light is totally internally reflected at B. The frequency of the red light is 4.40 × 10¹⁴ Hz. Calculate the wavelength of the red light inside the drop. Suggest why the light leaving the drop at C is much less intense than the light entering at A.
items.ms: The light slows down (its speed decreases) as it enters the water / water has a greater refractive index than air One side of each wavefront reaches the water (and slows down) before the other side, so the wavefront changes direction Use of n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂ (sin r = sin 59.0° ÷ 1.331) r = 40.1° Use of n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂ with 1.343 Angle of refraction for violet light = 39.66° Angle between the rays = 0.43° Use of sin C = 1/n C = 48.7° 40.1° is less than 48.7°, so the light is not totally internally reflected (most of it refracts out of the drop at B; only part is reflected) Use of n = c/v (v = 2.25 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹) Use of v = fλ λ = 5.12 × 10⁻⁷ m The light is not totally internally reflected at B, so most of it leaves the drop at B and only a small fraction is reflected towards C
items.why: Dispersion of red and violet light (Jun2021 Q13, Oct2025 Q13) and deciding whether TIR occurs (Jan2025 Q18b) recur; a raindrop, in which the reflection is only partial, is an unfamiliar context of the kind the Oct2022 report describes.

path: Unit 2 Waves and Electricity
Waves and Particle Nature of Light
S46 - calculate critical angle using 1 sin C  n Spe
items.question: An optical fibre has a core of refractive index 1.50 surrounded by cladding of refractive index 1.46. What is the critical angle at the core–cladding boundary? 2.3° 41.8° 43.2° 76.7°
items.ms: ncore sin C = ncladding sin 90°, so sin C = 1.46/1.50 = 0.973 and C = 76.7°. A uses sin C = 1.50 − 1.46; B is the critical angle for a core–air boundary (sin C = 1/1.50); C uses sin C = 1/1.46.
items.why: S46 has been asked in 7 of 21 sessions; the core–cladding critical angle was a show-that in Oct2022 Q16a, and Jan2025 Q18(d) asked how the cladding changes it.

path: Unit 2 Waves and Electricity
Waves and Particle Nature of Light
S46 - calculate critical angle using 1 sin C  n Spe
items.question: A gemmologist uses a refractometer to identify gemstones. A flat face of the gemstone is placed on the flat top surface of a hemisphere of glass of refractive index 1.81. Light inside the glass travels towards the centre of the flat surface at a range of angles of incidence θ, as shown in the diagram. Light with an angle of incidence greater than the critical angle is totally internally reflected to the viewer, where a scale shows the critical angle at the glass–gemstone boundary. The table gives the refractive indices of some gemstones. State the condition that the refractive index of a gemstone must meet for a critical angle to be measured. For one gemstone the critical angle is 63.5°. Identify the gemstone. The scale can show only critical angles from 55° to 75°. Deduce which of the gemstones in the table cannot be identified with this refractometer.
items.ms: The refractive index of the gemstone must be less than 1.81 (less than that of the glass) Use of n₁ sin C = n₂ sin 90° (n = 1.81 × sin 63.5°) n = 1.62 Topaz Use of n = 1.81 × sin C for either limit The refractive index must be between 1.48 and 1.75 Fluorite, ruby and diamond cannot be identified
items.why: S46 was asked in 7 of 21 sessions, mostly as a critical angle from two refractive indices (Oct2023 Q18b, Oct2022 Q16a); working back from a measured critical angle to identify a material from a table (as with the gemstones of Oct2021 Q11a) has not been asked.

path: Unit 2 Waves and Electricity
Waves and Particle Nature of Light
S47 - predict whether total internal reflection wil
items.question: Light travelling in material P meets a boundary with material Q. The angle of incidence is 50°. For which pair of materials is the light totally internally reflected? refractive index of P: 1.40; refractive index of Q: 1.00 refractive index of P: 1.50; refractive index of Q: 1.33 refractive index of P: 1.60; refractive index of Q: 1.45 refractive index of P: 1.70; refractive index of Q: 1.80
items.ms: TIR needs the light to travel towards a material of lower refractive index, with an angle of incidence greater than C, where sin C = nQ/nP. A: C = 45.6°, less than 50°, so TIR occurs. B: C = 62.5° and C: C = 65.0°, both greater than 50°. D: Q has the greater refractive index, so there is no critical angle.
items.why: S47 has come up in 15 of 21 sessions, including row-choice MCQs on the conditions for TIR (Jun2026 Q5, Jun2025 Q2); here each row needs its own critical angle, and the largest refractive index is a distractor.

path: Unit 2 Waves and Electricity
Waves and Particle Nature of Light
S47 - predict whether total internal reflection wil
items.question: An underwater camera uses a right-angled isosceles glass prism to turn light through 90°. The light enters one of the two shorter faces along the normal and meets the longest face at an angle of incidence of 45°. The longest face is in contact with water of refractive index 1.33. What is the least refractive index of the glass for which the light is totally internally reflected at the longest face? 0.94 1.33 1.41 1.88
items.ms: For TIR the critical angle must be no more than 45°: nglass sin 45° = 1.33 sin 90°, so nglass = 1.33 ÷ sin 45° = 1.88. A multiplies 1.33 by sin 45°; B is the same as water, so there would be no critical angle; C is the value for a prism in air (1 ÷ sin 45°).
items.why: Jan2025 Q18(b) and May2024 Q18(b) asked whether TIR occurs in a 45° prism in air; putting the prism in water, so that the critical angle depends on two refractive indices, is the likely next step.

path: Unit 2 Waves and Electricity
Waves and Particle Nature of Light
S47 - predict whether total internal reflection wil
items.question: Many cars have a rain sensor that switches on the windscreen wipers. An LED sends infrared radiation into the windscreen glass. The LED and a detector are attached to the inside of the windscreen by plastic blocks with the same refractive index as the glass. The diagram shows the path of the infrared when the outside of the windscreen is dry. The infrared meets the outer surface of the glass at P, where it makes an angle of 42° with the surface. refractive index of glass = 1.52 refractive index of water = 1.33 Show that the critical angle for the glass–air boundary is about 41°. A raindrop lands on the windscreen and covers P. Calculate the angle of refraction of the infrared in the raindrop. Explain how the sensor detects rain on the windscreen, and why it can be used to make the wipers move faster in heavier rain.
items.ms: Use of sin C = 1/n C = 41.1° Angle of incidence at P = 90° − 42° = 48° Use of n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂ with 1.52 and 1.33 θ = 58.1° IC1 When the windscreen is dry, the angle of incidence at P (48°) is greater than the critical angle for glass–air (41°) IC2 So the infrared is totally internally reflected at P and (almost) all of it reaches the detector IC3 Water has a higher refractive index than air, so the critical angle for glass–water is larger (61°), greater than 48° IC4 So when a drop covers P the infrared is not totally internally reflected; most of it refracts out into the water (as in (b)) IC5 So the intensity (power) of infrared reaching the detector decreases, and this fall in the detector's output is used to switch on the wipers IC6 In heavier rain more of the glass is covered by water, so more infrared escapes and the detector receives even less, which can be used to run the wipers faster
items.why: S47 has come up in 15 of 21 sessions; sensors whose output depends on whether TIR happens (the fingerprint scanner of Oct2023 Q18d, the dipstick of Jan2026 Q16c) are a favourite, and Oct2024 Q17b set a 6-mark question on TIR.

path: Unit 2 Waves and Electricity
Waves and Particle Nature of Light
S48 - how to measure the refractive index of a soli
items.question: A student wants to determine the refractive index of glass. She has a rectangular glass block, a ray box, a protractor, a pencil, a ruler and a sheet of white paper. Describe how she should obtain values of the angle of incidence i and the angle of refraction r. Her results are shown in the table. Plot a graph of sin i against sin r on the grid. Use your graph to determine the refractive index of the glass.
items.ms: Place the block on the paper and draw around its outline Direct a narrow ray of light from the ray box at one side of the block Draw the normal at the point where the ray enters the block Mark the ray emerging from the opposite side with two (widely spaced) crosses, then remove the block and join the point of entry to the point of exit to show the refracted ray Measure i and r from the normal with the protractor Repeat for a range of angles of incidence (e.g. 10° to 70°) All points plotted accurately (to within half a small square) Straight line of best fit Gradient determined using a large triangle (n = gradient) n = 1.50
items.why: S48 has never been examined as a method (the digest finds it tested only through ray diagrams such as Jun2022 Q11a and Jan2021 Q15b), so a describe-and-graph question is the likeliest surprise; the gradient of sin i against sin r gives n.

items.name: Plane polarisation
path: Unit 2 Waves and Electricity
Waves and Particle Nature of Light
S49 - what is meant by plane polarisation
items.question: Which of these waves can be plane polarised? sound waves in air ultrasound waves in soft tissue microwaves longitudinal waves on a stretched spring
items.ms: Only transverse waves can be plane polarised, because their oscillations are perpendicular to the direction of travel and can be restricted to one plane. Microwaves are electromagnetic, transverse waves. A, B and D are longitudinal waves, whose oscillations are along the direction of travel.
items.why: S49 has come up in 17 of 21 sessions; 'only transverse waves can be polarised' was tested in Oct2019 Q6 and Oct2020 Q8 and underlies the radio-aerial question of Jan2026 Q18(c).

items.name: Plane polarisation
path: Unit 2 Waves and Electricity
Waves and Particle Nature of Light
S49 - what is meant by plane polarisation
items.question: Unpolarised light passes through two polarising filters, X and then Y. The intensity of the light leaving Y is at its maximum. Filter Y is then rotated through 360° about the direction of the light, while X is kept still. At which angles of rotation of Y is the intensity of the light leaving Y zero? 90° only 90° and 270° 45°, 135°, 225° and 315° 90°, 180°, 270° and 360°
items.ms: The intensity is zero when Y's transmission plane is perpendicular to X's, which happens twice in a full turn: at 90° and 270°. A misses the second minimum; C gives the positions where the planes are at 45°, where some light passes; D also counts 180° and 360°, where the planes are parallel again and the intensity is a maximum.
items.why: Rotating-filter MCQs were set in Jan2024 Q9 and Oct2025 Q9, and Jun2025 Q12(b)(ii) rewarded 'maximum to minimum every 90°'; the Jun2022 report says polarisation remains a common difficulty.

items.name: Plane polarisation
path: Unit 2 Waves and Electricity
Waves and Particle Nature of Light
S49 - what is meant by plane polarisation
items.question: Unpolarised light is incident on two polarising filters P and R. The transmission planes of P and R are at 90° to each other, so no light emerges from R. A third polarising filter Q is placed between P and R, with its transmission plane at 45° to the planes of both P and R. Which statement is correct? No light emerges from R, because the planes of P and R are still at 90° to each other. Some light emerges from R, because the light leaving Q oscillates in a plane at 45° to the plane of R. Some light emerges from R, because Q makes the light unpolarised again. All of the light that passes through P also emerges from R.
items.ms: P plane polarises the light. Q transmits part of it, and the light leaving Q oscillates in Q's plane, at 45° to R's transmission plane, so it has a component parallel to R's plane and some passes through R. A ignores the change of plane at Q; C: a polarising filter cannot make light unpolarised; D: Q and R each remove part of the light, so not all of it emerges.
items.why: Oct2025 Q18(b) asked for a 5-mark explanation of three filters with the middle one rotated; with two-filter MCQs in Jan2024 Q9 and Oct2025 Q9, a three-filter MCQ is a likely next form.

items.name: Plane polarisation
path: Unit 2 Waves and Electricity
Waves and Particle Nature of Light
S49 - what is meant by plane polarisation
items.question: A student has a single polarising filter and a light meter. She wants to find out whether the light from a laser is plane polarised. Describe what she should do, and what she would observe if the light is plane polarised.
items.ms: Place the filter in the laser beam and measure the intensity of the light passing through it with the light meter Rotate the filter about the direction of the beam (in its own plane) through at least 180° If the light is plane polarised the intensity varies, from a maximum to a minimum (zero) every 90° of rotation If the light were unpolarised, the intensity would not change as the filter is rotated
items.why: Testing light with one rotating filter was asked in Jan2021 Q18a and Jan2023 Q16b(ii), and the Jun2019 report found many candidates applied two-filter ideas when only one filter was present.

items.name: Plane polarisation
path: Unit 2 Waves and Electricity
Waves and Particle Nature of Light
S49 - what is meant by plane polarisation
items.question: Sunlight is unpolarised. When sunlight is reflected from the flat surface of a lake, the reflected light is partially plane polarised. At one angle of incidence, θB, the reflected light is completely plane polarised. This happens when the reflected ray and the refracted ray are at 90° to each other, as shown in the diagram. refractive index of water = 1.33 Explain the difference between unpolarised light and plane polarised light. Show that θB is about 53°. A photographer looks at the reflection of the sky in the lake at the angle θB, through a polarising filter. She rotates the filter through 180°. Describe and explain how the brightness of the reflection changes.
items.ms: Unpolarised light: oscillations in all (many) planes Plane polarised light: oscillations in one plane only The plane(s) include the direction of travel of the wave (direction of energy transfer) Angle of refraction = 90° − θB (angles on a straight line with the 90° between the rays) Use of 1.00 sin θB = 1.33 sin(90° − θB), giving tan θB = 1.33 θB = 53.1° The brightness varies between a maximum and zero, with the maximum and the zero 90° apart (one zero in 180°) It is zero (the reflection disappears) when the filter's transmission plane is perpendicular to the plane of oscillation of the reflected light, because the reflected light is completely polarised
items.why: Defining plane polarisation has been asked in 6 sessions (most recently Oct2025 Q18a, 3 marks); polarisation by reflection (Jun2023 Q13b, Jun2026 Q11) and the Brewster-angle derivation from Snell's law (Oct2019 Q18c) are combined here.

path: Unit 2 Waves and Electricity
Electric Circuits
S74 - how the potential along a uniform current-car
items.question: Wire P and wire Q are uniform and made of the same metal. P has length 0.600 m and diameter 0.50 mm. Q has length 0.400 m and diameter 0.25 mm. The wires are joined at B and connected in series with a cell of e.m.f. 3.0 V and negligible internal resistance, as shown. A voltmeter is connected between end A of wire P and a sliding contact S. The distance of S from A is x. Explain why the voltmeter reading is directly proportional to x while S is on wire P. Show that the p.d. across wire P is about 0.8 V. S is moved from A to C. Sketch a graph on the axes to show how the voltmeter reading V varies with x.
items.ms: The current is the same at all points along wire P (it is in series) P is uniform (same ρ and A), so the resistance between A and S is proportional to x (R = ρx/A) V = IR, so V is proportional to x Use of R = ρl/A with A = πd²/4 (or R ∝ l/d²) RQ = 2.67 × RP (or RP : RQ = 3 : 8) Ratio of p.d.s = ratio of resistances, so V = 3.0 V × 3/11 = 0.82 V Straight line through the origin from x = 0 to x = 0.60 m Line reaches about 0.8 V at x = 0.60 m Straight line with a greater gradient from x = 0.60 m, reaching 3.0 V at x = 1.00 m
items.why: S74 came up in 5 of 21 sessions, always as a 1-mark item (Jun2023, Jan2024 and Jan2026 MCQs) apart from a V against l graph in Jan2021; a structured question with two wires of different thickness, linked to R = ρl/A, has not been set.

path: Unit 2 Waves and Electricity
Electric Circuits
S75 - the principles of a potential divider circuit
items.question: A potential divider consists of a 1.0 kΩ resistor in series with a variable resistor that can be set to any value from 0 to 5.0 kΩ. The divider is connected to a 6.0 V supply of negligible internal resistance. The output is the p.d. across the variable resistor. What is the range of the output p.d.? 0 to 1.0 V 0 to 5.0 V 0 to 6.0 V 1.0 V to 6.0 V
items.ms: Output = 6.0 V × R/(R + 1.0 kΩ): 0 when R = 0, and 6.0 × 5.0/6.0 = 5.0 V when R = 5.0 kΩ. A is the p.d. across the fixed resistor at the maximum setting. C ignores the share of the p.d. across the fixed resistor. D is the range of the p.d. across the fixed resistor.
items.why: S75 was asked as MCQs in Jan2024 and May2024; a divider with a variable resistor tests the same ratio idea at both ends of its range.

path: Unit 2 Waves and Electricity
Electric Circuits
S75 - the principles of a potential divider circuit
items.question: A student sets up the circuit shown. The battery has an e.m.f. of 9.0 V and negligible internal resistance. Calculate the reading on the voltmeter, assuming that the voltmeter has a very high resistance. The voltmeter has a resistance of 120 kΩ. Calculate the reading on the voltmeter. The student replaces the 33 kΩ and 15 kΩ resistors with resistors of 330 Ω and 150 Ω. The same voltmeter is used. Explain why the voltmeter reading is now much closer to the value calculated in (a).
items.ms: Use of Vout = V × R₂/(R₁ + R₂) (or I = 9.0 V ÷ 48 kΩ and V = IR) V = 2.81 V Use of 1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ for the voltmeter in parallel with the 15 kΩ resistor Combined resistance = 13.3 kΩ V = 9.0 V × 13.3/(33 + 13.3) = 2.59 V The voltmeter's resistance is very much greater than 150 Ω, so the parallel combination is almost exactly 150 Ω (149.8 Ω) so the ratio of the resistances, and so the ratio of the p.d.s, is almost unchanged / the voltmeter takes a negligible fraction of the current
items.why: S75 calculations came up in 5 of 21 sessions (Jan2026 Q16a); the Oct2020 report said very few candidates allowed for the voltmeter's own resistance, so a calculation of this loading effect is the likeliest new angle.

items.name: Potential dividers with sensors
path: Unit 2 Waves and Electricity
Electric Circuits
S76 - analyse potential divider circuits where one
items.question: An NTC thermistor is connected in series with a fixed resistor, an ammeter and a battery of negligible internal resistance. A voltmeter is connected across the thermistor. The temperature of the thermistor decreases. Which row describes the changes in the meter readings? ammeter reading: decreases; voltmeter reading: increases ammeter reading: decreases; voltmeter reading: decreases ammeter reading: increases; voltmeter reading: decreases ammeter reading: increases; voltmeter reading: increases
items.ms: Colder: fewer conduction electrons, so the thermistor's resistance increases. The total resistance increases, so the current falls; the thermistor has a larger share of the total resistance, so the p.d. across it rises. B gives the change in the p.d. across the fixed resistor (IR falls). C is what happens when the temperature rises (or for a metal resistor that is cooled). D has the current rising although the total resistance has increased.
items.why: Meter-reading MCQs on sensor circuits recur (Oct2022 Q3, Jan2023 Q6, Oct2024 Q6, Jun2025 Q6); a falling temperature with the voltmeter across the thermistor reverses the usual set-up.

items.name: Potential dividers with sensors
path: Unit 2 Waves and Electricity
Electric Circuits
S76 - analyse potential divider circuits where one
items.question: An LDR is connected in series with a 15 kΩ resistor across a 6.0 V supply of negligible internal resistance. The resistance of the LDR is 4.5 kΩ in daylight and 60 kΩ in darkness. By how much does the p.d. across the 15 kΩ resistor decrease when daylight changes to darkness? 1.2 V 1.4 V 3.4 V 4.6 V
items.ms: Daylight: 6.0 × 15/19.5 = 4.6 V. Darkness: 6.0 × 15/75 = 1.2 V. Decrease = 3.4 V. A is the p.d. in darkness, B the p.d. across the LDR in daylight, D the p.d. in daylight.
items.why: Divider calculations with an LDR resistance at two light levels recur (Oct2019 Q14b, Jun2026 Q14); a 'change in p.d.' MCQ needs both steps.

items.name: Potential dividers with sensors
path: Unit 2 Waves and Electricity
Electric Circuits
S76 - analyse potential divider circuits where one
items.question: An NTC thermistor and a fixed resistor are connected in series to a battery of negligible internal resistance. The temperature of the thermistor increases. Which of the following does not happen? The current in the fixed resistor increases. The p.d. across the thermistor decreases. The ratio (p.d. across the thermistor ÷ p.d. across the fixed resistor) decreases. The total power supplied by the battery decreases.
items.ms: The thermistor's resistance falls, so the total resistance falls and P = V²/Rtotal increases: D does not happen. A happens because the current rises. B happens because the thermistor has a smaller share of the total resistance. C happens because the ratio of the p.d.s equals the ratio of the resistances, which falls.
items.why: The Jan2022 'not' MCQ on an LDR divider caught most candidates (the report says most chose options that do happen); a thermistor version with a power option, as in the Jun2023 6-mark question, is a likely repeat of the format.

items.name: Potential dividers with sensors
path: Unit 2 Waves and Electricity
Electric Circuits
S76 - analyse potential divider circuits where one
items.question: A solar panel turns to follow the Sun. Two identical LDRs, L₁ and L₂, are mounted on the panel, one on each side of a small screen. When the panel faces the Sun, both LDRs receive the same light. When it does not, the screen shades one of the LDRs. The LDRs are connected in the circuit shown. The supply has an e.m.f. of 12.0 V and negligible internal resistance. The voltmeter has a very high resistance. Explain why the voltmeter reads zero when the panel faces the Sun. A motor turns the panel when the voltmeter reading is greater than 0.50 V. At one moment, L₁ has a resistance of 1.2 kΩ and L₂ has a resistance of 1.5 kΩ. Deduce whether the motor turns the panel. Suggest why the tracker uses two LDRs, rather than one LDR and a fixed resistor, in the left-hand side of the circuit.
items.ms: The LDRs have equal resistances, so the p.d. across each LDR is 6.0 V (half the e.m.f.) The p.d. across each 10 kΩ resistor is also 6.0 V, so X and Y are at the same potential (there is no p.d. between X and Y) Use of the potential divider equation for L₁ and L₂, e.g. p.d. across L₂ = 12.0 V × 1.5/(1.2 + 1.5) p.d. across L₂ = 6.67 V (or p.d. across L₁ = 5.33 V) p.d. across each 10 kΩ resistor = 6.0 V, so the voltmeter reading = 0.67 V 0.67 V is greater than 0.50 V, so the motor turns the panel With one LDR and a fixed resistor, the potential at X would change whenever the overall light level changes (e.g. when a cloud covers the Sun) so the reading would not be zero, and the panel would turn, even when the panel faces the Sun With two identical LDRs, a change in the overall light level changes both resistances in the same proportion so the p.d.s across L₁ and L₂ stay equal, and the reading is only non-zero when one LDR is shaded more than the other
items.why: Sensor dividers come up in about one question per paper; the Jun2022 MCQ (a voltmeter between points on two wires) shows two dividers side by side are fair game, but a bridge of two LDRs, where only the ratio of resistances matters, has not been set.

items.name: Potential dividers with sensors
path: Unit 2 Waves and Electricity
Electric Circuits
S76 - analyse potential divider circuits where one
items.question: An incubator keeps eggs warm. Its heater is controlled by the circuit shown. The battery has an e.m.f. of 6.0 V and negligible internal resistance. The heater control unit switches the heater on when the p.d. across the thermistor is greater than 2.40 V, and switches it off when the p.d. is less than 2.40 V. The control unit draws negligible current. The graph shows how the resistance R of the thermistor varies with temperature θ. The variable resistor is set to 8.0 kΩ. The eggs must be kept at 37 °C. Deduce whether the heater is switched off when the temperature of the thermistor is 37 °C. Calculate the resistance that the variable resistor should be set to, so that the heater switches off when the temperature rises to 37 °C. The variable resistor is now set correctly. Explain how the circuit keeps the temperature of the eggs close to 37 °C. Your answer should include why the resistance of the thermistor changes with temperature.
items.ms: R = 6.0 kΩ read from the graph at 37 °C Use of the potential divider equation: V = 6.0 V × R/(R + 8.0 kΩ) V = 2.57 V 2.57 V is greater than 2.40 V, so the heater is still on (not switched off) at 37 °C p.d. across the variable resistor = 6.0 V − 2.40 V = 3.60 V Ratio of resistances = ratio of p.d.s: R/6.0 kΩ = 3.60/2.40 R = 9.0 kΩ IC1 If the temperature falls (below 37 °C), fewer electrons gain enough energy to be released, so there are fewer conduction electrons (charge carriers) in the thermistor IC2 so the resistance of the thermistor increases IC3 so the thermistor has a larger share of the total resistance (and the current decreases) IC4 so the p.d. across the thermistor increases (the p.d. across the variable resistor, IR, decreases) IC5 when the p.d. across the thermistor exceeds 2.40 V the heater switches on, so the temperature rises IC6 when the temperature rises above 37 °C, there are more conduction electrons, the resistance and the p.d. across the thermistor fall, the p.d. drops below 2.40 V and the heater switches off
items.why: S76 came up in 15 of 21 sessions, usually as 'read R from the graph, find the p.d., compare with the threshold' (Oct2023 Q14, Oct2025 Q17); choosing the resistor setting for a required switching temperature has not been asked, and the Oct2023 report said candidates rarely explained what happens when the temperature changes.

items.name: E.m.f. and internal resistance
path: Unit 2 Waves and Electricity
Electric Circuits
S77 - the definition of electromotive force (e.m.f.
items.question: A battery has an e.m.f. of 1.5 V. Which statement is correct? 1.5 J of energy is transferred to electrical energy for each electron that passes through the battery. The p.d. across the terminals of the battery is 1.5 V whatever the current in it. The battery transfers 1.5 J of energy to electrical energy every second. 1.5 J of energy is transferred to electrical energy for each coulomb of charge that passes through the battery.
items.ms: E.m.f. is the energy transferred per unit charge (1 V = 1 J C⁻¹), so D. A: per electron the energy is 1.5 eV (2.4 × 10⁻¹⁹ J), not 1.5 J. B: the terminal p.d. is less than 1.5 V when there is a current, because of the internal resistance. C describes a power of 1.5 W, which depends on the current.
items.why: The definition of e.m.f. was asked in Jan2020, Jan2025, Jun2025 and Jun2026; the Jan2024 report found candidates confusing e.m.f. with terminal p.d.

items.question: A voltmeter of very high resistance is connected across a cell. A 4.0 Ω resistor and a switch are also connected across the cell. With the switch open, the voltmeter reads 1.60 V. With the switch closed, it reads 1.28 V. What is the internal resistance of the cell? 0.25 Ω 0.80 Ω 1.0 Ω 5.0 Ω
items.ms: Switch closed: I = 1.28 V ÷ 4.0 Ω = 0.32 A; lost volts = 1.60 − 1.28 = 0.32 V; r = 0.32 V ÷ 0.32 A = 1.0 Ω. A is the lost volts divided by the terminal p.d. (the 4.0 Ω is left out). B uses I = 1.60 V ÷ 4.0 Ω. D is the total resistance ε/I.
items.why: Finding r from the open-circuit and loaded readings recurs (Jan2020 Q17b, Jun2025 Q14a); it is a natural single-step MCQ, like Oct2025 Q10.

items.question: A student investigates a small solar cell in bright light. A voltmeter of very high resistance is connected directly across the cell and reads 0.58 V. A 47 Ω resistor is then also connected across the cell, and the voltmeter reading falls to 0.47 V. Explain why the first reading is almost equal to the e.m.f. of the cell. Calculate the internal resistance of the cell.
items.ms: The voltmeter has a very high resistance, so there is (almost) no current in the cell so there is (almost) no p.d. across the internal resistance (no lost volts), so the terminal p.d. equals the e.m.f. I = 0.47 V ÷ 47 Ω = 0.010 A Use of ε = V + Ir with ε = 0.58 V (lost volts = 0.11 V) r = 11 Ω

items.question: Space probes that travel far from the Sun use a thermoelectric generator to supply electrical power. The generator acts as a source of e.m.f. ε with an internal resistance r. It is connected to a load of resistance R. Show that the power P delivered to the load is given by P = ε²R/(R + r)² The power delivered to the load is greatest when R = r. Explain why the terminal p.d. of the generator is then equal to half its e.m.f. The graph shows how P varies with R for the generator. Use the graph to determine ε. On the probe, the generator is connected to a load of resistance 15 Ω. Calculate the power delivered to the load and the power dissipated in the generator. Suggest why the engineers chose a load of 15 Ω rather than 5.0 Ω, even though less power is delivered to the load.
items.ms: ε = I(R + r), so I = ε/(R + r) Substitutes I into P = I²R to give P = ε²R/(R + r)² The same current is in R and r, and R = r, so the p.d. across the load equals the p.d. across the internal resistance (V = IR) ε = V + Ir (the e.m.f. is the sum of the two p.d.s), so V = ε/2 r = 5.0 Ω, read as the value of R at the maximum of the graph Maximum P = 45 W, and use of P = V²/R (V = 15 V) or P = I²R (I = 3.0 A) ε = 30 V I = ε/(R + r) = 30 V ÷ 20 Ω = 1.5 A Power delivered to the load = I²R = 34 W Power dissipated in the generator = I²r = 11 W A smaller fraction of the generator's power is wasted in its internal resistance (25% instead of 50%) / it is more efficient
items.why: S77 came up in 20 of 21 sessions, with power comparisons as R changes in Jan2020 Q17c, Jan2023 Q17c and Oct2025 Q16c; a graph of load power against R with its maximum at R = r has not been set, and the specification names space technology as an application of this topic.

items.question: In an experiment to determine the e.m.f. ε and internal resistance r of a cell, a student plots a graph of the current I in the cell (y-axis) against the terminal p.d. V (x-axis). Which gives the gradient of the graph and the intercept on the V-axis? gradient: −r; intercept on V-axis: ε gradient: −1/r; intercept on V-axis: ε gradient: −1/r; intercept on V-axis: ε/r gradient: −r; intercept on V-axis: ε/r
items.ms: ε = V + Ir gives I = −V/r + ε/r, so the gradient is −1/r. I = 0 when V = ε, so the line meets the V-axis at ε. A and D give the gradient of a V against I graph. C gives the intercept on the I-axis (ε/r).

items.question: A student determines the e.m.f. ε and internal resistance r of a lithium coin cell. She uses a voltmeter, an ammeter and a variable resistor. Draw a circuit diagram of the circuit she should use. Her results are shown in the table. Plot a graph of V against I on the grid. Use your graph to determine ε and r. She disconnects the cell between readings. Explain why.

items.question: The temperature of a metal wire increases. Which row describes the changes in the wire? amplitude of lattice vibrations: decreases; number of conduction electrons per unit volume: about the same amplitude of lattice vibrations: increases; number of conduction electrons per unit volume: increases amplitude of lattice vibrations: increases; number of conduction electrons per unit volume: about the same amplitude of lattice vibrations: about the same; number of conduction electrons per unit volume: increases
items.ms: In a metal nearly all the conduction electrons are already free, so their number hardly changes; heating increases the amplitude of the lattice vibrations, so electrons collide with the lattice more often and the resistance rises. B describes an NTC thermistor (a semiconductor). A and D have the wrong change in the lattice vibrations and, in D, the carrier number.
items.why: Metal-versus-thermistor table MCQs recur (May2024 Q1, Oct2024 Q5); the Jan2025 report said many candidates described a thermistor when asked about a metal.

items.question: The temperature of an NTC thermistor increases. Which row describes the changes in the number of conduction electrons per unit volume n, the amplitude of the lattice vibrations and the resistance R of the thermistor? n: increases; lattice vibrations: increase; R: decreases n: increases; lattice vibrations: decrease; R: decreases n: increases; lattice vibrations: increase; R: increases n: decreases; lattice vibrations: increase; R: increases
items.ms: Heating releases more electrons to conduct and also makes the lattice vibrate with a greater amplitude; the rise in n has the greater effect, so R falls. B: the lattice vibrations do not decrease (the Jan2022 report found candidates thought they must for R to fall). C: R decreases for an NTC thermistor. D: n increases, not decreases.
items.why: S79 MCQs appeared in Jan2022, Jan2024, Oct2024, Jan2026 and twice in Jun2026; the Jan2022 report found candidates thought the lattice vibrations in a heated thermistor decrease.

items.question: A car headlamp has a tungsten filament. The lamp is connected to a 12.0 V supply of negligible internal resistance and switched on at time t = 0. The graph shows how the current I in the lamp varies with t. Explain, in terms of particles, why the current decreases after the lamp is switched on. Calculate the ratio resistance of the filament when the current is steady ÷ resistance of the filament at t = 0 An engineer suggests connecting an NTC thermistor in series with the lamp to reduce the current at switch-on. When cold, the thermistor has a resistance of 1.6 Ω. After a few seconds, the current has warmed the thermistor and its resistance has fallen to 0.10 Ω. Calculate the current at the instant the lamp is switched on. Explain why the resistance of the thermistor decreases as its temperature rises, even though the amplitude of its lattice vibrations increases.
items.ms: The current heats the filament, so its temperature rises The (amplitude of the) lattice vibrations increases so the (conduction) electrons collide with the lattice (ions) more frequently so the resistance increases (the number of conduction electrons stays about the same) and the current decreases Reads I = 30 A at t = 0 and 5.0 A when steady, and uses R = V/I (0.40 Ω and 2.4 Ω) Ratio = 6.0 Total resistance = 0.40 Ω + 1.6 Ω = 2.0 Ω I = 12.0 V ÷ 2.0 Ω = 6.0 A As the temperature rises, more electrons gain enough energy to become conduction electrons / the number of conduction electrons per unit volume increases This increase in the number of charge carriers has a greater effect than the increase in collisions with the lattice so the resistance decreases (from I = nqvA, more current for the same p.d.)
items.why: S79 came up in 14 of 21 sessions, mostly as 3-mark lattice-vibration explanations (Jan2025, Oct2025, Jan2026); a switch-on current surge, with an NTC thermistor used to limit it, sets the metal and thermistor models side by side, as only Jan2024 Q18 has done.

items.question: The intensity of the light falling on an LDR increases. Which statement explains why the resistance of the LDR decreases? The amplitude of the lattice vibrations decreases, so conduction electrons collide with the lattice less often. More photons are absorbed each second, so more electrons are released to become conduction electrons. Photons give the conduction electrons more kinetic energy, so their drift velocity increases. The light heats the LDR, so the amplitude of the lattice vibrations increases.
items.ms: More intense light means more photons per second; each absorbed photon can release an electron, so the number of charge carriers rises and the resistance falls (B). A uses the temperature model, and the lattice vibrations do not decrease. C: the change is in the number of carriers, not their speed. D would increase the resistance, not decrease it.
items.why: MCQs on why an LDR's resistance falls came up in Jun2022 (Q9) and Jan2024 (Q2); the Jun2026 mark scheme rewards 'more photons, more free electrons, lower resistance', and distractors from the temperature model test the spec's separate illumination model.

items.question: A student uses the circuit shown to investigate how an LDR responds to light from a small lamp. The battery has an e.m.f. of 4.5 V and negligible internal resistance. The lamp emits 0.24 W of light uniformly in all directions. Light from other sources is negligible. Calculate the intensity of the light at the LDR when d = 0.40 m. The lamp is moved from d = 0.40 m to d = 0.20 m. Explain how the voltmeter reading changes.
items.ms: Use of I = P/(4πd²) I = 0.12 W m⁻² IC1 Halving d makes the intensity at the LDR four times as great (I ∝ 1/d²) IC2 so more photons per second are incident on (absorbed by) the LDR IC3 more electrons gain energy and are released, so the number of conduction electrons (charge carriers) in the LDR increases IC4 so the resistance of the LDR decreases IC5 the total resistance decreases, so the current increases (or the LDR has a smaller share of the total resistance) IC6 so the p.d. across the fixed resistor (V = IR) increases: the voltmeter reading increases (and the p.d. across the LDR decreases)
items.why: S80 came up in 7 of 21 sessions, with 6-mark LDR chains in Jun2023 and Jan2025; linking the change in light to the inverse-square law for intensity (spec point 44, same unit) has not been asked.

Waves and Particle Nature of Light
S50 - what is meant by diffraction and use Huygens
items.question: Long-wave radio signals of wavelength 1500 m from a transmitter can be received in a valley behind a range of hills. VHF radio signals of wavelength 3 m from the same transmitter cannot be received in the valley. Which of the following is the best explanation? The long-wave signals diffract more around the hills because their wavelength is closer to the size of the hills. The long-wave signals have a higher frequency, so they diffract more around the hills. The VHF signals travel more slowly than the long-wave signals, so they do not reach the valley. The VHF signals are longitudinal waves, so they cannot spread out behind the hills.
items.ms: A is correct: waves spread out (diffract) most around an obstacle when the wavelength is similar to the size of the obstacle; 1500 m is comparable with the hills, while 3 m is far smaller, so the VHF waves hardly diffract into the valley. B: long-wave radio has the lower frequency (f = c/λ). C: all electromagnetic waves travel at the same speed in air. D: radio waves are transverse, and longitudinal waves diffract too.
items.why: S50 has come up in 5 of 21 sessions, almost always as waves passing through a gap (Jan2020, Oct2021, Jan2024, Jun2025); diffraction around an obstacle, also in the spec, was only touched by Jun2023 Q1.

path: Unit 2 Waves and Electricity
Waves and Particle Nature of Light
S50 - what is meant by diffraction and use Huygens
items.question: The diagram shows a view from above of straight wavefronts approaching the entrance to a harbour. The entrance is a gap of width 40 m between two harbour walls. A boat is moored at X, behind one of the walls. The diagram is drawn to scale. Explain, using Huygens' construction, why the waves spread out after passing through the gap. On the diagram, draw three wavefronts after they have passed through the gap. The diagram shows the waves on a day when they have a period of 5.0 s and a speed of 7.8 m s⁻¹. On this day the boat at X moves up and down a lot. On another day the waves approaching the harbour have the same amplitude but a wavelength of 4.0 m, and the boat at X hardly moves. Show that the wavelength of the waves shown in the diagram is about 40 m. Explain why the boat at X moves much more when the waves have the longer wavelength.
items.ms: Each point on a wavefront (in the gap) acts as a source of secondary wavelets The wavelets spread out (in all forward directions) and the new wavefront is the line that touches them all (their envelope), so it curves round behind the walls Curved wavefronts, approximately semicircular and centred on the gap, reaching into the regions behind both walls Spacing between the wavefronts equal to the spacing of the incident wavefronts Use of v = fλ with f = 1/T, giving λ = 7.8 × 5.0 = 39 m The longer wavelength (about 40 m) is about the same as the width of the gap, but 4.0 m is much smaller than the gap So the longer-wavelength waves diffract (spread out) much more after the gap and reach X, while the 4.0 m waves pass through with little spreading, leaving X sheltered
items.why: S50 has come up in 5 of 21 sessions, with Huygens' construction at a gap in Jan2020 and Jan2024; drawing the diffracted wavefronts and linking the amount of spreading to a wavelength found from v = fλ has not been asked.

items.question: Yellow light of wavelength 589 nm is incident normally on a diffraction grating that has 300 lines per mm. What is the angle between the second-order maximum and the straight-through direction? 10.2° 19.5° 20.7° 41.4°
items.ms: C is correct: d = 1/(300 × 10³) m = 3.33 × 10⁻⁶ m; sin θ = 2 × 589 × 10⁻⁹/3.33 × 10⁻⁶ = 0.353, so θ = 20.7°. A is the first-order angle; B uses tan⁻¹ instead of sin⁻¹; D is the angle between the two second-order maxima.
items.why: S51 has come up in 15 of 21 sessions; finding an angle from the lines per mm recurs (Jun2026 Q9, Oct2025 Q16b), and Oct2022 Q18a asked for a second-order angle.
