items.question: Light of wavelength 633 nm is incident normally on a diffraction grating that has 500 lines per mm. How many bright maxima are produced in total? 3 4 6 7
items.ms: D is correct: d = 1/(500 × 10³) m = 2.0 × 10⁻⁶ m; sin θ cannot exceed 1, so n ≤ d/λ = 3.16 and the highest order is 3. There are 3 orders on each side of the central (zero-order) maximum: 7 maxima. A counts the orders on one side only; B adds the central maximum to one side only; C leaves out the central maximum.
items.why: The highest order was asked in Oct2024 Q16c(ii) and Oct2025 Q16b(ii); counting all the maxima, including the central one, is the natural multiple-choice form.

items.question: White light is incident normally on a diffraction grating. In the spectra produced, light of wavelength 600 nm in the second order is at the same angle as light of wavelength λ in the third order. What is λ? 300 nm 400 nm 900 nm 1200 nm

items.question: A student uses a diffraction grating with 500 lines per mm to look at the light from a hydrogen discharge tube. A red line is seen in the first order at an angle of 19.2° to the straight-through direction. The diagram shows some of the energy levels of a hydrogen atom. Calculate the wavelength of the red light. Deduce which transition between the energy levels produces the red light. The student predicts that the second-order maximum for the red light will be at 38.4° to the straight-through direction. Deduce whether the student is correct.
items.ms: d = 1/(500 × 10³) m = 2.00 × 10⁻⁶ m Use of nλ = d sin θ with n = 1 λ = 6.58 × 10⁻⁷ m Use of E = hf and c = fλ (E = hc/λ = 3.02 × 10⁻¹⁹ J) Conversion to electronvolts: E = 1.89 eV −1.51 eV − (−3.40 eV) = 1.89 eV, so the transition is from n = 3 to n = 2 sin θ = 2λ/d (= 2 × sin 19.2°) = 0.658 θ = 41.1°, which is not 38.4°, so the student is incorrect
items.why: Past grating questions used only lasers and white light; using a grating to identify an energy-level transition (S63 is asked in most sessions) is a likely synoptic link, and Oct2022 Q18a asked for a second-order angle from the first.

path: Unit 2 Waves and Electricity
Waves and Particle Nature of Light
S51 - use n  dsin for a diffraction grating
items.question: A student directs a beam of light from a laser onto a diffraction grating that has 600 lines per mm. Bright dots are formed on a screen. The diagram shows, viewed from above, the central dot, the two first-order dots and the distances she measured. Explain why bright dots are formed only at certain angles. Determine the wavelength of the light, using the measurements on the diagram. The grating and the screen are now placed in a large glass tank filled with water. The laser beam enters the tank at right angles to the glass, and the grating is still 0.800 m from the screen. refractive index of water = 1.33 Explain why the first-order dots are now closer to the central dot. Deduce whether more bright dots can be formed in the water than in air. Assume that the screen is wide enough to show every dot.
items.ms: Light diffracts (spreads out) as it passes through each slit, so the waves from different slits overlap At a bright dot the path difference between waves from adjacent slits is a whole number of wavelengths (nλ) So the waves arrive in phase and interfere constructively (superpose to give maximum amplitude) At other angles the waves from the many slits arrive out of phase and cancel (destructive interference) Use of tan θ = 0.330/0.800 (half the separation), θ = 22.4° d = 1/(600 × 10³) m = 1.67 × 10⁻⁶ m Use of nλ = d sin θ with n = 1 λ = 6.36 × 10⁻⁷ m The speed of light in water is less than in air (v = c/n) The frequency is unchanged, so the wavelength in water is smaller (λ = v/f, so λ is divided by 1.33) d is unchanged, so from nλ = d sin θ a smaller λ gives a smaller θ In water λ = 6.36 × 10⁻⁷/1.33 = 4.78 × 10⁻⁷ m, so for n = 3, sin θ = 3λ/d = 0.86 (or n_max = d/λ = 3.5) In air sin θ would be 1.14 for n = 3, which is impossible (n_max = 2.6), so the third-order dots appear only in water: 7 dots instead of 5, so more dots can be formed
items.why: S51 has come up in 15 of 21 sessions and long grating questions open with why bright dots form and λ from the screen geometry (Jan2022, Jan2025, Jan2026); a grating in water, linking n = c/v (S45) to the number of orders, has never been asked.

items.question: A student determines the wavelength of the light from a green laser using a diffraction grating with 300 lines per mm. The laser beam is incident normally on the grating, and a screen is placed parallel to the grating. She measures the distance s between the two first-order maxima on the screen for different distances D between the grating and the screen. The table shows her results. Give one precaution she should take to use the laser safely. Plot a graph of s against D on the grid. Use your graph to determine the wavelength of the light. Another student suggests using a grating with 600 lines per mm to reduce the percentage uncertainty in the value of the wavelength. Explain whether this suggestion is correct.
items.ms: Any one of: do not look into the beam; point the laser away from people's eyes / stand behind the laser; remove or cover reflective surfaces; wear laser safety goggles Axes labelled s / m (vertical) and D / m (horizontal) Sensible scales, with the plotted points covering at least half the grid in each direction All points plotted accurately (to within half a small square) Straight line of best fit (passing close to the origin) Gradient calculated using a large triangle (about 0.32) tan θ = gradient/2 d = 1/(300 × 10³) m = 3.33 × 10⁻⁶ m and use of nλ = d sin θ with n = 1 λ = 5.3 × 10⁻⁷ m With more lines per mm, d is smaller, so for the same wavelength the angle θ is larger (sin θ = λ/d) So s is larger for each D, and the same uncertainty in measuring s is a smaller percentage of s, so the percentage uncertainty in λ is smaller and the suggestion is correct
items.why: Core practical 6 has been asked in 3 of 21 sessions (last Oct2024), only as set-up, measurements and safety; a graph of s against D, the likeliest way to test its graph skills, has never been asked.

S53 - how diffraction experiments provide evidence
items.question: Electrons are accelerated from rest through a potential difference and pass through a thin layer of graphite, forming rings on a screen. The accelerating potential difference is increased. Which statement is correct? The rings get smaller because the de Broglie wavelength of the electrons decreases. The rings get smaller because the electrons spend less time in the graphite. The rings get larger because the de Broglie wavelength of the electrons increases. The rings get larger because the momentum of the electrons increases.
items.ms: A is correct: a greater p.d. gives the electrons more kinetic energy and momentum, so λ = h/p is smaller; the electrons diffract less and the rings get smaller. B: the time spent in the graphite does not decide the size of the rings; the wavelength does. C: the wavelength decreases. D: the momentum does increase, but that makes the wavelength smaller and the rings smaller.
items.why: S53 has come up in 6 of 21 sessions; the effect of the accelerating p.d. on the rings was asked only in Oct2023 Q15(b)(iii) and never as a multiple-choice question.

S53 - how diffraction experiments provide evidence
items.question: The diagram shows an electron diffraction tube. Electrons are accelerated from rest through a potential difference of 3.5 kV and then pass through a very thin layer of graphite. A pattern of rings is seen on the fluorescent screen. Explain how the rings provide evidence that electrons can behave as waves. Show that the de Broglie wavelength of the electrons is about 2 × 10⁻¹¹ m. The spacing between neighbouring rows of carbon atoms in graphite is about 1.2 × 10⁻¹⁰ m. A student suggests that protons accelerated from rest through the same potential difference would give a ring pattern of a similar size. mass of proton = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg Deduce whether the student is correct.
items.ms: The electrons diffract as they pass through the graphite Diffraction is a property of waves (particles would not diffract) The diffracted electron waves superpose/interfere, and the rings are where the interference is constructive The regular arrangement of carbon atoms acts like a diffraction grating Use of W = QV: Ek = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C × 3500 V (= 5.6 × 10⁻¹⁶ J) Use of Ek = ½mv² and p = mv (or p = √(2mEk)) Use of λ = h/p: λ = 2.1 × 10⁻¹¹ m Use of λ = h/√(2mEk) with the proton mass (or λ ∝ 1/√m, ratio √(1.67 × 10⁻²⁷/9.11 × 10⁻³¹) = 43) λ = 4.8 × 10⁻¹³ m This is about 43 times smaller than the electron wavelength (and about 250 times smaller than the atomic spacing), so the protons are diffracted through much smaller angles and any rings would be far smaller: the student is incorrect
items.why: S53 has come up in 6 of 21 sessions, usually as 2–4 mark explanations of the rings (Oct2022, Oct2023, Oct2024); a heavier particle was compared only once (Oct2020 Q15b, neutrons), never protons accelerated through the same p.d.

items.question: An electron has a de Broglie wavelength of 2.6 × 10⁻¹⁰ m. Which expression gives the speed of the electron in m s⁻¹? 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ / (9.11 × 10⁻³¹ × 2.6 × 10⁻¹⁰) (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 2.6 × 10⁻¹⁰) / (9.11 × 10⁻³¹) 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ / (1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 2.6 × 10⁻¹⁰) (9.11 × 10⁻³¹ × 2.6 × 10⁻¹⁰) / (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴)

items.question: An electron is accelerated from rest through a potential difference V and then has a de Broglie wavelength λ. A second electron is accelerated from rest through a potential difference V/4. What is the de Broglie wavelength of the second electron? λ/4 λ/2 2λ 4λ
items.ms: C is correct: Ek = eV, so p = √(2meV) is proportional to √V, and λ = h/p is proportional to 1/√V. Dividing V by 4 halves p, so λ doubles. A assumes λ ∝ V; B assumes λ ∝ √V; D assumes λ ∝ 1/V.
items.why: S54 has come up in 15 of 21 sessions, usually as a calculation from an accelerating p.d. (Jan2026, Jun2025, Oct2023); how λ scales with the p.d. has not been asked.

items.question: In an electron microscope, electrons are accelerated from rest through a potential difference V. The size of the smallest detail the microscope can show depends on the de Broglie wavelength of the electrons. A designer wants the electrons to have a de Broglie wavelength of 2.2 × 10⁻¹¹ m. Calculate V. The microscope is used to see detail about 10⁻¹⁰ m across. Explain why this detail could not be seen with visible light.

S55 - that waves can be transmitted and reflected a
items.question: Ultrasound travelling through water is incident normally on the flat surface of a steel block. Which statement is correct? Some ultrasound is reflected and some is transmitted, and the transmitted ultrasound has a different frequency. Some ultrasound is reflected and some is transmitted, and the transmitted ultrasound has a different wavelength. All of the ultrasound is reflected because steel has a much greater density than water. All of the ultrasound is transmitted because it meets the surface at normal incidence.
items.ms: B is correct: at an interface between two media part of the wave is reflected and part is transmitted; the speed of ultrasound in steel is greater than in water and the frequency is set by the source, so the wavelength (λ = v/f) changes. A: the frequency does not change. C: a large difference in density reflects a large fraction, but not all of it. D: normal incidence means no change of direction, but some ultrasound is still reflected.
items.why: S55 has come up in 5 of 21 sessions, as reflection at cracks and at the lungs; what happens to the transmitted wave itself has not been asked.

items.question: Before an ultrasound scan, a layer of gel is spread on the patient's skin and the transducer is pressed onto the gel. The density of the gel is similar to the density of skin. The density of air is about 1/1000 of the density of skin. Explain why the gel is needed.
items.ms: Without the gel there would be a layer of air between the transducer and the skin At a boundary between different media some of the ultrasound is reflected; the very large difference in density between air and skin means most of it is reflected So very little ultrasound would enter the body, and the echoes from inside would be too weak to detect The gel and the skin have similar densities, so most of the ultrasound is transmitted from the gel into the skin
items.why: S55 has come up in 5 of 21 sessions (cracks in rails and beams, the lungs); the coupling gel, the standard medical example of reflection at an interface, has not been asked.

items.question: A pulse of laser light is sent from the Earth to a reflector on the Moon. The reflected pulse is detected back on the Earth 2.56 s after it was sent. speed of light = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ What is the distance from the Earth to the reflector? 1.17 × 10⁸ m 1.92 × 10⁸ m 3.84 × 10⁸ m 7.68 × 10⁸ m
items.ms: C is correct: the pulse travels to the Moon and back, so distance = ct/2 = 3.00 × 10⁸ × 2.56/2 = 3.84 × 10⁸ m. A divides c by t; B divides ct by 4; D is the whole distance travelled by the pulse (no factor of 2).

items.question: An ultrasound scanner sends pulses of ultrasound, each lasting 2.0 μs, into soft tissue. The speed of ultrasound in soft tissue is 1540 m s⁻¹. Two boundaries, one behind the other, can be distinguished only if their echoes do not overlap. What is the smallest distance between two boundaries that can be distinguished? 0.77 mm 1.5 mm 3.1 mm 6.2 mm
items.ms: B is correct: the echo from the far boundary arrives 2Δx/v after the echo from the near one, and the echoes do not overlap if this is at least the pulse duration, so Δx = vτ/2 = 1540 × 2.0 × 10⁻⁶/2 = 1.5 × 10⁻³ m. A divides by 4; C has no factor of 2; D multiplies by 2 instead of dividing.
items.why: Pulse duration limits were asked in Jan2021 Q3 and Jun2026 Q7 as statements and in Oct2025 Q12(b) for a sensor's range; the smallest separation of two boundaries, the resolution limit the spec names, has not been calculated.

items.question: A bat finds insects by emitting pulses of ultrasound and detecting the echoes. An insect can be detected only if the wavelength of the ultrasound is less than the length of the insect. speed of sound in air = 340 m s⁻¹ Which frequency would allow the bat to detect an insect of length 5.0 mm? 20 kHz 45 kHz 60 kHz 80 kHz
items.ms: D is correct: λ = v/f = 340/(80 × 10³) = 4.2 × 10⁻³ m = 4.2 mm, which is less than 5.0 mm. A, B and C give λ = 17 mm, 7.6 mm and 5.7 mm, all longer than the insect, so the ultrasound would diffract around it.

items.name: Pulse-echo techniques (ultrasound, radar, laser ranging)
path: Unit 2 Waves and Electricity

S56 - how a pulse-echo technique can provide inform
items.question: An ultrasound A-scan is used to measure the length of a patient's eye. A transducer placed on the front surface of the eye (the cornea) sends a short pulse of ultrasound into the eye. The ultrasound passes in turn through a liquid, the lens and a jelly before reaching the retina at the back of the eye. speed of ultrasound in the liquid and in the jelly = 1530 m s⁻¹ speed of ultrasound in the lens = 1640 m s⁻¹ The graph shows the signal from the transducer against time t. P is the pulse being sent. A, B and C are the echoes from the front of the lens, the back of the lens and the retina. Explain why an echo is received from the back of the lens as well as from the front of the lens. Calculate the thickness of the lens. Calculate the distance from the cornea to the retina. The A-scan uses pulses of ultrasound of frequency 10 MHz, each lasting about 0.5 μs. Explain how the wavelength of the ultrasound and the duration of the pulses limit the detail that the A-scan can show.
items.ms: At the front surface of the lens (a boundary between two media) only part of the ultrasound is reflected; the rest is transmitted into the lens The back of the lens is another boundary between different media (lens and jelly), so part of the transmitted ultrasound is reflected there Use of v = s/t with t = 10.0 μs − 5.0 μs = 5.0 μs Half the distance: thickness = 4.1 × 10⁻³ m Times read from the graph and measured from P: 4.0 μs in the liquid and 22.0 μs in the jelly Use of distance = 1530 m s⁻¹ × time/2 (3.06 mm and 16.8 mm) distance = 3.06 mm + 4.1 mm + 16.8 mm = 2.40 × 10⁻² m IC1 The wavelength is found from v = fλ: about 1.5 × 10⁻⁴ m (0.15 mm) at 10 MHz IC2 Ultrasound diffracts around features that are similar in size to, or smaller than, the wavelength IC3 So features smaller than about one wavelength cannot be detected; a higher frequency (shorter wavelength) shows finer detail IC4 Each echo lasts as long as the pulse (about 0.5 μs) IC5 If the time between the echoes from two boundaries is less than the pulse duration, the echoes overlap and the boundaries cannot be distinguished IC6 The smallest separation that can be distinguished = speed × pulse duration/2, about 0.4 mm, so shorter pulses distinguish boundaries that are closer together
items.why: S56 has come up in 18 of 21 sessions; its 6-mark questions (Jan2020 Q13, Jan2026 Q19) asked how the technique locates a boundary, while the second half of the spec point, how wavelength and pulse duration limit the information, has only had 1–2 mark parts; an eye A-scan with layers of different speeds is a fresh context.

Nuclear Decay
S133 - the concept of nuclear binding energy and be
items.question: A nucleus of an element X has proton number Z, nucleon number A and mass M. The mass of a proton is mp and the mass of a neutron is mn. c is the speed of light in a vacuum. Which expression gives the binding energy of the nucleus? (M − Zmp − (A − Z)mn)c² (Zmp + Amn − M)c² (Zmp + (A − Z)mn − M)c² ÷ A (Zmp + (A − Z)mn − M)c²
items.ms: The binding energy is c² × the mass deficit, and the mass deficit is the total mass of the separate nucleons (Z protons and A − Z neutrons) minus the mass of the nucleus. A has the subtraction the wrong way round, so it is negative. B uses A neutrons instead of A − Z. C is the binding energy per nucleon, not the binding energy of the nucleus.
items.why: S133 has come up in all 18 sessions; Jun2026 Q1 asked for the meaning of binding energy in words, but the expression in symbols, with the per-nucleon and wrong-way-round traps, has not been an MCQ.

items.question: Some old camping-lantern mantles contain thorium-232. Thorium-232 decays by alpha emission to radium-228: ²³²₉₀Th → ²²⁸₈₈Ra + ⁴₂α The table gives the masses of the nuclei. Calculate the energy released when one thorium-232 nucleus decays, in MeV. The alpha particles are emitted with a kinetic energy of 4.01 MeV. Explain why this is less than the energy calculated in (a).
items.ms: Mass difference = 231.988683 − (227.982795 + 4.001506) = 0.004382 u Conversion of u to kg (× 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg u⁻¹) Use of ΔE = c²Δm ΔE = 4.09 MeV The thorium nucleus is initially at rest, so the total momentum is zero (momentum is conserved) The radium nucleus recoils with momentum equal in size and opposite in direction to that of the alpha particle So some of the energy released becomes kinetic energy of the radium nucleus (a small share because its mass is much greater) The radium nucleus may be left in an excited state, so some energy is emitted as a gamma photon

items.question: Space probes that travel far from the Sun need a heat source to generate electricity. One design uses americium-241, which decays by alpha emission to an isotope of neptunium (Np). Americium-241 has a half-life of 432 years. Complete the nuclear equation for this decay by adding the nucleon number and proton number of each product. ²⁴¹₉₅Am → Np + α The table gives the masses of the nuclei. Calculate the energy released in one decay, in J. Show that the decay constant of americium-241 is about 5.1 × 10⁻¹¹ s⁻¹. Calculate the mass of americium-241 needed for an initial thermal power of 250 W. Assume that all the energy released by the decays is transferred to thermal energy in the heat source. The graph shows how the thermal power P of a plutonium-238 heat source, also with an initial power of 250 W, would vary with time t. Deduce which of the two heat sources would meet this requirement. items.question: Engineers add a small amount of sodium-24 to the water in a buried pipe to find a leak. Sodium-24 has a half-life of 15.0 hours. items.question: A gamma source is held in air in front of a detector. When the distance between them is doubled, the count rate due to the source falls to about one quarter. items.question: Two radioactive sources X and Y have the same activity at time t = 0. The half-life of X is 2.0 hours and the half-life of Y is 6.0 hours. What is the value of (number of undecayed nuclei in X) ÷ (number of undecayed nuclei in Y) at t = 12 hours? 1/48 1/16 3/16 1/3
items.ms: Same activity means λXNX = λYNY; λX = 3λY, so initially NX/NY = 1/3. In 12 hours X goes through 6 half-lives (× 1/64) and Y through 2 (× 1/4), so the ratio = (1/3) × (1/64) ÷ (1/4) = 1/48. B is the ratio of the activities (or forgets the initial ratio). C uses an initial ratio of 3 instead of 1/3. D is the initial ratio only.

items.question: Living trees take in carbon, including a small fraction of radioactive carbon-14. When a tree dies, it stops taking in carbon and the carbon-14 in the wood decays. Carbon-14 has a half-life of 5730 years. Assume the fraction of carbon-14 in living trees has always been the same. Show that the decay constant of carbon-14 is about 3.8 × 10⁻¹² s⁻¹. items.question: A student determines the half-life of protactinium-234m, a beta emitter. She records the number of counts in 10 s intervals, starting at the times t shown in the table. Before starting, she recorded 300 counts in 600 s with no source present. R is the corrected count rate. Explain why the count rates must be corrected for background radiation before their logarithms are taken. Complete the table. The graph shows ln (R / s⁻¹) against t for the other results. Plot the two remaining points and draw a line of best fit. Use the graph to determine the half-life of protactinium-234m. Explain why the points for larger values of t would be expected to lie further from the line of best fit. Suggest why she counted for 10 s at each time rather than for 60 s.
items.ms: The background count rate is (roughly) constant: it does not decay So the measured count rate does not fall exponentially (it levels off at the background), so the ln graph would curve / its gradient would be too small So the half-life found would be too large R = 21.7 s⁻¹ and ln (R / s⁻¹) = 3.08 Points at t = 90 s and t = 210 s plotted accurately (to within half a small square) Best-fit straight line Gradient calculated using a large triangle (at least half the length of the line) λ = −gradient (about 0.0097 s⁻¹) Use of t½ = ln 2 ÷ λ t½ = 72 s Decay is random, so the number of counts in each interval fluctuates When the counts are small the fluctuations are a larger fraction (percentage) of the count / the background is a larger fraction of the count The half-life is short (about 70 s), so the count rate would change a lot during a 60 s count

items.question: Iridium-192 is used to check welds in steel. Gamma radiation from the source passes through the weld onto a photographic film, as shown. Iridium-192 decays by beta-minus emission to platinum (Pt), and the platinum nucleus then emits gamma radiation. Complete the nuclear equation for the beta-minus decay by adding the nucleon number and proton number of each product. ¹⁹²₇₇Ir → Pt + β + ν̄ A new source has an activity of 3.7 × 10¹² Bq. The half-life of iridium-192 is 73.8 days. Calculate the mass of iridium-192 in the source. The source is replaced when its activity has fallen to 1.1 × 10¹² Bq. S143 - that the condition for simple harmonic motion
items.question: A mass hangs from a vertical spring and oscillates with simple harmonic motion. The resultant force F on the mass is given by F = −kx. What does x represent? the amplitude of the oscillation the distance moved by the mass since it was released the extension of the spring the displacement of the mass from its equilibrium position
items.ms: x is the displacement from the equilibrium position, where the resultant force is zero. A: the amplitude is the maximum value of x, a constant. B: the distance moved since release is measured from the release point, not from the equilibrium position. C: a vertical spring is already extended at the equilibrium position, so the resultant force is not k × extension.
items.why: S143 has come up in 15 of 18 sessions; Oct2025 Q15(a)(i) asked what x means in F = −kx as a written part, but it has never been an MCQ.

items.name: The condition for SHM; F = -kx
path: Unit 5 Thermodynamics, Radiation, Oscillations and Cosmology
Oscillations
S143 - that the condition for simple harmonic motion
items.question: Which graph shows how the resultant force F on an object varies with its displacement x from the equilibrium position when the object moves with simple harmonic motion? Graph A Graph B Graph C Graph D
items.ms: For SHM F = −kx: a straight line through the origin with a negative gradient (A). B has the force in the same direction as the displacement, so the object would accelerate away. C is a restoring force of constant size (not proportional to x). D is a restoring force that is not proportional to the displacement.
items.why: Graphs that show SHM recur (Jan2025 Q17(a) a–x graph, Oct2024 Q4); an F–x version with restoring-force distractors that are not proportional to x has not been asked.

items.name: The condition for SHM; F = -kx
path: Unit 5 Thermodynamics, Radiation, Oscillations and Cosmology
Oscillations
S143 - that the condition for simple harmonic motion
items.question: A cylinder of mass 0.30 kg and cross-sectional area 4.0 × 10⁻³ m² floats upright in water of density 1.0 × 10³ kg m⁻³. The cylinder is pushed down so that it is 2.0 cm below its equilibrium position, and is then released. Which gives the resultant force on the cylinder at the moment it is released? 0.78 N downwards 0.78 N upwards 2.2 N upwards 3.7 N upwards
items.ms: At equilibrium the upthrust equals the weight. Pushing the cylinder down 2.0 cm displaces an extra 4.0 × 10⁻³ × 0.020 m³ of water, so the upthrust increases by ρVg = 0.78 N while the weight is unchanged: the resultant is 0.78 N upwards, opposite to the displacement and proportional to it, so the cylinder moves with SHM. A has the wrong direction. C subtracts the extra upthrust from the weight. D is the total upthrust (weight + extra upthrust), not the resultant force.
items.why: S143 asks students to identify situations in which SHM will occur, but past papers only use springs and pendulums; showing F ∝ −x for a new system (a floating object) is the likeliest surprise.

items.name: The condition for SHM; F = -kx
path: Unit 5 Thermodynamics, Radiation, Oscillations and Cosmology

items.question: A student drops a small rubber ball onto a hard floor. The ball bounces back up to almost the same height each time, so its motion repeats at regular time intervals. State the conditions necessary for an object to move with simple harmonic motion. The student says that the ball moves with simple harmonic motion because its motion repeats at regular time intervals. Explain why the student is wrong.
items.ms: The (resultant) force / acceleration is proportional to the displacement (from the equilibrium position) and is (always) directed towards the equilibrium position / in the opposite direction to the displacement While the ball is in the air the only force on it is its weight, so the (resultant) force / acceleration (g) is constant so the force is not proportional to the displacement (from the mid-point of the motion) / it acts downwards even when the ball is below the mid-point, so it is not always directed towards a fixed point
items.why: The SHM conditions have been a 2-mark part in 11 of 18 papers (most recently Jun2026 Q20(a)); recognising a periodic motion that is not SHM, as the spec's 'identify situations' requires, has not been asked.

items.question: An object moves with simple harmonic motion of amplitude A and angular frequency ω. Timing starts (t = 0) as the object passes through its equilibrium position moving in the positive direction. Which equation gives the velocity v of the object at time t? v = Aω cos ωt v = −Aω cos ωt v = Aω sin ωt v = −Aω sin ωt
items.ms: Starting from the equilibrium position, x = A sin ωt; its gradient is v = Aω cos ωt, which gives v = +Aω (the maximum, in the positive direction) at t = 0. B gives the maximum velocity in the negative direction at t = 0. C and D give v = 0 at t = 0, which is true only if timing starts at an extreme position (D is the equation when the object starts at x = +A).
items.why: S144 MCQs recur (Jan2024 Q7, Jan2023 Q9); the spec equations assume timing starts at maximum displacement, and a different starting point has never been tested.

items.question: An object oscillates with simple harmonic motion. Its maximum speed is v₀ and its maximum acceleration is a₀. The amplitude is halved and the frequency is doubled. Which gives the new maximum speed and the new maximum acceleration? v₀ and a₀ v₀ and 4a₀ v₀ and 2a₀ 2v₀ and 4a₀
items.ms: v_max = Aω and a_max = Aω². Halving A and doubling ω gives (A/2)(2ω) = Aω = v₀ and (A/2)(2ω)² = 2Aω² = 2a₀. A treats a_max like v_max. B ignores the halved amplitude in a_max. D ignores the halved amplitude altogether.
items.why: May2024 Q3 asked how the maximum kinetic energy changes with amplitude; ratio MCQs are the hardest in the reports, and a two-factor change to v_max and a_max together has not been set.

items.question: The needle of a sewing machine moves vertically with simple harmonic motion. It makes 720 complete oscillations per minute and its amplitude is 9.0 mm. items.question: A vibration plate in a gym has a platform that moves vertically with simple harmonic motion. In one setting the platform oscillates at 35 Hz with an amplitude of 2.0 mm. Calculate the maximum speed of the platform. Calculate the maximum acceleration of the platform. A small block is placed on the platform. At this setting the block does not stay in contact with the platform for the whole of each cycle. Explain why the block loses contact with the platform. You should state where in the cycle this happens. Calculate the maximum frequency at which the platform could oscillate with an amplitude of 2.0 mm without the block losing contact.

items.question: A mass hangs from a spring and oscillates vertically with period T. A second spring, identical to the first, is then attached alongside the first so that the mass hangs from both springs side by side. What is the new period of oscillation? T/2 T/√2 √2 T 2T

items.question: A child sits on a swing that oscillates with a small amplitude. The swing can be treated as a simple pendulum whose length is the distance from the pivot to the child's centre of mass. The child then stands up on the seat, which raises her centre of mass. items.question: A student wants to measure the acceleration of free fall g using a long pendulum in a stairwell. The pivot is out of reach, so she cannot measure the full length of the pendulum. Instead she measures the distance h from a mark M on the string to the centre of the bob. M is a fixed distance c below the pivot, as shown. She changes h by changing the length of string between M and the bob, and measures the period T for each value of h. Describe how the student should measure T for one value of h so that her value is as accurate as possible. Explain why a graph of T² against h should be a straight line that does not pass through the origin. The graph shows her results and the line of best fit. Use the graph to determine a value for g. Use the graph to determine c. For h = 0.750 m the bob is pulled 6.0 cm to one side and released. Use the graph to calculate the maximum speed of the bob. Give a reason why the amplitude of the oscillations should be small.
items.ms: Time a number of oscillations (at least 10) and divide the total time by that number Start and stop timing as the bob passes through the equilibrium position / use a fiducial marker at the equilibrium position Repeat the timing and calculate a mean T = 2π√((h + c)/g), so T² = (4π²/g)h + 4π²c/g Compared with y = mx + c: the gradient 4π²/g is constant and the intercept 4π²c/g is not zero (positive) Gradient calculated using a large triangle (about 4.0 s² m⁻¹) Use of gradient = 4π²/g g = 9.8 m s⁻² Intercept on the T² axis read (1.0 s²) / line extended to T² = 0 at h = −0.25 m c = intercept ÷ gradient = 0.25 m T² read from the graph at h = 0.750 m (4.0 s²), so T = 2.0 s Use of ω = 2π/T and v = Aω v_max = 0.19 m s⁻¹ The pendulum moves with SHM (so T = 2π√(l/g) applies) only for small amplitudes, when the restoring force is (approximately) proportional to the displacement

items.name: Displacement-time graphs; gradient is velocity
path: Unit 5 Thermodynamics, Radiation, Oscillations and Cosmology
Oscillations
S146 - draw and interpret a displacement-time graph
items.question: The graph shows how the displacement x of an object moving with simple harmonic motion varies with time t. At which point are both the velocity and the acceleration of the object positive? P Q R S
items.ms: The velocity is the gradient of the graph, and the acceleration is opposite to the displacement (a = −ω²x). At R the gradient is positive and x is negative, so a is positive. At P the gradient and the acceleration are both negative. At Q the gradient is negative. At S the gradient is positive but x is positive, so a is negative.
items.why: S146 MCQs have appeared in 7 of 18 papers as graph matching (most recently Jan2026 Q9); reading the signs of v and a at points on one graph has not been asked.

items.name: Displacement-time graphs; gradient is velocity

items.question: The displacement x of an object moving with simple harmonic motion is given by x = A cos ωt, where A = 3.0 cm and the period is 0.50 s. What is the gradient of the displacement–time graph at t = 0.125 s? −0.38 m s⁻¹ −0.24 m s⁻¹ 0 m s⁻¹ +0.38 m s⁻¹
items.ms: The gradient is the velocity v = −Aω sin ωt. At t = 0.125 s = T/4, ωt = π/2, so v = −Aω = −0.030 m × (2π/0.50 s) = −0.38 m s⁻¹. B is the average velocity over the first quarter cycle (−0.030 m ÷ 0.125 s). C confuses the velocity with the acceleration, which is zero where x = 0. D has the wrong sign: the object is moving towards negative x.
items.why: Jun2025 Q15(b) allowed v_max to be found from the gradient at the equilibrium crossing; the sign of that gradient has not been tested.

items.question: A buoy floating in a harbour moves up and down as waves pass it. The graph shows how the vertical displacement x of the buoy varies with time t. Add a line to the graph to show how the velocity of the buoy varies with time over the same interval. No values are needed on the velocity axis. items.question: The graph shows how the velocity v of an object moving with simple harmonic motion varies with time t. At which point is the object at its maximum negative displacement? P Q R S
items.ms: The acceleration is the gradient of the v–t graph and a = −ω²x. At S the velocity is zero and the gradient is positive and at its greatest, so x is most negative. At Q v = 0 but the gradient is negative: maximum positive displacement. At P and R the speed is a maximum, so the object is at the equilibrium position.

items.name: Resonance
path: Unit 5 Thermodynamics, Radiation, Oscillations and Cosmology
Oscillations
S148 - what is meant by resonance
items.question: A parent pushes a child on a swing. The natural period of the swing is 2.4 s. The parent gives the swing one short push at regular time intervals. Which time interval between pushes makes the amplitude increase most quickly? 0.6 s 1.2 s 2.4 s 3.6 s
items.ms: Pushing every 2.4 s makes the driving frequency equal to the natural frequency, so every push is at the same point in the cycle and in the direction of motion: resonance, with the most efficient transfer of energy. With 1.2 s or 3.6 s, every other push comes half a cycle later and opposes the motion. With 0.6 s the pushes come at four different points in each cycle and some of them oppose the motion.
items.why: Resonance MCQs recur (Oct2025 Q1, Jun2025 Q2, Jun2021 Q3); choosing the driving period for an everyday forced oscillation has not been asked.

items.name: Resonance
path: Unit 5 Thermodynamics, Radiation, Oscillations and Cosmology
Oscillations
S148 - what is meant by resonance
items.question: A road has raised strips across it, spaced 0.50 m apart. When a car drives over them, its steering wheel vibrates. The natural frequency of vibration of the steering wheel is 30 Hz. At which speed does the steering wheel vibrate with the greatest amplitude? 0.017 m s⁻¹ 15 m s⁻¹ 60 m s⁻¹ 94 m s⁻¹
items.ms: The strips give a driving frequency f = v/d. Resonance occurs when v/d = 30 Hz, so v = 30 Hz × 0.50 m = 15 m s⁻¹. A is d/f, C is f/d and D uses ω = 2πf instead of f.
items.why: Speed-bump resonance was asked in Jan2023 Q19(a) and Jan2026 Q20(b); a 1-mark version using the driving frequency v/d is a likely MCQ.

items.name: Resonance
path: Unit 5 Thermodynamics, Radiation, Oscillations and Cosmology
Oscillations
S148 - what is meant by resonance
items.question: A mass on a spring is driven at its natural frequency. After some time it oscillates with a large, constant amplitude. Which statement about each complete cycle is correct? The driver transfers no energy to the system, because the amplitude is constant. The energy transferred by the driver is greater than the energy transferred to the surroundings. The energy transferred by the driver is equal to the maximum kinetic energy of the mass. The energy transferred by the driver is equal to the energy transferred to the surroundings by damping.
items.ms: At a constant amplitude the energy of the oscillating system is constant, so the energy supplied by the driver in each cycle equals the energy dissipated by damping. A: energy is still supplied, to replace what damping removes. B would make the amplitude keep increasing. C confuses the energy stored in the oscillator with the energy transferred each cycle.
items.why: Jun2023 Q19(b)(ii) asked about energy flow at resonance and the ER says few answered well; a steady-state energy-balance MCQ tests the same misconception.

items.question: The diagram shows a demonstration called Barton's pendulums. A horizontal string is tied between two fixed supports. Pendulum D has a heavy bob. Pendulums P, Q, R and S are light paper cones. R has the same length as D; P, Q and S have different lengths. D has a length of 0.60 m. Calculate the frequency of oscillation of D. D is pulled to one side and released. Explain the motion of the light pendulums P, Q, R and S a short time later. Each light pendulum is fitted with a large card disc, which greatly increases the air resistance on it. D is released again as before. Explain how the motion of R differs from its motion in (b).
items.ms: Use of T = 2π√(l/g) f = 0.64 Hz IC1 D oscillates and exerts a periodic force on the string, which passes it to each light pendulum IC2 So P, Q, R and S undergo forced oscillations IC3 They all oscillate at the frequency of D (the driving frequency), not at their own natural frequencies IC4 R has the same length as D, so the natural frequency of R equals the driving frequency IC5 R resonates: there is maximum transfer of energy from D to R, so R has the largest amplitude IC6 The natural frequencies of P, Q and S are different from the driving frequency, so their amplitudes are small (the closer the length to that of D, the larger the amplitude) The amplitude of R is smaller because more energy is transferred to the surroundings in each cycle (more work is done against air resistance / the damping is greater) R still has the largest amplitude (it still resonates) because its natural frequency depends only on its length The amplitude of R is now closer to the amplitudes of the other pendulums (the resonance is less sharp)
items.why: Resonance has come up in 14 of 18 sessions, often as a 6-mark answer (Jan2025 Q15, Jun2022 Q14) where the ER wants both the driving and the driven system named; Barton's pendulums, the standard demonstration, has not been used.

items.question: A student carries out an experiment to determine the value of an unknown mass M. She hangs a spring from a vibration generator, which is connected to a signal generator, and adds known masses m to the bottom of the spring, as shown. For each mass she finds the resonant frequency f of the mass–spring system. Describe how the student should find the resonant frequency for one mass. Explain why a graph of 1/f² against m should be a straight line through the origin. The table shows her results. Complete the table and plot a graph of 1/f² against m on the grid. For the unknown mass M, the resonant frequency was 1.65 Hz. Use your graph to determine M. Use your graph to determine the stiffness k of the spring.
items.ms: Increase the frequency of the signal generator slowly (from a low value) Observe the amplitude of oscillation of the masses using the metre rule (or a fixed pointer) The resonant frequency is the frequency at which the amplitude is a maximum Make smaller changes in frequency near the maximum / approach it from higher and from lower frequencies and take the mean f = 1/T and T = 2π√(m/k), so 1/f² = T² = (4π²/k)m Compared with y = mx: 4π²/k is a constant (the gradient) and there is no intercept 1/f² values correct to 3 s.f. (0.156, 0.240, 0.316, 0.396, 0.469, 0.557) Axes labelled with quantity and unit, and sensible scales (points cover more than half the grid) All points plotted accurately (to within half a small square) Best-fit straight line drawn 1/f² = 0.367 s² M read from the graph = 0.23 kg Gradient determined from a large triangle (about 1.58 s² kg⁻¹) k = 4π²/gradient = 25 N m⁻¹

items.name: Conservation of energy in damped and undamped oscillations
path: Unit 5 Thermodynamics, Radiation, Oscillations and Cosmology
Oscillations
S150 - how to apply conservation of energy to damped
items.question: A mass attached to a horizontal spring oscillates with simple harmonic motion of amplitude A on a frictionless surface. At which displacement from the equilibrium position is the kinetic energy of the mass equal to the elastic potential energy stored in the spring? A/2 A/√2 √3A/2 A
items.ms: The total energy ½kA² is constant. When Ek = Ep, Ep is half the total: ½kx² = ¼kA², so x = A/√2. A assumes the potential energy is proportional to x. C is where the kinetic energy is a quarter of the total (the speed is half its maximum). D is the amplitude, where the kinetic energy is zero.
items.why: Jun2026 Q4–Q5 and Jan2021 Q5 tested energy against amplitude and displacement; the point where E_{k} = E_{p} has not been asked.

path: Unit 5 Thermodynamics, Radiation, Oscillations and Cosmology

S150 - how to apply conservation of energy to damped
items.question: A glider of mass 0.20 kg on a horizontal air track is attached to one end of a spring. The other end of the spring is fixed. The glider oscillates with simple harmonic motion of amplitude 5.0 cm, and frictional forces are negligible. The graph shows how the elastic potential energy Ep stored in the spring varies with the displacement x of the glider from its equilibrium position. Add a line to the graph to show how the total energy of the oscillating system varies with displacement. Determine the speed of the glider when its displacement is 2.0 cm. The air supply to the track is switched off, so that friction acts on the glider. After six oscillations the amplitude has fallen to 4.0 cm. Calculate the percentage of the original energy of the system that has been transferred to the surroundings. Explain why the amplitude decreases when friction acts on the glider.
items.ms: Horizontal line at 20 mJ from x = −5.0 cm to x = +5.0 cm Ep at 2.0 cm read from the graph (3.2 mJ) Ek = 20 mJ − 3.2 mJ = 16.8 mJ v = 0.41 m s⁻¹ Energy at amplitude 4.0 cm = 12.8 mJ (from the graph, or ½kA²) Energy transferred = 20 mJ − 12.8 mJ = 7.2 mJ Percentage = 36% Work is done against friction (the resistive force) so energy is transferred from the oscillating system to the thermal energy store of the surroundings; the total energy (½kA²) decreases, so the amplitude decreases
items.why: Jan2023 Q14 asked for a total-energy line and a speed from an energy–displacement graph; the fraction of energy lost when the amplitude falls (E ∝ A²) has not been asked.

items.name: Free and forced oscillations
path: Unit 5 Thermodynamics, Radiation, Oscillations and Cosmology
Oscillations
S151 - the distinction between free and forced oscil
items.question: A tuning fork is struck and then held in the air. Its prongs vibrate at 256 Hz. The stem of the vibrating fork is then pressed onto a wooden table top, which also vibrates at 256 Hz. Explain why the vibration of the prongs is a free oscillation but the vibration of the table top is a forced oscillation.
items.ms: Prongs: after a single disturbance (being struck) they oscillate at their natural frequency, with no periodic external force acting Table top: a periodic (driving) force from the fork makes it oscillate at the fork's frequency, which is not (necessarily) its own natural frequency
items.why: Free and forced oscillations have been tested in only 3 of 18 sessions (MCQs May2024 Q4 and Oct2025 Q5; Jan2022 Q17(a) for a loudspeaker); the Jun2022 Q14 ER found the two confused, so a short written distinction is likely.

items.name: Amplitude near the natural frequency; effect of damping
path: Unit 5 Thermodynamics, Radiation, Oscillations and Cosmology
Oscillations
S152 - how the amplitude of a forced oscillation cha
items.question: A system is made to oscillate by a periodic driving force of constant size. A graph of the amplitude of oscillation against driving frequency has a sharp peak. The damping of the system is then increased. Which statement describes the new peak? It is lower and broader, and is at a slightly lower frequency. It is lower and narrower, and is at the same frequency. It is higher and narrower, and is at a slightly higher frequency. It is the same height, but is broader and at a lower frequency.
items.ms: More damping transfers more energy to the surroundings at every frequency, so the amplitude is smaller, most of all near the natural frequency: the peak becomes lower and flatter (broader) and moves to a slightly lower frequency. B: the peak broadens, it does not narrow. C describes a decrease in damping. D: the height of the peak falls as the damping increases.
items.why: Oct2022 Q10 asked how lighter damping changes the resonance peak; the digest notes that the amplitude–frequency curve itself has not been examined, so a matching MCQ is likely.

items.question: Engineers test a model of a tall building by fixing it to a shaking table. The table oscillates horizontally with a constant amplitude of 2.0 mm at a driving frequency that can be varied. The graph shows how the amplitude of oscillation of the top of the model varies with the driving frequency. State the natural frequency of the model. Explain why the amplitude is a maximum at this frequency. The engineers then fit dampers to the model. Sketch a curve on the graph to show how the amplitude of the top of the model now varies with the driving frequency.

items.name: Damping and plastic deformation of ductile materials
path: Unit 5 Thermodynamics, Radiation, Oscillations and Cosmology
Oscillations
S153 - how damping and the plastic deformation of du
items.question: Some buildings in earthquake zones contain steel braces that are designed to deform plastically when the building sways. Which statement explains how this reduces the amplitude of the building's oscillations? The braces store elastic strain energy and return it to the building in each cycle. The braces make the building stiffer, so its natural frequency increases. Work is done in permanently deforming the braces, so energy is transferred away from the oscillating building. The braces exert a force on the building that is always in the same direction as its velocity.
items.ms: Plastic deformation is permanent: the work done deforming the ductile steel is not returned to the building, so energy is removed from the oscillation and the amplitude falls. A describes elastic deformation, which returns the energy. B: plastic deformation does not stiffen the frame, and a change of natural frequency removes no energy. D: a force in the direction of the velocity would do work on the building and increase its energy.
items.why: S153 MCQs appeared in Jan2026 Q2, Jan2025 Q2 and Oct2024 Q2 (ductile materials in earthquake zones); the energy-transfer reason is the core idea behind all of them.

items.question: A pendulum swings in air and its oscillations are lightly damped. Which quantity stays approximately constant as the oscillations die away? amplitude maximum speed period total energy

items.why: The damped pendulum (Jan2025 Q8) was one of the hardest MCQs in its paper; that light damping leaves the period unchanged has not been tested directly.

items.question: Buildings in earthquake zones are designed so that the amplitude of their oscillations stays small. One design uses diagonal steel braces in the frame of the building. The steel is ductile, and the braces are designed to deform plastically when the building sways by a large amount. State what is meant by a ductile material. Explain how the plastic deformation of the braces reduces the amplitude of the oscillations of the building. Another design rests the whole building on flexible bearings. A building of mass 2.4 × 10⁶ kg rests on bearings with a total horizontal stiffness of 2.6 × 10⁷ N m⁻¹. Most of the energy of earthquake ground vibrations is at frequencies between 2 Hz and 10 Hz. items.question: The radiation from star X has a peak wavelength of 950 nm. Which statement about X is correct? Of the visible light that X emits, the greatest intensity is at the red end of the visible spectrum. X emits no visible light because its peak wavelength is in the infrared. X has a higher surface temperature than a star with a peak wavelength of 500 nm. The surface temperature of X is about 3000 K, so X must be a red giant.
items.ms: The intensity rises towards the peak at 950 nm, so within the visible range (400–700 nm) it is greatest at the red end. items.question: Astronomers measure the position of a nearby star against the background of distant stars, and measure it again six months later. Why are the two measurements made six months apart? So that the nearby star has moved half-way round its orbit. So that the Earth is at opposite ends of a diameter of its orbit around the Sun. So that the distant stars have moved relative to the Earth. So that the light from the star has travelled a measurable distance.
items.ms: In six months the Earth moves to the opposite side of its orbit, giving the largest possible baseline (the diameter of the orbit), so the nearby star's apparent shift is as large as possible. A: the shift is caused by the Earth's motion, not the star's. C: the distant stars are the fixed background. D: the time for light to travel plays no part in the method.
items.why: Parallax MCQs come up often (Oct2023 Q2, Jan2024 Q2, May2024 Q2, Jan2025 Q5, Jan2026 Q4); the Oct2021 report notes that the role of the Earth's orbit is often only implied.

items.question: Astronomers use trigonometric parallax to determine the distances to nearby stars. Describe how trigonometric parallax is used to determine the distance to a nearby star. You may include a labelled diagram in your answer. Proxima Centauri has a parallax angle of 3.72 × 10⁻⁶ rad, measured using the radius of the Earth's orbit, 1.50 × 10¹¹ m. Calculate the distance to Proxima Centauri. In 2020 the New Horizons spacecraft, far out in the Solar System, photographed Proxima Centauri at the same time as telescopes on the Earth. The diagram shows the positions of the Earth, New Horizons and Proxima Centauri at that time. Calculate the angle θ. Explain why observations from a spacecraft far from the Sun could be used to determine the distances to stars that are too far away for parallax measurements from the Earth.
items.ms: The position of the star is measured against the background of distant (fixed) stars The measurement is repeated 6 months later, when the Earth is at the opposite end of a diameter of its orbit The (change in) angle / parallax angle is determined The radius of the Earth's orbit (the Earth–Sun distance) must be known Trigonometry is used to calculate the distance: d = r/tan θ Use of tan θ = r/d (or d = r/θ for a small angle) d = 4.03 × 10¹⁶ m θ = 1.74 × 10⁻⁴ rad The separation of the two observing positions (the baseline) is much greater than the radius of the Earth's orbit, so the angle is much greater for a star at a given distance For distant stars the parallax angle from the Earth's orbit is too small to measure precisely; with the larger baseline the angle is large enough to measure
items.why: Describing parallax recurs (Oct2021 Q17, Jan2023 Q18, Oct2025 Q21) and so does its distance limit (Jan2022, Jun2025, Jun2026); a longer baseline from a spacecraft (New Horizons, 2020) is an untested angle on the same idea.

items.question: The H-R diagram shows the main sequence. P shows the position of a star with a mass similar to the Sun's while it is on the main sequence. Q and R show the positions of the same star at two later stages of its life. Explain how the star evolves from P to Q, and then from Q to R.
items.ms: IC1 At P the star is fusing hydrogen into helium in its core IC2 When the hydrogen in the core runs out, fusion in the core stops (so the outward pressure falls) IC3 The core contracts under gravity and its temperature increases IC4 The temperature rises enough for helium fusion to start (with hydrogen fusing in a shell around the core) IC5 The outer layers expand and cool, so at Q the star is a red giant: a larger surface area and a lower surface temperature, with a greater luminosity IC6 When fusion stops, the outer layers are lost and the core contracts to a white dwarf at R: small, hot and of low luminosity

items.question: A clothes steamer turns 200 g of water at 20 °C into steam at 100 °C. specific heat capacity of water = 4180 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ specific latent heat of vaporisation of water = 2.26 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹ What is the total energy needed? 6.7 × 10⁴ J 4.5 × 10⁵ J 5.2 × 10⁵ J 5.4 × 10⁵ J
items.ms: ΔE = mcΔθ + LΔm = 0.200 × 4180 × 80 + 0.200 × 2.26 × 10⁶ = 6.69 × 10⁴ + 4.52 × 10⁵ = 5.2 × 10⁵ J. A is the heating term only; B is the latent heat term only (forgetting one of the two energies); D uses Δθ = 100 K instead of 80 K.
items.why: S125 has come up in 17 of 18 sessions and 'heat then boil' is its commonest set-up; the Jun2023 and Jun2024 examiners' reports single out forgetting one of the two energy terms.

items.question: Two blocks, P and Q, have equal masses. Each block is heated from 20 °C. The graph shows how the temperature θ of each block varies with the energy supplied to it. What is (specific heat capacity of P) ÷ (specific heat capacity of Q)? 0.16 0.40 2.5 6.3
items.ms: For the same energy (20 kJ) and the same mass, c = ΔE/(mΔθ), so c ∝ 1/Δθ. Δθ for P = 40 K and Δθ for Q = 16 K, so c_P/c_Q = 16/40 = 0.40. C is the ratio the wrong way up (it compares the gradients, not the heat capacities); A and D square these ratios.
items.why: Jan2026 Q16 and Oct2025 Q16 needed values read from energy graphs; a graph of temperature against energy, whose gradient is 1/mc, has not been set as an MCQ.

items.question: In a ballistics laboratory, a lead pellet of mass 0.90 g travelling at 340 m s⁻¹ hits a steel plate and stops. 40% of its kinetic energy is transferred to the pellet as thermal energy. specific heat capacity of lead = 130 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ What is the rise in temperature of the pellet? 178 K 267 K 356 K 445 K
items.ms: 0.40 × ½mv² = mcΔθ, so the mass cancels: Δθ = 0.40 × ½ × 340² ÷ 130 = 178 K. B uses 60% (the energy that is not transferred to the pellet); C leaves out the ½ in ½mv²; D assumes that all of the kinetic energy heats the pellet.
items.why: The Jun2022 Q20(b)(i) mark scheme rewarded 'mass cancels, so Δθ is independent of the mass'; a kinetic-to-thermal energy MCQ in which the given mass is not needed has not been set.

items.question: A cook's hand is scalded by 2.5 g of steam at 100 °C, which condenses on the skin. The water formed then cools to skin temperature, 35 °C. specific heat capacity of water = 4180 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ specific latent heat of vaporisation of water = 2.26 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹ Calculate the total energy transferred to the skin. Compare your answer to (a) with the energy transferred to the skin by 2.5 g of water at 100 °C that cools to 35 °C. Hence explain why a scald from steam is much more severe than a scald from the same mass of boiling water.
items.ms: Use of ΔE = LΔm (5650 J) Use of ΔE = mcΔθ with Δθ = 65 K (679 J) ΔE = 6.3 × 10³ J Water at 100 °C transfers only 679 J (mcΔθ), about one ninth of the energy from the steam Steam also transfers its latent heat to the skin as it condenses, so much more energy is transferred

items.question: During a marathon, a runner of mass 64 kg produces thermal energy in her body at a rate of 1100 W. average specific heat capacity of the human body = 3500 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ Calculate the increase in her body temperature in 10 minutes if none of this energy were transferred away from her body. Explain, in terms of the molecules, why the evaporation of sweat cools her skin.
items.ms: Use of ΔE = Pt with t = 600 s (ΔE = 6.6 × 10⁵ J) Use of ΔE = mcΔθ Δθ = 2.9 K Use of 75% of the power and t = 3.0 × 3600 s (ΔE = 8.9 × 10⁶ J) Use of ΔE = LΔm Δm = 3.7 kg The molecules in the sweat have a (random) range of kinetic energies / speeds The molecules with the most kinetic energy (the fastest) escape from the surface of the liquid So the mean kinetic energy of the molecules that remain decreases The (absolute) temperature is proportional to the mean kinetic energy of the molecules, so the temperature of the sweat falls (and energy is transferred from the skin to the sweat)

items.question: Some homes store thermal energy in a 'thermal battery' that contains a wax which melts at 58 °C. A student investigates a sample of the wax. She places 0.250 kg of solid wax in an insulated container with an electric heater. The heater transfers energy to the wax at a constant rate of 30.0 W. The graph shows how the temperature θ of the wax varies with time t. Determine the specific heat capacity of the solid wax. Show that the specific latent heat of fusion of the wax is about 2.0 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹. A thermal battery in a home contains 180 kg of this wax. When the battery is fully charged, the wax is liquid at 75 °C. The manufacturer claims that, as the wax cools to 35 °C, the battery can supply heat to the home at an average rate of 1.5 kW for 12 hours. specific heat capacity of liquid wax = 2400 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ Assume that all the energy released by the wax is transferred to the home. Deduce whether the manufacturer's claim is correct. The student's container was not perfectly insulated. Explain how this affects the value of the specific latent heat found in (b), and suggest one change to the experiment that would reduce this effect.
items.ms: Use of ΔE = Pt with t = 720 s (ΔE = 2.16 × 10⁴ J) Use of ΔE = mcΔθ with Δθ = 40 K c = 2160 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ Time for melting read from the graph: 2400 s − 720 s = 1680 s Use of ΔE = LΔm with ΔE = Pt L = 2.02 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹ Use of ΔE = mcΔθ for the liquid cooling from 75 °C to 58 °C (7.3 × 10⁶ J) Use of ΔE = LΔm for the wax solidifying (3.6 × 10⁷ J) Use of ΔE = mcΔθ for the solid cooling from 58 °C to 35 °C (8.9 × 10⁶ J) Total energy = 5.3 × 10⁷ J and use of P = ΔE/t, giving t = 3.5 × 10⁴ s (9.7 h) [or energy needed for the claim = 6.5 × 10⁷ J] Comparison and conclusion: 9.7 h < 12 h (or 5.3 × 10⁷ J < 6.5 × 10⁷ J), so the claim is not correct Some of the energy supplied by the heater is transferred to the surroundings / not all of the energy Pt is used to melt the wax So the energy used in the calculation is greater than the energy that melted the wax, and the value of L is too large Add more insulation / a lid to the container, or use a more powerful heater so that the wax melts in a shorter time
items.why: S125 has come up in 17 of 18 sessions, and Jan2026 Q16 and Oct2025 Q16 both evaluated a claim with values read from a graph; finding c and L from a heating curve, and phase-change heat stores, have not been set.

items.name: Core Practical 12: calibrate a thermistor in a potential divider as a thermostat
path: Unit 5 Thermodynamics, Radiation, Oscillations and Cosmology
Thermodynamics
S126 - CORE PRACTICAL 12 Calibrate a thermistor in a
items.question: A thermostat uses an NTC thermistor in series with a fixed resistor R and a 6.0 V supply. A control unit switches a heater off when the p.d. across R rises to 2.4 V. The heater switches off at a lower temperature than is needed. Which change would make the heater switch off at a higher temperature? Replace R with a resistor of smaller resistance. Replace R with a resistor of greater resistance. Increase the e.m.f. of the supply. Connect the control unit across the thermistor instead of across R.
items.ms: The heater switches off when the p.d. across R is 2.4 V, i.e. when the thermistor resistance has fallen to R × (6.0 − 2.4)/2.4 = 1.5R. The thermistor's resistance falls as its temperature rises, so with a smaller R this resistance is reached at a higher temperature. B does the opposite. C: a larger e.m.f. makes the p.d. across R reach 2.4 V while the thermistor resistance is still larger, so at a lower temperature. D: the p.d. across the thermistor rises as the temperature falls, so the heater would switch off as the water cooled.
items.why: No WPH15 question has yet asked about the potential-divider (thermostat) part of Core Practical 12 (a coverage gap in the digest), so it is the likeliest surprise for this practical.

items.question: A student calibrates a thermistor in a potential divider circuit, so that it can be used as the temperature sensor of a thermostat for a sous-vide cooker (a water bath for slow cooking). The circuit is shown. The thermistor is placed in a beaker of water with a thermometer. The water is heated from 0 °C to 100 °C, and the student records the voltmeter reading Vout at different temperatures θ. Explain why Vout increases as the temperature of the water increases. State two precautions the student should take so that each reading of Vout corresponds to the temperature recorded. The graph shows the student's calibration curve. The thermistor is placed in the cooker and Vout is 2.0 V. Use the graph to determine the temperature of the water in the cooker. Explain why this circuit is more suitable for a thermostat that controls the water at 60 °C than for one that controls water at 10 °C.
items.ms: The resistance of the (NTC) thermistor decreases as its temperature increases So the total resistance decreases and the current increases / the fixed resistor's share of the 5.0 V increases So the p.d. across the 2.2 kΩ resistor (V = IR) increases Stir the water (so that its temperature is uniform) Wait until the readings are steady / heat the water slowly / remove the heat source before taking a reading Place the thermometer bulb close to the thermistor Read the thermometer and the voltmeter at the same time θ = 52 °C (accept 51 °C to 53 °C) The gradient of the graph (the change in Vout per °C) is greater at 60 °C than at 10 °C So a small change in temperature near 60 °C gives a larger change in Vout, so the thermostat responds to smaller changes in temperature (it is more sensitive)
items.why: Core Practical 12 was set as a 6-mark method in Oct2023 and Oct2024, but the potential divider, the calibration curve and its sensitivity have never been asked (digest coverage gap).

items.question: A student determines the specific latent heat of vaporisation of water. She uses an electric heater of known power to boil water in a beaker, and measures the mass of water boiled away in a measured time. Her value is greater than the accepted value. Which of the following could explain this? The heater was switched on for longer than the time she recorded. Some water splashed out of the beaker while it boiled. The balance read 2.0 g too high for every reading. Energy was transferred from the beaker to the surroundings.
items.ms: L = Pt/Δm. D: some of the energy Pt is transferred to the surroundings, so less water boils away than the energy assumes, and L is too large. A: more energy was supplied than Pt, so L is too small. B: Δm is too large, so L is too small. C: a constant zero error cancels when the change in mass is found, so it has no effect.
items.why: Jan2022 Q2, Jan2026 Q10 and Jun2026 Q9 all asked which error makes a measured latent heat too low; the reverse, a value that is too high, has not been asked.

items.name: Internal energy: random distribution of potential and kinetic energy
path: Unit 5 Thermodynamics, Radiation, Oscillations and Cosmology
Thermodynamics
S128 - the concept of internal energy as the random
items.question: Which statement about internal energy is correct? The internal energy of a block of ice increases when the block is lifted onto a higher shelf. The internal energy of ice increases as it melts at 0 °C, although its temperature does not change. Most of the internal energy of an ideal gas is the potential energy of its molecules. Two objects at the same temperature must have the same internal energy.
items.ms: Internal energy is the sum of the randomly distributed kinetic and potential energies of the molecules. B: when ice melts the potential energy of the molecules increases while their mean kinetic energy is unchanged. A: the gravitational potential energy of the whole block is not internal energy. C: there are no forces between the molecules of an ideal gas, so it has no molecular potential energy. D: internal energy also depends on the number of molecules and on the state of the object.
items.why: Jan2024 Q1 and Oct2020 Q8 asked about molecular energies during melting; the meaning of 'random distribution' (energy of the object as a whole is not internal energy) has not been tested.

items.name: Internal energy: random distribution of potential and kinetic energy
path: Unit 5 Thermodynamics, Radiation, Oscillations and Cosmology
Thermodynamics
S128 - the concept of internal energy as the random
items.question: Some crushed ice at −30 °C is heated at a constant rate until all of the water has boiled away. The graph shows how the temperature θ varies with time. Explain the shape of the graph in terms of the energies of the molecules. Your answer should include why section ST is longer than section QR.
items.ms: IC1 Internal energy is the sum of the (randomly distributed) kinetic and potential energies of the molecules IC2 In PQ and RS the energy supplied increases the mean kinetic energy of the molecules, so the temperature rises IC3 In QR and ST the temperature is constant, so the mean kinetic energy of the molecules is constant IC4 In QR and ST the energy supplied increases the potential energy of the molecules (bonds are broken / the molecules move further apart), so the internal energy still increases IC5 ST is longer because, at a constant rate of heating, more energy is needed to boil the water than to melt the same mass of ice (the specific latent heat of vaporisation is greater than that of fusion) IC6 On boiling the molecules are separated completely (all the bonds are broken), so the increase in potential energy is much greater than on melting, when the molecules stay close together
items.why: Jun2023 Q18 was a 6-mark question on the internal energy of cooling wax; a heating curve that also asks why boiling takes longer than melting has not been asked.

items.name: Absolute zero; mean KE and absolute temperature
path: Unit 5 Thermodynamics, Radiation, Oscillations and Cosmology
Thermodynamics
S129 - the concept of absolute zero and how the aver
items.question: A student investigates how the pressure p of a fixed mass of air varies with its temperature θ at constant volume. The air is in a sealed flask that is placed in a water bath. The graph shows her results. Draw a line of best fit and extend it to determine a value for absolute zero in °C. Explain why the pressure of the gas would be zero at absolute zero. The student removes some air from the flask so that it contains half as many molecules. She then repeats the experiment. Sketch, on the same axes, the line you would expect. Explain your answer.
items.ms: Straight line of best fit drawn through the points and extended to p = 0 Absolute zero in the range −260 °C to −290 °C At absolute zero the molecules would have no kinetic energy / would stop moving (the mean kinetic energy is proportional to the absolute temperature) So there would be no collisions with (no change of momentum at) the walls, so no force on the walls and the pressure (p = F/A) is zero Straight line that meets the θ axis at the same point (absolute zero) Line with half the gradient (half the pressure at each temperature) p = NkT/V, so at constant V and T the pressure is proportional to N
items.why: S129 has been asked in only 3 of 18 sessions and absolute zero has never been asked directly (digest coverage gap); extrapolating a pressure–temperature graph is the likeliest way to ask it.

items.name: Ideal gas equation pV = NkT
path: Unit 5 Thermodynamics, Radiation, Oscillations and Cosmology

S130 - use the equation pV  NkT for an ideal gas
items.question: A sealed food jar has an internal volume of 750 cm³. It contains air at a pressure of 1.01 × 10⁵ Pa and a temperature of 20 °C. How many gas molecules are in the jar? 1.9 × 10¹⁹ 1.9 × 10²² 2.7 × 10²³ 1.9 × 10²⁵
items.ms: N = pV/kT = (1.01 × 10⁵ × 7.50 × 10⁻⁴) ÷ (1.38 × 10⁻²³ × 293) = 1.9 × 10²². A uses the pressure in kPa; C uses the temperature in °C; D converts cm³ to m³ by multiplying by 10⁻³ instead of 10⁻⁶.
items.why: S130 has come up in 16 of 18 sessions and finding N from p, V and T recurs (Jun2021 Q11, Oct2021 Q14, Jan2025 Q19); unit conversion is the commonest slip.

items.name: Ideal gas equation pV = NkT
path: Unit 5 Thermodynamics, Radiation, Oscillations and Cosmology

items.question: A fixed mass of ideal gas is at a temperature of 27 °C. Its pressure is tripled and its volume is halved. What is the new temperature of the gas? −73 °C 41 °C 177 °C 1527 °C
items.ms: pV/T is constant, so T₂ = T₁ × (p₂V₂)/(p₁V₁) = 300 K × 3 × ½ = 450 K = 177 °C. A uses the ratio the wrong way up (200 K); B multiplies the Celsius temperature by 1.5; D multiplies by 3 and by 2 (1800 K).
items.why: The combined gas law with a kelvin conversion recurs (Jun2026 Q11, Jan2026 Q15, Oct2025 Q14), and the examiners' reports note candidates who leave the temperature in °C.

items.question: A cylinder of compressed nitrogen is stored outdoors. Over one week, the pressure in the cylinder falls from 8.0 MPa to 6.0 MPa and the temperature of the gas falls from 27 °C to 7 °C. The volume of the cylinder does not change. What percentage of the nitrogen molecules have leaked out of the cylinder? 20% 25% 30% 80%
items.ms: N = pV/kT, so N₂/N₁ = (p₂/p₁)(T₁/T₂) = (6.0/8.0)(300/280) = 0.80. So 20% have leaked out. B ignores the fall in temperature; C uses the temperature ratio the wrong way up (0.75 × 280/300 = 0.70); D is the percentage that remains.
items.why: Jan2021 Q14(b) and Jun2023 Q12(b) asked for the amount of gas lost from a container; combining a leak with a fall in temperature is the multi-step version that suits a late MCQ.

items.question: In a diesel engine, air is drawn into a cylinder and then compressed by a piston. The valves are closed during the compression. Fuel is then sprayed into the hot compressed air and ignites without a spark. At the start of the compression the air has a volume of 5.0 × 10⁻⁴ m³, a pressure of 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa and a temperature of 30 °C. Calculate the number of air molecules in the cylinder. items.name: Ideal gas equation pV = NkT
path: Unit 5 Thermodynamics, Radiation, Oscillations and Cosmology
Thermodynamics
S130 - use the equation pV  NkT for an ideal gas
items.question: A disposable tank of helium is sold for filling party balloons. The tank has an internal volume of 9.0 × 10⁻³ m³. When the tank is full, the helium in it is at a pressure of 1.80 × 10⁶ Pa and a temperature of 20 °C. Show that there are about 4.0 × 10²⁴ helium atoms in the full tank. Each balloon is filled until it is a sphere of diameter 23 cm. The helium in a filled balloon is at a pressure of 1.03 × 10⁵ Pa and a temperature of 20 °C. Helium flows from the tank into a balloon only while the pressure in the tank is greater than the pressure in the balloon. Assume that the temperature of the helium in the tank stays at 20 °C. Calculate the maximum number of balloons that can be filled from the tank. The tank carries the warning: 'Do not store above 50 °C.' Explain, in terms of the helium atoms, why the pressure in the tank increases when its temperature increases.
items.ms: T = 293 K Use of pV = NkT N = 4.01 × 10²⁴ Volume of one balloon V = 4/3 πr³ = 6.37 × 10⁻³ m³ Use of pV = NkT to find the number of atoms in one balloon (1.62 × 10²³) Atoms left in the tank at 1.03 × 10⁵ Pa (2.29 × 10²³) subtracted from the total 23 balloons IC1 The atoms move randomly and collide with the walls of the tank IC2 In each collision the momentum of an atom changes, so the wall exerts a force on the atom and the atom exerts an equal and opposite force on the wall IC3 When the temperature increases, the mean kinetic energy of the atoms increases (½m<c²> = (3/2)kT), so the atoms move faster on average IC4 So the change in momentum in each collision with the wall increases IC5 And the atoms hit the walls more often (the rate of collisions with the walls increases) IC6 So the rate of change of momentum, and so the force on the walls, increases; the area is constant, so the pressure (p = F/A) increases
items.why: S130 has come up in 16 of 18 sessions; how many balloons a cylinder can fill (with gas left in the tank) has not been asked, and the molecular explanation of pressure rising with temperature was the 6-mark question in Oct2020, Jan2023, Oct2025 and Jan2026.

items.name: Derive and use (1/2)m<c^2> = (3/2)kT
path: Unit 5 Thermodynamics, Radiation, Oscillations and Cosmology

items.question: A container holds a mixture of two ideal gases, X and Y, at the same temperature. A molecule of X has 4 times the mass of a molecule of Y. Which row of the table is correct? ¼ and ½ 1 and ¼ 1 and ½ 1 and 2
items.ms: Mean kinetic energy ½m<c²> = (3/2)kT depends only on temperature, so the ratio of mean kinetic energies is 1. A wrongly makes the kinetic energy depend on mass; B forgets the square root; D has the speed ratio the wrong way up.

items.question: The graph shows how the gravitational potential V due to Venus varies with distance r from the centre of Venus. The graph starts at the surface of Venus. items.question: Mercury is the closest planet to the Sun. It has almost no atmosphere. mass of Mercury = 3.30 × 10²³ kg radius of Mercury = 2.44 × 10⁶ m Show that the minimum speed v that an object at the surface of Mercury needs to escape from Mercury's gravitational field is given by v = √(2GM/R) where M and R are the mass and the radius of Mercury. Calculate the escape velocity from the surface of Mercury. The surface of Mercury facing the Sun reaches a temperature of about 700 K. Calculate the root-mean-square speed of nitrogen molecules at this temperature. mass of a nitrogen molecule = 4.65 × 10⁻²⁶ kg The r.m.s. speed of nitrogen molecules on Mercury is much less than the escape velocity. However, Mercury could not have kept an atmosphere of nitrogen over billions of years. Explain why.
items.ms: Kinetic energy at the surface = gain in gravitational potential energy to reach infinity: ½mv² = GMm/R Rearranging (m cancels) to give v = √(2GM/R) Use of v = √(2GM/R) v = 4.25 × 10³ m s⁻¹ Use of ½m⟨c²⟩ = (3/2)kT √⟨c²⟩ = 789 m s⁻¹ IC1 The molecules have a (wide) range/distribution of speeds; the r.m.s. speed is only a typical value IC2 A small fraction of the molecules have speeds several times the r.m.s. speed, greater than the escape velocity IC3 These molecules, if near the top of the atmosphere and moving away from Mercury, escape from the gravitational field and do not return IC4 Collisions between the remaining molecules continually give some molecules speeds above the escape velocity / the speed distribution is restored IC5 Radiation from the Sun keeps the gas at a high temperature, so the mean kinetic energy of the molecules (∝ T) stays high and the loss continues IC6 Over billions of years almost all the nitrogen escapes; Mercury's escape velocity is low because its mass is small (compared with the Earth's)
items.why: Escape velocity from ½mv² = GMm/R recurs (Jan2023 Q12, Oct2025 Q13), and molecules escaping despite a low mean speed has appeared as a short part twice (Jan2023, Jan2026); a 6-mark extended answer on it would be new.
