items.question: The Hubble Space Telescope has a mass of 1.11 × 10⁴ kg. It moves in a circular orbit 540 km above the Earth's surface. mass of Earth = 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg radius of Earth = 6.37 × 10⁶ m Show that the orbital speed v of a satellite in a circular orbit of radius r around the Earth is given by v = √(GM/r) where M is the mass of the Earth. Calculate the orbital speed of the telescope. The very thin upper atmosphere exerts a small drag force on the telescope, so the radius of its orbit slowly decreases. A student states: 'The drag force acts against the motion of the telescope, so the telescope must be slowing down.' Assess the validity of the student's statement. You should consider the energy of the telescope in your answer.
items.ms: Equates GMm/r² to mv²/r Algebra (m cancels) leading to v = √(GM/r) Use of v = √(GM/r) with r = 6.37 × 10⁶ m + 5.40 × 10⁵ m v = 7.59 × 10³ m s⁻¹ From v = √(GM/r), as r decreases v increases, so the statement is not valid As r decreases the gravitational potential energy (−GMm/r) decreases / becomes more negative Ek = ½mv² = GMm/2r, so the gain in kinetic energy is half the loss of gravitational potential energy The other half of the lost gravitational potential energy is the work done against the drag force (transferred to thermal energy) The gravitational force has a component along the motion as the telescope spirals inwards, and does more work on it than the drag removes, so its speed increases
items.why: S160 carries 5.8% of the unit's marks; v = √(GM/r) was derived in Jan2026, and atmospheric drag has been asked only as heating (Jan2021 Q17), never the speed increase that follows.

items.name: Orbits: gravity provides the centripetal force
path: Unit 5 Thermodynamics, Radiation, Oscillations and Cosmology
Astrophysics and Cosmology
S160 - apply Newtons laws of motion and universal gr
items.question: Astronomers can detect a planet orbiting a distant star by observing the star's spectrum. The gravitational pull of the planet makes the star move in a small circular orbit with the same period as the planet. Assume that the Earth lies in the plane of these orbits. The graph shows how the change in wavelength Δλ of a line in the star's spectrum varies with time t. The wavelength of this line measured in a laboratory is 589.0 nm. Explain why the observed wavelength of the line varies as shown. Use the graph to determine the orbital period of the planet, in seconds. The mass of the star is 2.10 × 10³⁰ kg. The mass of the planet is very much smaller than this, so the planet can be assumed to orbit the centre of the star. Show that the radius of the planet's orbit is about 8 × 10⁹ m. Use the graph to calculate the maximum speed of the star along the line of sight from the Earth. The gravitational forces on the star and on the planet are equal in magnitude, and they orbit with the same period. It follows that (mass of star × orbital speed of star) = (mass of planet × orbital speed of planet) The orbital speed of the star is the speed calculated in (d). Calculate the mass of the planet. In practice, the plane of the orbits may be tilted relative to the line of sight from the Earth. Explain why the mass calculated in (e) would then be less than the actual mass of the planet.
items.ms: Doppler effect: the observed wavelength changes because the source (the star) moves relative to the Earth As the star orbits it moves alternately away from the Earth (wavelength increases) and towards the Earth (wavelength decreases) The component of the star's velocity along the line of sight varies, so Δλ varies regularly with the orbital period (greatest when the star moves directly towards or away from the Earth) Period read from the graph, preferably over several cycles (4.23 days) T = 3.65 × 10⁵ s Use of F = GMm/r² with F = mω²r (or F = mv²/r) Use of ω = 2π/T (or v = 2πr/T) with T from (b) r = 7.80 × 10⁹ m Use of Δλ/λ = v/c with Δλ = 1.2 × 10⁻¹³ m v = 61 m s⁻¹ Use of v = 2πr/T for the planet Use of M vstar = m vplanet m = 9.6 × 10²⁶ kg The Doppler shift gives only the component of the star's velocity along the line of sight So the star's actual orbital speed is greater than the value from (d), and the planet's mass (∝ speed of star) is greater than calculated
items.why: Orbit calculations are in almost every paper; combining T² = 4π²r³/GM with the Doppler shift of a star's spectrum, the way most planets around other stars are found, has never been asked.

path: Unit 5 Thermodynamics, Radiation, Oscillations and Cosmology
Astrophysics and Cosmology
S169 - how the movement of a source of waves relativ
items.question: A police car moves at constant velocity directly towards a pedestrian who is standing still. The siren on the car emits sound of constant frequency. Which of the following describes the sound received by the pedestrian, compared with the sound received when the car is at rest? wavelength shorter, frequency higher, speed higher wavelength shorter, frequency higher, speed unchanged wavelength unchanged, frequency higher, speed higher wavelength longer, frequency lower, speed unchanged
items.ms: Each wavefront is emitted from a point closer to the pedestrian than the one before, so the wavefronts are closer together and the wavelength received is shorter. The speed of sound depends only on the air, so it is unchanged, and f = v/λ is therefore higher. A and C wrongly add the car's speed to the speed of sound; D describes a source moving away from the pedestrian.
items.why: S169 has been asked in 6 of 18 sessions, always with light from stars; the spec says 'a source of waves', and the Doppler effect for a moving sound source has never been asked.

items.question: Many stars are in binary systems, in which two stars orbit their common centre of mass. Astronomers study the spectrum of star A in a binary system. Star A moves in a circular orbit at constant speed, and the Earth lies in the plane of the orbit. The graph shows how the wavelength λ of one line in the spectrum of star A, received at the Earth, varies with time t. The wavelength of this line measured in a laboratory is 656.28 nm. Explain why the received wavelength varies with time. Calculate the orbital speed of star A. Deduce whether the binary system as a whole is moving towards or away from the Earth.
items.ms: As star A orbits, the component of its velocity towards or away from the Earth changes (Doppler effect) When star A moves away from the Earth the received wavelength is longer (red shift); when it moves towards the Earth the received wavelength is shorter (blue shift) The shift is greatest when star A moves directly towards or directly away from the Earth Δλ = (656.42 − 656.18) nm ÷ 2 = 0.12 nm Use of Δλ/λ = v/c v = 5.49 × 10⁴ m s⁻¹ The mean of the maximum and minimum wavelengths is 656.30 nm, which is greater than 656.28 nm So the system (its centre of mass) is moving away from the Earth / the system is red-shifted
items.why: Written S169 questions explain a varying shift from an orbiting or rotating source (Oct2020 Q12(a), Oct2021 Q16(b), Oct2024 Q17(a)) and the half-range trap is the factor of 2 missed in Jan2025 Q18(b); S169 has not appeared since Oct2024.

items.question: Light from a distant galaxy is red-shifted. The wavelengths of several lines in the galaxy's spectrum are compared with the wavelengths of the same lines measured in a laboratory. Which quantity has the same value for every line? the fractional change in wavelength, Δλ/λ the change in wavelength, Δλ the change in frequency, Δf the change in photon energy, ΔE
items.ms: z = Δλ/λ ≈ v/c depends only on the galaxy's speed, so it is the same for every line. Δλ = zλ is larger for lines of longer wavelength (B); Δf = zf is larger for lines of higher frequency (C); ΔE = hΔf varies in the same way as Δf (D).
items.why: S170 has come up in all 18 sessions; MCQs on what a red-shifted spectrum shows recur (Jan2022 Q9, Oct2023 Q5), but the fact that Δλ/λ is the same for every line has not been asked.

items.question: A line in the hydrogen spectrum has a frequency of 6.17 × 10¹⁴ Hz when measured in a laboratory. A galaxy is moving away from the Earth at 1.8 × 10⁴ km s⁻¹. What is the frequency of this line in the light received from the galaxy? 3.70 × 10¹³ Hz 5.80 × 10¹⁴ Hz 6.17 × 10¹⁴ Hz 6.54 × 10¹⁴ Hz
items.ms: z = v/c = 1.8 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹ / 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ = 0.060, so Δf = 0.060 × 6.17 × 10¹⁴ Hz = 3.70 × 10¹³ Hz, and the frequency falls for a receding source: f = 5.80 × 10¹⁴ Hz. A is the shift Δf only; C comes from using 1.8 × 10⁴ m s⁻¹ (km not converted to m), which gives a shift too small to change the value to 3 s.f.; D adds the shift, as for a source moving towards the Earth.
items.why: Shift-and-speed calculations appear in almost every session (Jun2025 Q5 asked for an observed wavelength); the frequency version with a km s⁻¹ trap follows Oct2025 Q12 and Jan2024 Q13, which used frequencies.

items.question: Quasars are extremely luminous objects at very great distances from the Earth. The Lyman-alpha line in the spectrum of hydrogen has a wavelength of 121.6 nm when measured in a laboratory. In the spectrum of a quasar this line is received with a wavelength of 571.5 nm. Show that the redshift z of the quasar is about 3.7. A student uses z = v/c to calculate the speed of the quasar. Deduce whether the student's method is valid for this quasar.
items.ms: Δλ = 571.5 nm − 121.6 nm = 449.9 nm z = Δλ/λ = 449.9 / 121.6 = 3.70 v = zc = 3.70 × 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ = 1.1 × 10⁹ m s⁻¹ This is greater than the speed of light, so the calculated value cannot be correct So the method is not valid: z ≈ v/c only applies when v is much less than c (z much less than 1)
items.why: Every S170 calculation in the past papers has had z of 0.1 or less (Jun2025 Q5 is the largest); whether z ≈ v/c still holds at large z has never been asked and is the likeliest surprise.

items.question: Astronomers measured the distances d of six galaxies using Type Ia supernovae as standard candles. They also measured the wavelength λ of a calcium absorption line in the spectrum of each galaxy. The wavelength of this line measured in a laboratory is 393.4 nm. The table shows their results and the recession velocity v calculated for five of the galaxies. Calculate the recession velocity v of galaxy D. Write your answer in the table. Plot a graph of v against d on the grid. Explain how the graph supports Hubble's law. Use your graph to determine a value for the Hubble constant H0 in km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹. Calculate a value for the age of the universe in years. 1 Mpc = 3.09 × 10²² m, 1 year = 3.15 × 10⁷ s
items.ms: Use of v = cΔλ/λ with Δλ = 15.2 nm and 393.4 nm in the denominator v = 1.16 × 10⁴ km s⁻¹ Axes labelled with quantities and units, with sensible scales (plotted points cover at least half the grid in each direction) All six points plotted correctly, to within ± half a small square Best-fit straight line drawn The graph is a straight line through the origin So v is (directly) proportional to d, as v = H0d predicts The points lie close to the line / the scatter is small All the lines are red-shifted (λ > 393.4 nm), so all the galaxies are moving away, the more distant ones faster Gradient calculated using a large triangle (at least half the length of the line) H0 = 70 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹ Conversion of H0 to s⁻¹, e.g. H0 = 70 × 10³ m s⁻¹ / 3.09 × 10²² m = 2.27 × 10⁻¹⁸ s⁻¹ Use of age = 1/H0 Age = 1.4 × 10¹⁰ years
items.why: S170 has come up in all 18 sessions; Hubble-law graphs (Oct2022 Q15, Oct2023 Q14(b)) and the H0-to-age chain (Jun2022 Q12, Jan2024 Q18(c)) recur, and plotting the data for the gradient is the natural long-question form not among the recent past questions.

path: Unit 5 Thermodynamics, Radiation, Oscillations and Cosmology
Astrophysics and Cosmology
S171 - the controversy over the age and ultimate fat
items.question: Astronomers estimate the mass of a cluster of galaxies in two ways: from the total electromagnetic radiation that the galaxies emit, and from the gravitational force needed to keep the galaxies moving as they do within the cluster. The second method gives a much larger mass. Which of the following is the best explanation? The light from the cluster is red-shifted, so the luminosity of the galaxies is underestimated. The galaxies are moving away from each other, as Hubble's law predicts. The cluster contains matter that does not emit electromagnetic radiation. The cluster contains many stars that emit mainly infrared radiation.
items.ms: Mass that shows up through its gravitational effect but not through the radiation emitted must be matter that emits no electromagnetic radiation: dark matter. A: a red shift changes wavelengths by a small fraction and cannot account for a much larger mass; B: Hubble's law describes the recession of distant galaxies, not the motion of galaxies held together in a cluster; D: infrared is electromagnetic radiation, so it is already included in the first method.
items.why: Dark-matter MCQs appear in Jan2021 Q2 and Jun2026 Q3 and S171 has come up in 14 of 18 sessions; the motion of galaxies in a cluster is a fresh context for the same evidence.

items.question: A new measurement gives a larger value for the Hubble constant H0. Which of the following describes the effect on the estimated age of the universe and on the distance calculated for a galaxy from its measured red shift? age greater, distance greater age greater, distance smaller age smaller, distance greater age smaller, distance smaller
items.ms: Age ≈ 1/H0, so a larger H0 gives a smaller age. For a measured red shift, v = zc is fixed and d = v/H0, so the distance is smaller too. A and B take the age to increase with H0; C takes d to increase with H0.
items.why: Jan2025 Q7, Jun2025 Q4 and Oct2025 Q4 all link H0 to the age of the universe; the effect of a revised H0 on calculated distances has not been asked.

items.question: The mean density of the universe is equal to the critical density. Which statement describes the future of the universe? It will expand for ever, and its rate of expansion will not fall towards zero. Its expansion will stop and then the universe will contract. Its rate of expansion will decrease towards zero, but it will never contract. It will expand to a maximum size and then stay at that size.
items.ms: At the critical density (a flat universe) gravity slows the expansion so that its rate tends to zero, but the expansion never reverses. A describes an open universe (density less than critical); B a closed universe (density greater than critical); D: the universe does not stop at a fixed size, because the expansion rate only approaches zero.
items.why: Fate-versus-density MCQs came up in Oct2024 Q7, Jan2026 Q3 and Jan2026 Q5; the flat (critical-density) case is the one not yet asked.

items.question: The graph shows three possible ways, P, Q and R, in which the size of the universe could change with time. The present time is marked 'now'. State which curve represents a universe with a mean density greater than the critical density. Give a reason for your answer. Use the graph to explain why the age of the universe depends on its mean density. Suggest how the spectra of distant galaxies observed while the universe is contracting would differ from those observed now.
items.ms: R The size reaches a maximum and then decreases: the gravitational attraction is large enough to stop the expansion and make the universe contract The curves have the same gradient now (the same present rate of expansion) but reach zero size at different times in the past The greater the density, the more gravity has slowed the expansion, so the expansion was faster in the past So a universe of greater density (R) took less time to reach its present size: it is younger The galaxies would be moving towards the observer (towards each other) So the spectral lines would be shifted to shorter wavelengths / higher frequencies: a blue shift instead of a red shift
items.why: Open, closed and flat universes are tested by MCQ (Jun2023 Q1, Oct2024 Q7, Jan2026 Q5) but never with a size–time graph; linking the fate to the age and to the Doppler shift has not been asked.

items.question: Astronomers use two different methods to measure the Hubble constant H0. The table shows their results. Calculate the difference between the ages of the universe given by the two values of H0. 1 Mpc = 3.09 × 10²² m, 1 year = 3.15 × 10⁷ s Explain why there is uncertainty about the age and the ultimate fate of the universe.
items.ms: Conversion of a value of H0 to s⁻¹, e.g. 73.0 × 10³ m s⁻¹ / 3.09 × 10²² m = 2.36 × 10⁻¹⁸ s⁻¹ Use of age = 1/H0 for both values Difference = 1.12 × 10⁹ years IC1 The age of the universe is estimated as 1/H0, so any uncertainty in H0 gives an uncertainty in the age IC2 H0 is found from the gradient of a graph of recession velocity against distance; the distances of remote galaxies are difficult to measure accurately, so H0 is uncertain (different methods give different values, as in the table) IC3 1/H0 assumes the universe has always expanded at the same rate; gravity may have changed the rate of expansion, so the true age is not exactly 1/H0 IC4 The ultimate fate depends on the mean density of the universe compared with the critical density IC5 If the mean density is greater than the critical density, gravity will stop the expansion and the universe will contract; if it is less, the universe will expand for ever IC6 Dark matter does not emit electromagnetic radiation and is detected only by its gravitational effect, so the amount of it, and hence the mean density of the universe, is uncertain
items.why: S171 has come up in 14 of 18 sessions but never as a 6-mark answer; the spec's wording ('the controversy over the age and ultimate fate of the universe') suits one, and the disagreement between measured values of H0 gives a fresh numerical lead-in.

items.question: The graph shows how the orbital speed v of stars in a spiral galaxy varies with their distance r from the centre of the galaxy. Curve X shows the measured speeds. Curve Y shows the speeds predicted from the mass of the stars and gas that can be observed. State what is meant by dark matter. A star in the galaxy moves in a circular orbit at a distance of 1.5 × 10²¹ m from the centre. Assume that the mass inside its orbit acts as if it were concentrated at the centre of the galaxy. Show that the mass inside the star's orbit is about 1 × 10⁴² kg. Determine the percentage of the mass inside the star's orbit that is dark matter. Explain why curve Y decreases at large values of r.
items.ms: Matter that has mass / exerts a gravitational force but does not emit (or absorb) electromagnetic radiation v = 2.2 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹ read from curve X Use of GMm/r² = mv²/r M = 1.09 × 10⁴² kg v = 1.1 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹ read from curve Y M ∝ v² at the same r, so observed mass = (1.1/2.2)² × M = 0.25M (= 2.7 × 10⁴¹ kg) Percentage that is dark matter = 75% Nearly all the observed mass is close to the centre, so the mass inside an orbit hardly increases as r increases v² = GM/r (from GMm/r² = mv²/r), so with M (nearly) constant v decreases as r increases
